questions.relatedConcept: Data alignment and memory addressing
questions.interviewTip: Candidates should understand that 'char' is the basic unit of measurement in C (1 byte), while pointer sizes are tied to hardware addressing capabilities.

questions.question: In the C standard, what is the effect of using the 'restrict' keyword on a pointer parameter within a function definition?
options: It forces the pointer to be stored in a read-only memory segment by the hardware.
It informs the compiler that the pointer address will not be modified by any other pointer within the function's scope.
It prevents the function from being called with NULL or uninitialized memory pointers.
It instructs the compiler to ignore aliasing optimizations for the duration of the function call.
questions.correctAnswer: It informs the compiler that the pointer address will not be modified by any other pointer within the function's scope.
questions.explanation: The 'restrict' keyword is a type qualifier that informs the compiler that for the lifetime of the pointer, only the pointer itself (or a value derived from it) will be used to access the object it points to. This allows the compiler to perform more aggressive optimizations like vectorization or register caching, assuming no other pointer aliases the same memory region.
questions.hint: Think about memory aliasing and how compilers optimize store operations.
questions.relatedConcept: Pointer Aliasing and Compiler Optimization
questions.codeSnippet: void merge(int * restrict dest, const int * restrict src, size_t n);
questions.interviewTip: Understanding 'restrict' demonstrates that a candidate cares about low-level performance tuning and how high-level code maps to machine instructions.

questions.question: In the C language, what is the result of the expression 'sizeof(char)' compared to 'sizeof(signed char)' and 'sizeof(unsigned char)' when targeting standard compliant compilers?
options: sizeof(char) is 1, but signed/unsigned variants may differ due to alignment requirements.
All three expressions evaluate to 1.
sizeof(char) is platform-dependent, while the others are fixed at 1.
The expressions are invalid because 'char' is not an integer type.
questions.correctAnswer: All three expressions evaluate to 1.
questions.explanation: According to the ISO C standard, 'char', 'signed char', and 'unsigned char' are guaranteed to have the same representation size, which is explicitly defined as 1 byte (where a byte is defined by CHAR_BIT, not necessarily 8 bits).
questions.hint: Recall the C standard definition of the byte and the relationship between char types.
questions.relatedConcept: Data representation and standard compliance
questions.interviewTip: Understanding the C standard's definition of a 'byte' is crucial for writing cross-platform, portable low-level code.

questions.question: In the C++ language, what is the observable behavior of using the 'alignas' specifier on an object that is smaller than its natural alignment requirement?
options: The object will occupy less memory than the original alignment requirement, potentially increasing CPU cycle cost for access.
The compiler issues a diagnostic error because 'alignas' cannot be used to reduce the alignment requirement of a type.
The object will be padded to 1 byte, ignoring the underlying 'double' requirements for compatibility.
The compiler ignores the 'alignas' specifier and maintains the 'double' type's default alignment.
questions.correctAnswer: The compiler issues a diagnostic error because 'alignas' cannot be used to reduce the alignment requirement of a type.
questions.explanation: According to the C++ standard, an alignment specifier cannot be used to decrease the alignment of a type to be less strict than the alignment of its members. Attempting to do so results in a compilation error.
questions.hint: Consider the relationship between struct member requirements and the aggregate's alignment constraints.
questions.relatedConcept: Memory Alignment and Type Constraints
questions.codeSnippet: struct alignas(1) Data { double x; };
questions.interviewTip: This tests depth of knowledge regarding how C++ handles low-level memory layouts and compiler enforcement of type safety.

questions.question: In C, what is the result of the variable `a` after executing the following code?
options: Undefined behavior
questions.correctAnswer: Undefined behavior
questions.explanation: The expression `a = a++ + ++a;` modifies `a` twice without an intervening sequence point, which the C standard classifies as undefined behavior. Therefore the program's result cannot be reliably predicted, making "Undefined behavior" the only correct answer. The numeric options assume a particular evaluation order, which the language does not guarantee.
questions.hint: Think about how many times `a` is modified between sequence points.
questions.relatedConcept: Sequence points and undefined behavior in C expressions
questions.codeSnippet:
int a = 5;
a = a++ + ++a;
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates understand that not all expression evaluations are well-defined in C, revealing depth of language knowledge.

title: IBM - Test 3: Technical Assessment
description: Test 3 for IBM. Every question is unique against the whole question database — no repeats, no renumbered or reworded variants of an existing question.

questions.question: In the context of the C++17 memory model, what is the observable behavior when multiple threads perform non-atomic concurrent writes to the same memory location, where at least one of these writes is not atomic?
options: The last writer wins, with the value being updated atomically due to CPU cache consistency.
Data race, resulting in undefined behavior regardless of the values written.
The compiler guarantees sequential consistency for primitive types, preventing race conditions.
The hardware will serialize the operations, ensuring the memory location eventually holds one of the written values.
questions.correctAnswer: Data race, resulting in undefined behavior regardless of the values written.
questions.explanation: According to the C++ memory model, a data race occurs when two or more threads access the same memory location concurrently, at least one of the accesses is a write, and no atomic operations are used. This is strictly undefined behavior (UB), not a platform-dependent race condition.
questions.hint: Focus on the formal definition of 'data race' in the C++ memory model standard.
questions.relatedConcept: Memory Model and Concurrency Semantics
questions.interviewTip: Senior candidates should recognize that concurrent non-atomic access is never safe, even if it 'works' on a specific x86 architecture.

questions.question: Which of the following scenarios best describes the side-effect behavior of a Python 'decorator' function executed at definition time?
options: The string 'Decorated' is printed every time 'task()' is invoked.
The string 'Decorated' is printed only if 'task' is imported into another module.
The string 'Decorated' is printed exactly once when the 'task' function is defined.
The code fails to compile because 'log' must be a class to act as a decorator.
questions.correctAnswer: The string 'Decorated' is printed exactly once when the 'task' function is defined.
questions.explanation: Decorators in Python are executed at the time the function is defined (when the module is loaded), not when the function is called. Therefore, the print statement inside the decorator executes during the definition phase.
questions.hint: Distinguish between function definition time and invocation time in the Python interpreter.
questions.relatedConcept: Decorator Execution Lifecycle
questions.interviewTip: Testing this demonstrates understanding of the Python interpreter's bytecode execution flow during module initialization.

questions.question: In the context of the C memory model and ISO C11 standard, what is the well-defined behavior of accessing an object through an lvalue of a type that is not a compatible type, specifically regarding the 'effective type' rule?
options: The compiler performs an implicit bitwise cast, resulting in a valid bit-representation of 2.0 in the int object.
The compiler is allowed to assume 'i' and 'd' do not overlap, potentially caching 'i' in a register prior to the store through 'd'.
The program executes correctly because 'double' and 'int' are both arithmetic types and thus compatible.
The operation results in undefined behavior due to a violation of the strict aliasing rule.
questions.correctAnswer: The operation results in undefined behavior due to a violation of the strict aliasing rule.
questions.explanation: According to the ISO C standard (C11 6.5/7), an object shall have its stored value accessed only by an lvalue expression that has a compatible type or certain other specific exceptions (like char*). Accessing an int via a double pointer violates strict aliasing, leading to undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Consider the strict aliasing rule and the requirements for accessing memory locations of different types.
questions.relatedConcept: Strict Aliasing Rule and Effective Types
questions.codeSnippet: int i = 10; double *d = (double *)&i; *d = 2.0;
questions.interviewTip: This tests if a candidate understands how compilers optimize memory access based on type assumptions.

questions.question: In Python, what is the architectural reason that executing `list.append` within a tight loop is often more memory-efficient than using the `+` operator to concatenate lists?
options: Method A creates a new list object in each iteration, whereas Method B utilizes list over-allocation (amortized O(1) growth).
Method A triggers immediate garbage collection on the previous list, while Method B defers memory reclamation.
Method B forces the interpreter to use a specialized C-level primitive that bypasses the global object heap.
Method A maintains the original list's memory block, while Method B forces a re-allocation of the underlying array buffer every time.
questions.correctAnswer: Method A creates a new list object in each iteration, whereas Method B utilizes list over-allocation (amortized O(1) growth).
questions.explanation: Python lists are implemented as dynamic arrays. Using the `+` operator creates a new list object and copies elements, which is O(N). The `append` method, however, takes advantage of the list's pre-allocated capacity, making it amortized O(1).
questions.hint: Think about how dynamic arrays manage memory capacity to avoid frequent reallocations.
questions.relatedConcept: Dynamic Array Amortization
questions.codeSnippet:
data = []
for i in range(10000):
    data += [i] # Method A
    # vs
    data.append(i) # Method B
questions.interviewTip: An interviewer uses this to gauge if a developer understands the hidden cost of Python's dynamic list management.

questions.question: In the context of the C11 memory model, what is the fundamental difference in the behavior of atomic_load and atomic_load_explicit with memory_order_relaxed regarding non-atomic memory accesses in the same thread?
options: atomic_load_explicit with memory_order_relaxed enforces a compiler barrier that prevents all non-atomic reordering, while atomic_load does not.
There is no difference in ordering constraints; both permit reordering of non-atomic accesses around the atomic load.
atomic_load provides sequential consistency, whereas atomic_load_explicit with memory_order_relaxed allows the compiler and hardware to reorder non-atomic stores.
atomic_load_explicit prevents the compiler from performing constant folding on the value, whereas atomic_load does not.
questions.correctAnswer: There is no difference in ordering constraints; both permit reordering of non-atomic accesses around the atomic load.
questions.explanation: In the C11 memory model, both standard atomic_load and atomic_load_explicit(..., memory_order_relaxed) are considered atomic operations. Since memory_order_relaxed provides no synchronization or ordering guarantees with respect to other memory operations, both allow the compiler and CPU to reorder non-atomic accesses around the load.
questions.hint: Focus on the definition of memory_order_relaxed in the C11 standard.
questions.relatedConcept: C11 Memory Model atomics
questions.interviewTip: Understanding atomic ordering is crucial for low-latency concurrent systems engineering.

questions.question: In a distributed system, why is the use of a Lamport Timestamp strictly less informative than a Vector Clock when detecting causality?
options: Vector Clocks are faster to compute because they do not require a global counter shared across nodes.
Lamport Timestamps require infinite bandwidth to transmit the state of the entire system for every event.
Lamport Timestamps cannot determine if two events are concurrent; they only provide a total ordering that may not reflect true causality.
Vector Clocks ensure that the system remains consistent even in the event of a total network partition.
questions.correctAnswer: Lamport Timestamps cannot determine if two events are concurrent; they only provide a total ordering that may not reflect true causality.
questions.explanation: Lamport timestamps only provide a partial order (if a->b then T(a) < T(b)), but if T(a) < T(b), it does not necessarily mean a->b. Vector clocks explicitly track the history of updates per process, allowing the system to distinguish between causal relationships and concurrent events.
questions.hint: Think about the distinction between total order and partial order in distributed events.
questions.relatedConcept: Distributed logical clocks and causality
questions.interviewTip: Distributed systems architects often differentiate candidates based on their understanding of logical vs. physical time.

questions.question: In C++, when employing the Rule of Five, why is it considered a defect to implement a move constructor that merely copies the resource pointer without nulling the source object's pointer?
options: The move constructor will implicitly call the copy constructor, causing a memory leak.
The compiler will throw an error for violating the 'noexcept' requirement of move semantics.
The underlying memory manager will flag an alignment error due to pointer aliasing.
The source object's destructor will trigger a double-free on the shared resource.
questions.correctAnswer: The source object's destructor will trigger a double-free on the shared resource.
questions.explanation: A move operation must transfer ownership. If the source object is not left in a null state (or another valid 'moved-from' state), its destructor will eventually execute and deallocate the memory that the new object now owns, resulting in a double-free runtime crash.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to the source object once it goes out of scope after the move.
questions.relatedConcept: Move semantics and resource ownership safety
questions.interviewTip: Senior candidates should immediately recognize the lifecycle impact of move operations on resource management.

questions.question: When utilizing asynchronous functions in Python's asyncio, what is the impact of performing a CPU-bound operation (e.g., intensive matrix calculation) directly within an 'async def' function without offloading?
options: The event loop is blocked, preventing other concurrent tasks from progressing.
The CPU-bound code is implicitly executed in a thread pool, potentially causing race conditions.
The Python interpreter automatically serializes the task to prevent GIL contention.
The asyncio event loop throws a RuntimeWarning and forces the task to execute synchronously.
questions.correctAnswer: The event loop is blocked, preventing other concurrent tasks from progressing.
questions.explanation: Asyncio uses a single-threaded event loop. If a task performs a long-running CPU computation without 'await'-ing an I/O task or yielding control, the entire loop freezes, halting all other scheduled tasks.
questions.hint: Think about the threading model of the asyncio event loop.
questions.relatedConcept: Concurrency models and event loop blocking
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands the difference between concurrency (asyncio) and parallelism (multiprocessing).

questions.question: In the context of the Linux kernel's OOM (Out of Memory) Killer, what happens when a process is assigned a negative value (e.g., -1000) to its 'oom_score_adj' file in /proc/[pid]/oom_score_adj?
options: The process is prioritized to be killed first when memory pressure exceeds 90%.
The process is permanently exempted from being selected for termination by the OOM killer.
The process will trigger an immediate panic of the entire kernel to prevent data corruption.
The process loses its ability to allocate further heap memory until the score is reset to 0.
questions.correctAnswer: The process is permanently exempted from being selected for termination by the OOM killer.
questions.explanation: Setting 'oom_score_adj' to -1000 effectively disables the OOM killer for that specific process, making it unkillable by the OOM mechanism. Distractors suggest priority or panic scenarios which are not the function of this specific adjustment.
questions.hint: Consider the semantic meaning of 'adj' (adjustment) in the context of kernel process selection heuristics.
questions.relatedConcept: Linux Kernel Memory Management
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how system-level processes manage stability under pressure is critical for SRE and backend engineering roles.

questions.question: When using 'epoll' on Linux, what is the fundamental functional difference between Edge-Triggered (EPOLLET) mode and Level-Triggered mode regarding file descriptor readiness?
options: Level-Triggered mode causes the kernel to block the thread entirely until the entire file descriptor buffer is emptied.
Edge-Triggered mode ignores all signals from the file descriptor if the system load average exceeds 1.0.
In Edge-Triggered mode, the event is reported only when a state change occurs, requiring the application to drain the buffer completely.
Level-Triggered mode requires the application to set the file descriptor to non-blocking mode, whereas Edge-Triggered does not.
questions.correctAnswer: In Edge-Triggered mode, the event is reported only when a state change occurs, requiring the application to drain the buffer completely.
questions.explanation: Edge-triggered mode notifies the user space only when an event occurs (a state change). If the buffer is not drained, no further events for that read/write will be generated, unlike Level-Triggered mode which persists the event until handled.
questions.hint: Think about the frequency of notifications and whether the kernel expects the application to 'consume' the status.
questions.relatedConcept: I/O Multiplexing
questions.interviewTip: Distinguishing between these modes demonstrates deep understanding of Linux high-performance network programming.

questions.question: In the context of the C11 memory model, what is the fundamental difference between memory_order_acquire and memory_order_consume when performing an atomic load operation?
options: memory_order_consume is deprecated in C11 and behaves identically to memory_order_relaxed, while memory_order_acquire is a full fence.
memory_order_acquire requires a complete system-wide synchronization barrier, whereas memory_order_consume only synchronizes with the specific thread that performed the store.
Both orderings are architecturally identical on x86, but differ only on ARMv8 due to the presence of hardware-level data dependency tracking.
memory_order_consume establishes a dependency chain only for operations that depend on the value loaded, whereas memory_order_acquire prevents all subsequent reordering.
questions.correctAnswer: memory_order_consume establishes a dependency chain only for operations that depend on the value loaded, whereas memory_order_acquire prevents all subsequent reordering.
questions.explanation: memory_order_consume is specifically designed to leverage the hardware data-dependency property (e.g., pointer dereferencing) to avoid the heavy cost of a full acquire barrier, which acts as a broader compiler and hardware reordering fence.
questions.hint: Think about the scope of compiler optimizations allowed after the load.
questions.relatedConcept: C11 Memory Model and Data Dependencies
questions.interviewTip: Distinguishing between acquire and consume shows a deep understanding of hardware-level memory models and performance optimization.

questions.question: What is the primary technical risk when relying on 'test-and-set' atomic operations in a high-contention spinlock implementation across a multi-socket NUMA architecture?
options: Cache line bouncing (ping-ponging) caused by continuous invalidation of the cache line across socket inter-connects.
The risk of a 'spurious wakeup' that causes the lock to be released prematurely by the scheduler.
Integer overflow of the atomic counter resulting in a deadlock state.
Violation of the strong consistency model required for hardware-level instruction reordering.
questions.correctAnswer: Cache line bouncing (ping-ponging) caused by continuous invalidation of the cache line across socket inter-connects.
questions.explanation: In NUMA systems, multiple cores attempting to 'test-and-set' the same memory location cause the cache line containing the lock to constantly bounce between caches, leading to significant interconnect congestion and performance degradation.
questions.hint: Consider the impact of the MESI protocol on shared memory synchronization.
questions.relatedConcept: NUMA memory contention and cache coherence
questions.interviewTip: This tests awareness of low-level hardware architecture implications on high-level concurrency primitives.

questions.question: In a C++ application utilizing RTTI (Run-Time Type Information), what causes a `dynamic_cast` from a base class pointer to a derived class pointer to return `nullptr` instead of throwing an exception?
options: The base class does not have at least one virtual function.
The `dynamic_cast` operator only throws `std::bad_cast` when casting references, not pointers.
The target class type is not registered in the linker's RTTI metadata table.
The compiler optimization flag -fno-rtti is enabled globally.
questions.correctAnswer: The `dynamic_cast` operator only throws `std::bad_cast` when casting references, not pointers.
questions.explanation: According to the C++ standard, dynamic_cast returns a null pointer when a pointer cast fails, but throws a std::bad_cast exception when a reference cast fails.
questions.hint: Consider the difference in error reporting mechanisms between pointer and reference casting.
questions.relatedConcept: C++ RTTI and exception handling
questions.codeSnippet:
Base* b = new Base();
Derived* d = dynamic_cast<Derived*>(b);
questions.interviewTip: This tests depth of knowledge regarding C++ standard behavior versus common assumptions about error handling.

questions.question: When debugging a Node.js process experiencing high memory pressure, you notice the heap size remains stable but the Resident Set Size (RSS) continues to grow unbounded. What is the most likely cause?
options: A circular reference in the JavaScript object graph is preventing the Mark-Sweep algorithm from reclaiming memory.
The Event Loop is saturated, causing asynchronous task queues to grow until they exceed the system's memory.
The V8 engine's external memory (Buffer/ArrayBuffer) allocated outside the V8 heap is not being garbage collected.
The process is leaking file descriptors, which are being incorrectly accounted for as resident memory by the OS kernel.
questions.correctAnswer: The V8 engine's external memory (Buffer/ArrayBuffer) allocated outside the V8 heap is not being garbage collected.
questions.explanation: Node.js (specifically V8) manages objects within the V8 heap, but Buffers are allocated in external memory. Since the GC is unaware of the external memory footprint, the RSS grows while the heap usage stays within reported limits.
questions.hint: Think about where Buffers and external C++ objects live in the Node.js memory architecture.
questions.relatedConcept: V8 memory management and external buffers
questions.interviewTip: Distinguishing between heap memory and RSS is vital for senior-level backend performance debugging.

questions.question: In the context of the C++ standard library, what is the behavior of the `std::atomic<T>::exchange` method when the provided argument is a reference to the same atomic object?
options: The operation is undefined behavior.
The atomic value becomes indeterminate due to a self-assignment race.
The compiler optimizes the call into a simple load operation.
The atomic value is set to its own current value effectively performing a no-op.
questions.correctAnswer: The atomic value is set to its own current value effectively performing a no-op.
questions.explanation: According to the C++ standard (atomic.exchange), the member function performs an atomic swap. When passing a reference to the same object, the load and store operations are conceptually atomic; since the value being stored is the current value, it effectively results in no change to the underlying state.
questions.hint: Check the C++ standard requirements for atomic exchange arguments.
questions.relatedConcept: Atomic operation semantics
questions.codeSnippet:
std::atomic<int> x(10);
x.exchange(x);
questions.interviewTip: This tests depth of knowledge regarding concurrency primitives and standard library safety guarantees.

questions.question: When using Python's `multiprocessing.Queue` to share data between processes, what is the fundamental technical reason why passing a large, complex object might cause a 'BrokenPipeError' or hang during execution?
options: The object exceeds the internal buffer size of the underlying pipe, causing a deadlock if not drained.
The GIL prevents the main process from serializing objects larger than 64KB.
The object contains non-pickleable local references that trigger an immediate process termination.
The underlying socket connection is dropped by the OS due to inactivity during the serialization process.
questions.correctAnswer: The object exceeds the internal buffer size of the underlying pipe, causing a deadlock if not drained.
questions.explanation: Multiprocessing Queues in Python use pipes. If the object size exceeds the system-level pipe buffer (which is finite), the sender will block until the receiver reads the data. If the receiver isn't actively consuming, or if the buffer is exhausted, the pipe can break or result in a deadlock, specifically under high load.
questions.hint: Think about the inter-process communication mechanism under the hood.
questions.relatedConcept: Inter-Process Communication constraints
questions.interviewTip: Understanding IPC limitations is crucial for building robust distributed or multi-processing Python backends.

questions.question: In the context of the C11 standard, what is the mandatory result of evaluating `(1.0 / 0.0)` in an implementation that defines `__STDC_IEC_559__`?
options: The expression triggers a floating-point exception (SIGFPE) by default.
The expression results in positive infinity.
The behavior is undefined, as division by zero is prohibited in standard C.
The expression results in a quiet NaN (Not-a-Number).
questions.correctAnswer: The expression results in positive infinity.
questions.explanation: When the `__STDC_IEC_559__` macro is defined, the implementation must conform to the IEC 60559 (IEEE 754) floating-point standard, where division of a positive finite number by zero yields positive infinity.
questions.hint: Check the implications of the IEC 60559 macro.
questions.relatedConcept: Floating-point IEEE 754 compliance in C
questions.codeSnippet: double result = 1.0 / 0.0;
questions.interviewTip: Understanding hardware-level floating-point behavior is critical for embedded or high-performance financial systems.

questions.question: Which of the following scenarios in Python correctly describes the 'MRO' (Method Resolution Order) conflict handled by the C3 linearization algorithm?
options: A situation where a method is defined in a base class but shadowed by a decorator, requiring explicit super() calls.
The accidental use of multiple inheritance resulting in a circular dependency at the module import level.
A class hierarchy that creates a non-monotonic precedence graph, preventing a consistent linearization.
When an abstract base class (ABC) forces a method implementation that conflicts with a mixin class's interface.
questions.correctAnswer: A class hierarchy that creates a non-monotonic precedence graph, preventing a consistent linearization.
questions.explanation: C3 linearization is designed to ensure that the MRO is consistent and monotonic; if a class hierarchy violates the constraints of the C3 algorithm, Python will raise a TypeError during class creation.
questions.hint: Recall the conditions under which Python's inheritance engine throws a TypeError.
questions.relatedConcept: C3 linearization and inheritance conflicts
questions.interviewTip: Distinguishing between runtime errors and compile-time (definition-time) errors in Python shows deep language mastery.

questions.question: In a C++ environment, when analyzing a core dump of a program that crashed due to a stack overflow, what is the most definitive indicator that the stack pointer has exceeded the guard page boundaries versus a standard heap corruption error?
options: A Bus Error (SIGBUS) caused by the alignment mismatch between the stack frame pointer and the instruction pointer.
The stack frame chain in the debugger appears infinite or circular due to recursive function calls.
The heap's heap-metadata-canary has been overwritten by a local variable residing on the stack.
The presence of a Segmentation Fault (SIGSEGV) with an access address mapping directly to an unallocated memory region just below the stack segment.
questions.correctAnswer: The presence of a Segmentation Fault (SIGSEGV) with an access address mapping directly to an unallocated memory region just below the stack segment.
questions.explanation: A stack overflow causes a segmentation fault when the stack pointer tries to access the protected guard page at the boundary of the thread's stack memory. Distractor 3 describes recursion, which is a cause, not the definitive indicator of the crash mechanism itself.
questions.hint: Consider how the operating system memory protection mechanism interacts with stack growth.
questions.relatedConcept: Stack memory segmentation and protection mechanisms
questions.interviewTip: IBM interviewers value deep knowledge of OS-level failures; linking crashes to memory segments demonstrates practical debugging experience.

questions.question: When configuring a distributed system's observability pipeline using Prometheus/Grafana, what is the fundamental risk of setting an excessively high 'scrape_interval' for high-cardinality metrics?
options: Metric aliasing occurs, where distinct time series are compressed into a single bucket, leading to loss of granular data integrity.
The 'PromQL' query engine will return incomplete results due to timestamp interpolation artifacts known as 'aliasing'.
The target service experiences increased CPU saturation due to the frequent overhead of the exporter process recalculating labels.
The persistent storage overhead increases exponentially due to the influx of redundant metadata headers for every scrap cycle.
questions.correctAnswer: Metric aliasing occurs, where distinct time series are compressed into a single bucket, leading to loss of granular data integrity.
questions.explanation: High cardinality combined with high frequency causes severe resource exhaustion and, more importantly, loss of data integrity during the aggregation phase (aliasing). Option 3 is a side effect but not the primary analytical risk.
questions.hint: Focus on what happens to distinct data series when the resolution is too high relative to the number of possible label combinations.
questions.relatedConcept: Prometheus high-cardinality performance implications
questions.interviewTip: This tests the candidate's understanding of monitoring infrastructure at scale, a critical skill for IBM Cloud SRE roles.

questions.question: In the context of the C11 `atomic_signal_fence` primitive, what is the specific technical justification for its inclusion in the C standard library compared to a standard `atomic_thread_fence`?
options: It prevents the compiler from reordering non-atomic memory accesses across the fence, which atomic_thread_fence ignores.
It provides synchronization between a thread and a signal handler executing on the same thread, which atomic_thread_fence cannot guarantee.
It forces an immediate write-through from the CPU cache to main memory to satisfy hardware-level coherency protocols.
It is required for compatibility with legacy systems that do not support lock-free atomic operations at the hardware level.
questions.correctAnswer: It provides synchronization between a thread and a signal handler executing on the same thread, which atomic_thread_fence cannot guarantee.
questions.explanation: atomic_signal_fence is specifically designed to manage the visibility and ordering of memory operations between a thread and a signal handler running on the same execution context. Standard thread fences are intended for multi-threaded memory visibility, whereas signal fences handle the asynchronous interruption of the same thread.
questions.hint: Consider the relationship between a signal handler and the thread that interrupted it.
questions.relatedConcept: C11 Memory Model and Asynchronous Signal Safety
questions.interviewTip: Understand the difference between multi-core thread synchronization and single-core asynchronous interruption.

questions.question: When utilizing `WeakReference` in Java to cache large objects, why might an application still suffer from an `OutOfMemoryError` even when the heap is technically under pressure?
options: Weak references prevent the objects they point to from being moved during heap compaction, leading to massive memory fragmentation.
The JVM treats WeakReference objects as GC roots, keeping the entire reference object graph alive indefinitely.
The garbage collector may not clear weak references until the memory pressure reaches a critical threshold or a full GC is triggered.
The overhead of the reference queue management consumes significant native memory that is not accounted for by the JVM heap limit.
questions.correctAnswer: The garbage collector may not clear weak references until the memory pressure reaches a critical threshold or a full GC is triggered.
questions.explanation: Weak references are only cleared by the collector when it deems the memory is needed. If the heap fill-rate is higher than the collector's ability to trigger and reclaim weak-referenced memory, an OOM can occur before the references are cleared.
questions.hint: Focus on the timing and the trigger mechanism of the garbage collector.
questions.relatedConcept: Java GC and Reachability Analysis
questions.interviewTip: Recognize that 'Weak' does not imply 'Immediate' in garbage collection contexts.

questions.question: In the context of the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), what is the definitive consequence of explicitly invoking System.gc() in a high-concurrency production environment?
options: It forces an immediate cleanup of the Young Generation, ensuring that short-lived objects are promoted to the Old Generation synchronously.
It clears all soft references in the heap regardless of memory pressure, effectively bypassing the LRU cache eviction policies.
It instructs the JIT compiler to flush the code cache and re-profile the bytecode for optimization, potentially increasing CPU usage temporarily.
It acts as a non-binding hint that triggers a full garbage collection event, potentially causing a 'stop-the-world' pause across all application threads.
questions.correctAnswer: It acts as a non-binding hint that triggers a full garbage collection event, potentially causing a 'stop-the-world' pause across all application threads.
questions.explanation: System.gc() is a hint to the JVM, but it typically forces a Full GC, which induces a 'stop-the-world' event, causing latency spikes in production. Distractors incorrectly suggest it affects specific generations or the JIT compiler.
questions.hint: Consider the impact of 'Stop-the-World' events on application responsiveness.
questions.relatedConcept: JVM Garbage Collection Internals
questions.interviewTip: An interviewer asks this to see if you understand the operational risks of manual memory management in managed runtimes.

questions.question: When implementing a Read-Write lock pattern (e.g., ReentrantReadWriteLock) in a multi-threaded system, which scenario is most likely to cause 'Writer Starvation'?
options: Multiple readers repeatedly acquiring the shared read lock, effectively preventing the pending write lock from ever being granted.
A single thread holding a write lock while simultaneously attempting to acquire a read lock within the same execution path.
The OS scheduler de-prioritizing threads that are currently waiting for a monitor condition inside the lock's internal queue.
Excessive context switching caused by the lock's internal state transition from 'shared' to 'exclusive' mode.
questions.correctAnswer: Multiple readers repeatedly acquiring the shared read lock, effectively preventing the pending write lock from ever being granted.
questions.explanation: If a system is read-heavy, a continuous stream of readers can keep the lock in 'shared' mode indefinitely, preventing writers from ever obtaining exclusive access. This is a classic concurrency design flaw known as reader-writer starvation.
questions.hint: Think about how shared access modes interact with the availability of exclusive access modes.
questions.relatedConcept: Concurrency Design Patterns
questions.interviewTip: This tests if you can move beyond simple threading primitives to architectural implications of high-level synchronization constructs.

questions.question: In Python, what is the consequence of inheriting from both a class that defines __slots__ and a class that does not?
options: Class C will effectively have no slots, allowing arbitrary attribute assignment.
Class C will gain a __dict__ attribute, effectively nullifying the memory optimization provided by A's __slots__.
Class C will throw a TypeError at runtime due to a conflict in object layout.
Class C will inherit only the slots from A and prohibit any new instance attributes.
questions.correctAnswer: Class C will gain a __dict__ attribute, effectively nullifying the memory optimization provided by A's __slots__.
questions.explanation: If any base class in the MRO does not define __slots__, the derived class will automatically generate a __dict__ unless it defines its own __slots__, meaning the memory optimization is lost.
questions.hint: Consider how Python handles dynamic attribute assignment when multiple inheritance is involved.
questions.relatedConcept: Python Object Internals and Slots
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how __slots__ impacts memory usage and inheritance is key for senior Python developers optimizing long-running processes.

questions.question: In the context of the C11 memory model, what is the observable effect of performing an atomic load operation with 'memory_order_relaxed' compared to 'memory_order_acquire' on non-atomic variables?
options: Both orderings provide identical visibility guarantees for non-atomic memory, differing only in compiler instruction reordering restrictions.
memory_order_relaxed causes a hardware stall to flush the store buffer, whereas memory_order_acquire uses branch prediction to optimize access.
Only memory_order_acquire creates a happens-before relationship that synchronizes non-atomic writes from other threads.
memory_order_acquire is deprecated in C11 and will trigger a compiler warning, defaulting to sequentially consistent behavior.
questions.correctAnswer: Only memory_order_acquire creates a happens-before relationship that synchronizes non-atomic writes from other threads.
questions.explanation: memory_order_relaxed provides no synchronization or ordering guarantees for other memory accesses, whereas memory_order_acquire ensures that subsequent reads/writes cannot be reordered before the load and synchronizes with release operations in other threads.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between atomicity of a single variable and synchronization of the surrounding memory state.
questions.relatedConcept: C11 Memory Model synchronization primitives
questions.interviewTip: Understanding memory barriers is critical for high-performance concurrent systems where race conditions occur even with atomic variables.

questions.question: In a distributed system using eventual consistency, if a database operation utilizes a 'quorum' read/write strategy with N=3, R=2, and W=2, what is the primary consequence if a network partition limits the node visibility to only 2 nodes?
options: The system maintains strong consistency for writes but may return stale data for reads if the surviving nodes were not part of the latest write quorum.
The system becomes unavailable for both reads and writes because a quorum of 2 is insufficient to satisfy the N=3 redundancy requirement during a failure.
The system will automatically switch to N=2 mode, causing a permanent reduction in data durability and replication factor.
The system remains available for both reads and writes because it satisfies the R+W > N requirement.
questions.correctAnswer: The system remains available for both reads and writes because it satisfies the R+W > N requirement.
questions.explanation: With N=3, R=2, and W=2, the condition R+W > N (2+2 > 3) is satisfied, which ensures that at least one node in the read set overlaps with the write set, preserving consistency even with one node failure.
questions.hint: Check the mathematical condition for quorum intersection in distributed storage.
questions.relatedConcept: Distributed Systems Quorum-based Consensus
questions.interviewTip: This tests the fundamental trade-offs in CAP theorem implementations for distributed databases like Cassandra or DynamoDB.

questions.question: In the context of the Linux kernel's Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS), how does the 'vruntime' (virtual runtime) variable influence task scheduling fairness for processes with different nice values?
options: It normalizes execution time by scaling the actual runtime by the weight associated with the process's nice value.
It tracks the raw wall-clock time spent by a task and preempts tasks immediately upon exceeding a global slice duration.
It assigns a constant static priority to tasks, ignoring the nice value until the task reaches the end of the runqueue.
It forces tasks with higher nice values to execute before lower ones to minimize context switching overhead.
questions.correctAnswer: It normalizes execution time by scaling the actual runtime by the weight associated with the process's nice value.
questions.explanation: The CFS scheduler uses vruntime to track how long a task has run, weighted by its priority (nice value). A process with a higher priority (lower nice value) has its actual runtime scaled down when calculating vruntime, allowing it to run 'virtually' slower, thus granting it more CPU time than a lower priority task.
questions.hint: Consider how CFS handles priority-based scaling of execution time.
questions.relatedConcept: Operating System Scheduling Algorithms
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how modern schedulers handle fairness versus priority is critical for systems-level performance tuning.

questions.question: When configuring a Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) system in a relational database, what is the specific performance implication of setting 'synchronous_commit' to 'off' in a high-concurrency environment?
options: The system executes the commit asynchronously by ignoring the WAL entirely, leading to potential corruption of the data files.
The system acknowledges the transaction as complete before the log buffer is flushed to persistent storage, increasing throughput but risking data loss.
The system uses a background thread to force a synchronous flush every millisecond, negating any performance benefits of the setting.
The system disables the ACID transaction property, causing subsequent reads to return stale data from the transaction log instead of the table.
questions.correctAnswer: The system acknowledges the transaction as complete before the log buffer is flushed to persistent storage, increasing throughput but risking data loss.
questions.explanation: Setting synchronous_commit to 'off' allows the database to return a 'success' response to the client after the transaction is committed to memory but before the WAL is physically persisted to disk. This improves throughput significantly but introduces a risk of losing the most recent transactions if a power failure or OS crash occurs.
questions.hint: Think about the trade-off between durability and latency in database durability settings.
questions.relatedConcept: Database Transaction Durability
questions.interviewTip: Engineers are often tested on their understanding of the CAP theorem and the 'D' in ACID when designing resilient systems.

questions.question: In the context of the C++20 memory model, when a memory location is updated via a std::atomic_ref without a specified memory order, which implicit constraint applies, and how does it affect compiler optimizations?
options: It defaults to std::memory_order_relaxed, allowing the compiler to reorder non-atomic accesses but enforcing atomicity on the specific memory location.
It requires an explicit memory_order argument; failing to provide one results in a compilation error.
It defaults to std::memory_order_seq_cst, prohibiting reordering of atomic operations with surrounding non-atomic memory accesses.
It defaults to std::memory_order_acquire_release, forcing a hardware fence that flushes all pending store buffers.
questions.correctAnswer: It defaults to std::memory_order_seq_cst, prohibiting reordering of atomic operations with surrounding non-atomic memory accesses.
questions.explanation: std::atomic_ref (introduced in C++20) defaults to std::memory_order_seq_cst for all operations. Sequential consistency is the strictest memory order, which not only guarantees atomicity but also enforces a total global ordering of operations, effectively preventing the compiler and CPU from reordering atomic operations relative to surrounding memory accesses.
questions.hint: C++20's std::atomic_ref has a stricter default memory ordering than typical low-level atomic operations.
questions.relatedConcept: C++20 std::atomic_ref memory semantics
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers look for candidates who understand that 'convenience' defaults in modern C++ often carry significant performance trade-offs compared to explicit, weaker memory orders.

title: Infosys - Test 1: OA Screening Assessment
description: Official technical screening test pattern for Infosys campus and off-campus recruitment drives.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q1] In a C program, what is the consequence of calling `malloc()` inside a signal handler after a segmentation fault has occurred?
options: It safely allocates memory and allows the handler to write to it, as the kernel guarantees atomicity of `malloc` during signal handling.
It typically causes undefined behavior or a deadlock because `malloc` is not async-signal-safe and may try to acquire a heap lock that was interrupted.
It fails with `NULL` return value only if the system is out of memory, but is otherwise safe to use for logging purposes.
It automatically switches the process to a new address space, preventing any corruption of the original heap.
questions.correctAnswer: It typically causes undefined behavior or a deadlock because `malloc` is not async-signal-safe and may try to acquire a heap lock that was interrupted.
questions.explanation: Calling non-async-signal-safe functions like `malloc` inside a signal handler is dangerous. If the fault occurred while holding an internal heap lock, the handler might attempt to re-acquire the same lock, leading to a deadlock or further corruption. The standard dictates that only specific async-signal-safe functions should be used in handlers.
questions.hint: Consider the state of mutexes or locks if the signal interrupted a critical section.
questions.relatedConcept: Async-signal-safety and heap locking
questions.interviewTip: Tests understanding of why crash handlers must be minimal and avoid dynamic allocation.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q2] In a Go program, what happens to a goroutine's stack memory if the goroutine is suspended at a blocking I/O call when the main program exits?
options: The memory is immediately reclaimed by the OS because the goroutine is no longer running on a CPU thread.
The garbage collector frees the stack if no references to the goroutine's closure variables exist.
The memory remains allocated until the goroutine explicitly finishes or calls `runtime.Goexit()`, even if paused.
The runtime forcibly terminates the goroutine and leaks the memory to prevent resource exhaustion.
questions.correctAnswer: The memory remains allocated until the goroutine explicitly finishes or calls `runtime.Goexit()`, even if paused.
questions.explanation: In Go, a goroutine's stack is a contiguous block of memory that grows and shrinks as needed. When a goroutine blocks, its stack is still mapped in memory. The Go runtime does not unmap or free the stack while the goroutine object exists; it is released only when the goroutine terminates (completes or exits).
questions.hint: The existence of the OS thread is separate from the logical goroutine's memory footprint.
questions.relatedConcept: Goroutine stack memory lifetime
questions.interviewTip: Distinguishes between CPU scheduling and memory lifecycle in concurrent runtimes.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q3] What is the primary consequence of accessing an uninitialized local variable of automatic storage duration in C?
options: The variable is guaranteed to be implicitly initialized to zero by the runtime environment.
The variable contains an indeterminate value, and reading it invokes undefined behavior.
The compiler issues a fatal build error halting compilation.
The stack pointer automatically shifts to allocate a new safe memory location.
questions.correctAnswer: The variable contains an indeterminate value, and reading it invokes undefined behavior.
questions.explanation: In C, local variables with automatic storage duration are not automatically initialized to zero. They retain whatever garbage values happen to reside in that stack memory frame, and reading them before assignment results in undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Think about stack garbage values and standard compliance.
questions.relatedConcept: Automatic storage duration and uninitialized variables
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers test this to see if the candidate understands memory semantics beyond high-level languages like Java or Python.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q4] How does the scope of a variable declared with the 'static' keyword inside a block differ from a standard local variable?
options: Its scope becomes global across all translation units in the project.
Its value is re-initialized to zero every time the enclosing block is entered.
Its scope is restricted to the block, but its lifetime spans the entire execution of the program.
Its memory is allocated on the heap rather than the data segment.
questions.correctAnswer: Its scope is restricted to the block, but its lifetime spans the entire execution of the program.
questions.explanation: A local static variable retains block scope (it can only be referenced by name within that function), but it possesses static storage duration, meaning its lifetime persists throughout the entire program run and its value is preserved across function calls.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between lifetime and visibility/scope.
questions.relatedConcept: Static storage duration vs block scope
questions.interviewTip: Frequently asked to ensure candidates understand storage classes and where state is preserved in procedural programs.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q5] What is the primary behavioral hazard of calling a non-reentrant function (such as `strtok`) inside a POSIX signal handler?
options: It triggers an immediate segmentation fault because signal handlers execute in kernel space where strtok is unmapped.
It automatically upgrades the signal handler execution context to a multi-threaded pool, causing a race condition.
It results in a compile-time warning or linker error regarding forbidden symbols in signal contexts.
It causes undefined behavior due to potential data corruption if the signal interrupted a normal function call that was also modifying internal static state of strtok.
questions.correctAnswer: It causes undefined behavior due to potential data corruption if the signal interrupted a normal function call that was also modifying internal static state of strtok.
questions.explanation: Non-reentrant functions like `strtok` rely on internal static state to keep track of parsing across calls. If a signal interrupts the main thread while it is mid-way through modifying or reading that internal state, and the handler invokes the same function, the state becomes corrupted, leading to unpredictable program behavior.
questions.hint: Think about what `strtok` uses internally to remember the state between successive calls.
questions.relatedConcept: Async-signal-safety and non-reentrant state corruption
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test deep knowledge of low-level concurrency, OS signals, and thread safety nuances beyond basic multi-threading.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q6] What is the exact consequence under the C standard of modifying a const-qualified object through a non-const pointer obtained via explicit casting?
options: Undefined behavior, even if the underlying storage location is located in writable memory (such as the stack).
Guaranteed modification of the variable 'a', resulting in its value becoming 20 safely.
A strict compilation error emitted by any standard-conforming compiler due to type-system violation.
A guaranteed hardware trap or segmentation fault at the moment the assignment statement executes.
questions.correctAnswer: Undefined behavior, even if the underlying storage location is located in writable memory (such as the stack).
questions.explanation: According to the C standard, modifying an object that is defined with const-qualification results in undefined behavior. Even if a cast removes the qualifier and allows code to compile and run without an explicit crash, optimizers assume const objects never change and can optimize aggressively, leading to subtle bugs.
questions.hint: Cast operators do not change the underlying constness contract made with the compiler.
questions.relatedConcept: Const qualification violation and undefined behavior
questions.interviewTip: This tests whether candidates understand that C type casting is a directive to the compiler, not necessarily a runtime safety guarantee.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q7] When designing a high-throughput REST API using Spring Boot, under what architectural condition does connection pooling for an external HTTP client (like WebClient or RestTemplate) become a critical performance bottleneck?
options: When connection timeouts are set too high, causing all HTTP requests to default to synchronous execution regardless of asynchronous reactive declarations.
When the application threads block synchronously waiting for available connections from the pool while downstream latency spikes, exhausting thread pool resources.
When the maximum connection pool size exceeds the physical core count of the server, triggering excessive CPU context switching.
When connection keep-alive headers are stripped by a reverse proxy, forcing TLS renegotiation on every packet.
questions.correctAnswer: When the application threads block synchronously waiting for available connections from the pool while downstream latency spikes, exhausting thread pool resources.
questions.explanation: If downstream services experience latency spikes, an under-provisioned connection pool will cause threads to block waiting for a free connection. This quickly depletes the application's thread pool, leading to cascading failures across the API.
questions.hint: Consider what happens when caller threads outnumber available socket connections during a downstream slowdown.
questions.relatedConcept: HTTP connection pooling saturation and thread exhaustion
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if you understand how underlying transport-layer bottlenecks propagate upward into application thread management.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q8] What is the primary trade-off when configuring a relational database index with a very high cardinality column compared to a low cardinality column?
options: High cardinality indexes can only be utilized for equality checks and cannot participate in range queries.
Low cardinality indexes speed up write operations exponentially but cause full table scans on every read query.
High cardinality indexes provide selective filtering but require significantly more storage and incur higher maintenance overhead during write operations.
Low cardinality indexes prevent query optimizers from using execution plans efficiently due to multi-column collation conflicts.
questions.correctAnswer: High cardinality indexes provide selective filtering but require significantly more storage and incur higher maintenance overhead during write operations.
questions.explanation: Columns with high cardinality (many unique values like UUIDs or timestamps) yield highly selective index leaf nodes, but the resulting B-Tree structure is larger, more fragmented, and consumes more memory and disk I/O during inserts and updates.
questions.hint: Think about how many rows match a specific key value and how that affects tree depth and modification cost.
questions.relatedConcept: Database index cardinality performance trade-offs
questions.interviewTip: Expected answer in system design and database tuning rounds to check your grasp of write amplification vs. read performance.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q9] During a code review for an enterprise Spring Boot microservice, a reviewer flags the use of `field-based` dependency injection (`@Autowired` on private fields). What is the primary architectural or testability drawback that prompts this flag?
options: It makes the class immutable and prevents runtime reconfiguration of dependencies.
It silently causes memory leaks due to circular references that constructor injection detects eagerly.
It forces the class to be thread-unsafe because fields cannot be marked as final.
It prevents instantiation of the class entirely outside of the Spring container unless reflection is explicitly used to inject mocks.
questions.correctAnswer: It prevents instantiation of the class entirely outside of the Spring container unless reflection is explicitly used to inject mocks.
questions.explanation: Field injection relies heavily on reflection by the container to set private fields. If you attempt to instantiate the class in a plain unit test using 'new OrderProcessor()', the 'paymentService' will be null, and manual setter or reflection workarounds are required, defeating the simplicity of pure JUnit tests.
questions.hint: Consider how you would unit test this class without starting up the Spring IoC container.
questions.relatedConcept: Spring Dependency Injection Best Practices and Testability
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers look for practical framework experience beyond basic annotations; knowing why constructor injection is preferred shows an understanding of maintainable design.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q10] In a high-throughput enterprise REST API using JPA/Hibernate, a developer encounters an N+1 select problem and attempts to fix it by fetching multiple child collections simultaneously in a single JPQL query using `JOIN FETCH`. What critical runtime exception or design issue can this introduction inadvertently trigger?
options: MultipleBagFetchException due to attempting to fetch multiple collection-valued associations simultaneously via Cartesian product.
OptimisticLockException due to concurrent updates on the fetched child collections during the same read transaction.
StackOverflowError during query parsing because Hibernate cannot resolve nested joins beyond two levels.
LazyInitializationException when accessing the returned list outside the transaction boundary.
questions.correctAnswer: MultipleBagFetchException due to attempting to fetch multiple collection-valued associations simultaneously via Cartesian product.
questions.explanation: Hibernate throws a MultipleBagFetchException (specifically an IllegalArgumentException) when a query tries to fetch multiple collection bags (List mapped without ordering) simultaneously, because it results in a Cartesian product multiplication of rows, leading to memory inflation and duplicate entities.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when you combine two independent collection relationships in a single SQL JOIN in relational databases mapped as Lists.
questions.relatedConcept: Hibernate ORM Performance Antipatterns
questions.codeSnippet:
@Query("SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.items JOIN FETCH o.deliveries")
List<Order> findAllOrdersWithDetails();
questions.interviewTip: This is a classic senior-level ORM gotcha that separates developers who blindly apply annotations from those who understand the underlying SQL translation.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q11] What is the primary runtime implication of allocating large objects directly on the heap instead of the stack in managed runtime environments like the .NET CLR or JVM?
options: Large objects are automatically thread-confined, preventing cross-thread sharing without explicit synchronization blocks.
Large objects bypass generation-0/1 nurseries and are allocated in a specialized heap region, increasing vulnerability to fragmentation and full garbage collection pauses.
Stack allocation overflow is prevented by spilling local reference handles directly to kernel page files.
The runtime converts large object allocations into immutable strings to optimize deduplication passes.
questions.correctAnswer: Large objects bypass generation-0/1 nurseries and are allocated in a specialized heap region, increasing vulnerability to fragmentation and full garbage collection pauses.
questions.explanation: Managed runtimes typically feature a Large Object Heap (LOH) or dedicated regions where objects exceeding a specific threshold bypass minor generational garbage collection cycles. Because these objects are collected less frequently and are expensive to move, they lead to memory fragmentation and trigger costly full garbage collections.
questions.hint: Think about generational garbage collection thresholds and memory fragmentation.
questions.relatedConcept: Large Object Heap and Generational Garbage Collection
questions.interviewTip: Interweaves garbage collection mechanics with performance tuning for enterprise applications.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q12] In Unix-like systems, what occurs when a parent process terminates without calling wait() or waitpid() on a child process that has already finished execution?
options: The operating system immediately terminates the child process and frees all its virtual memory pages and file descriptors.
The child process becomes a daemon process attached directly to the root session ID.
The child process entry remains in the kernel process table as a zombie process until the init process adopts and reaps it.
A segmentation fault signal is propagated to the parent process namespace.
questions.correctAnswer: The child process entry remains in the kernel process table as a zombie process until the init process adopts and reaps it.
questions.explanation: When a child process exits, its exit status and process descriptor are retained in the process table so the parent can read them via wait(). If the parent terminates first, the child becomes an orphan and is re-parented by init (PID 1), which automatically invokes wait() to clean up the table entry. If the parent is alive but fails to call wait(), the entry remains a zombie, consuming a process ID.
questions.hint: Consider the distinction between orphaned processes and process descriptor cleanup states.
questions.relatedConcept: Process Lifecycle Management and Zombie Processes
questions.interviewTip: Tests fundamental understanding of operating system resource accounting and process synchronization.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q13] In the C memory model, what defines the behavior when two concurrent threads access the same memory location without synchronization, and at least one access is a write?
options: It is safely handled via lock-free atomic fallback by modern compilers.
It triggers a segmentation fault immediately at the runtime level.
It forces sequential consistency automatically for scalar variables.
It results in undefined behavior due to a data race.
questions.correctAnswer: It results in undefined behavior due to a data race.
questions.explanation: According to the C and C++ standards, concurrent accesses to the same memory location where at least one is a write and neither is atomic form a data race, which results in undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Think about what the ISO standard states regarding concurrent conflicting non-atomic accesses.
questions.relatedConcept: Data races and undefined behavior in concurrent memory access
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers test this to check if candidates understand that multi-threaded correctness requires explicit synchronization rather than hoping hardware handles simultaneous writes safely.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q14] Which of the following describes the execution guarantee provided by `std::call_once` in modern C++ when paired with a `std::once_flag`?
options: It guarantees that the specified function is called exactly once, even across multiple concurrent threads, establishing a happens-before relationship.
It guarantees thread-safe execution only if the callable returns a boolean success status.
It executes the callable asynchronously on a background thread pool to avoid blocking the caller.
It acts as a spinlock that continuously yields the CPU until the target function completes.
questions.correctAnswer: It guarantees that the specified function is called exactly once, even across multiple concurrent threads, establishing a happens-before relationship.
questions.explanation: std::call_once ensures that a function is called exactly once regardless of the number of threads that execute it, synchronizing all subsequent calls with the completion of the initialization.
questions.hint: Look for the mechanism designed specifically for thread-safe lazy initialization.
questions.relatedConcept: std::call_once and thread-safe initialization semantics
questions.interviewTip: Often asked when discussing singleton patterns or one-time configuration loading in multi-threaded enterprise applications.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q15] During production maintenance, a client service experiences intermittent core dumps with a stack trace pointing to 'pthread_mutex_unlock' called from a signal handler. What is the fundamental root cause of this defect?
options: Signal handlers run in a separate process space where pthread locks are invalid.
Mutex locking and unlocking operations are not async-signal-safe, leading to undefined behavior and deadlocks when interrupting a thread already holding the lock.
The mutex was not initialized with the PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE attribute.
The signal was caught by the main thread instead of a dedicated worker thread.
questions.correctAnswer: Mutex locking and unlocking operations are not async-signal-safe, leading to undefined behavior and deadlocks when interrupting a thread already holding the lock.
questions.explanation: Functions like pthread_mutex_lock and pthread_mutex_unlock are not async-signal-safe. If a signal interrupts a thread that already holds the mutex and the handler attempts to lock it again, it results in self-deadlock or heap corruption.
questions.hint: Consider what functions are permitted inside an asynchronous signal context.
questions.relatedConcept: Async-signal-safety and mutex locking in POSIX threads
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify understanding of concurrency primitives and safe interrupt handling in systems programming.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q16] A production microservice written in Go logs intermittent memory corruption and unexpected panics only under high concurrent load. Profiling reveals a goroutine mutating a map concurrently accessed by another goroutine. What is the primary reason Go's runtime does not protect built-in maps with internal mutexes by default?
options: Go maps are implemented as read-only structures after initialization.
Built-in maps rely on external database transactions for thread safety.
To avoid unnecessary synchronization overhead for single-threaded or thread-confined map usage, since most maps do not require concurrent access.
The Go compiler automatically inserts locks only when race detection flags are enabled at build time.
questions.correctAnswer: To avoid unnecessary synchronization overhead for single-threaded or thread-confined map usage, since most maps do not require concurrent access.
questions.explanation: Go intentionally leaves map implementation without internal locking to avoid performance penalties in scenarios where synchronization is unnecessary. Developers must use sync.RWMutex or sync.Map when concurrent access occurs.
questions.hint: Think about performance trade-offs in language design for common data structures.
questions.relatedConcept: Go map concurrency semantics and performance design
questions.interviewTip: Frequently asked to test concurrency safety patterns and language runtime philosophy.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q17] When utilizing the standard C `strtok()` function to parse a string, what critical side-effect or constraint regarding the input string and concurrency must developers account for?
options: It allocates a new heap-allocated copy of each token that must be manually freed to avoid memory leaks.
It is fully thread-safe because it relies on standard thread-local storage for state tracking.
It leaves the original input string completely unmodified and read-only.
It modifies the original string by replacing delimiter characters with null-terminators and uses a static internal buffer, making it non-thread-safe.
questions.correctAnswer: It modifies the original string by replacing delimiter characters with null-terminators and uses a static internal buffer, making it non-thread-safe.
questions.explanation: strtok() modifies the source string in place by inserting '\0' at delimiter positions and stores parsing state in a static, internal variable, rendering it non-reentrant and thread-unsafe.
questions.hint: Think about how strtok remembers its position across multiple calls without passing the string pointer again.
questions.relatedConcept: Standard library function side effects and thread safety
questions.interviewTip: Intervers love asking about library functions that modify state or aren't thread-safe, as it highlights production debugging skills.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q18] What is the primary reason that standard JSON parsing libraries throw an error or handle integers incorrectly when parsing numeric values exceeding 9007199254740991 (Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER in IEEE 754 double-precision floats)?
options: JavaScript and many standard parsers represent all numeric JSON types as 64-bit binary floating-point numbers, leading to precision loss above 2^53 - 1.
JSON specification limits numbers to 32 bits, forcing parsers to reject anything larger.
RFC 8259 explicitly mandates that any integer over 16 digits must be encrypted.
Network transmission protocols automatically truncate integers to avoid buffer overflows.
questions.correctAnswer: JavaScript and many standard parsers represent all numeric JSON types as 64-bit binary floating-point numbers, leading to precision loss above 2^53 - 1.
questions.explanation: JSON numbers are often parsed into IEEE 754 double-precision floats by default in languages like JavaScript, which can precisely represent integers only up to 2^53 - 1.
questions.hint: Consider how floating-point representation limits exact integer storage ranges.
questions.relatedConcept: JSON numeric parsing limits and IEEE 754 precision
questions.interviewTip: Useful for backend developers dealing with large database 64-bit IDs (like Twitter/Snowflake IDs) consumed by web frontends.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q19] What is the primary portability risk when using the 'char' type without an explicit 'signed' or 'unsigned' qualifier in C cross-platform development?
options: 'char' is guaranteed to be 16 bits on some embedded platforms, breaking standard 8-bit ASCII assumptions.
The standard leaves the signedness of 'char' implementation-defined, so values above 127 may be interpreted as negative on some architectures.
Character literals like 'A' will produce compiler warnings on GCC if not explicitly qualified.
Pointers to 'char' cannot participate in pointer arithmetic across different translation units.
questions.correctAnswer: The standard leaves the signedness of 'char' implementation-defined, so values above 127 may be interpreted as negative on some architectures.
questions.explanation: According to the C standard, 'char', 'signed char', and 'unsigned char' are three distinct types. The plain 'char' type adopts the signedness of the hardware platform (e.g., signed on x86, unsigned on certain ARM or PowerPC implementations), introducing portability bugs when storing byte values > 127.
questions.hint: Think about how architectures differ regarding negative values in bytes.
questions.relatedConcept: C language portability, implementation-defined types, and signedness of plain char
questions.interviewTip: Interrogates whether a candidate understands subtle standard-defined ambiguities that surface during cross-compiler migrations.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q20] According to the C and C++ standards, what is the behavior of performing pointer arithmetic past one element beyond the end of an array (e.g., `arr + 2` for a 2-element array `int arr[2];`)?
options: Both 'arr + 2' and 'arr + 3' are fully valid as long as they do not cross a 4KB page boundary.
Pointer arithmetic is permitted to span any address space, but dereferencing causes a segmentation fault.
Pointing to 'arr + 2' is valid for comparison purposes only, whereas dereferencing it or evaluating 'arr + 3' invokes Undefined Behavior.
Both pointers are guaranteed to wrap around circularly to the beginning of the array.
questions.correctAnswer: Pointing to 'arr + 2' is valid for comparison purposes only, whereas dereferencing it or evaluating 'arr + 3' invokes Undefined Behavior.
questions.explanation: The C standard permits a pointer to point to the element dynamically positioned one past the last element of an array solely for loop termination comparisons. Dereferencing that pointer or generating any pointer pointing further beyond (`arr + 3`) yields strict Undefined Behavior.
questions.hint: Consider the strict boundaries enforced by the language standard for loop end conditions.
questions.relatedConcept: Pointer arithmetic boundaries, one-past-the-end pointers, and Undefined Behavior
questions.interviewTip: Essential for assessing deep comprehension of memory safety hazards and standards compliance in low-level systems programming.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q21] When configuring application log levels in a production microservice, what is the primary risk of using 'DEBUG' mode continuously over an extended duration?
options: Automatic suppression of all error logs due to buffer overflow in the logging framework
Unencrypted transmission of internal variables across all network boundaries
Compilation warnings becoming errors and crashing the production build pipeline
Excessive I/O disk writes and log file inflation leading to storage exhaustion and performance degradation
questions.correctAnswer: Excessive I/O disk writes and log file inflation leading to storage exhaustion and performance degradation
questions.explanation: Running at DEBUG level generates an immense volume of trace messages, which saturate disk I/O, consume vast amounts of disk space rapidly, and can severely impact application latency due to synchronous log flushing.
questions.hint: Consider the physical resources consumed by verbose logging over time.
questions.relatedConcept: Production telemetry and logging overhead
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to check if candidates understand the operational impact of configuration choices in production environments.

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q22] In distributed systems observability, what distinguishes a 'Metric' from a 'Trace'?
options: Metrics are point-in-time aggreg数値 (counters/gauges) measuring system health, whereas Traces follow the end-to-end journey of a single transaction across services
Metrics provide the exact stack trace of a failed function, whereas Traces only show CPU utilization over time
Metrics are exclusively collected by front-end clients, whereas Traces are strictly confined to database queries
Metrics can only be queried via SQL, whereas Traces require manual log file parsing
questions.correctAnswer: Metrics are point-in-time aggreg数値 (counters/gauges) measuring system health, whereas Traces follow the end-to-end journey of a single transaction across services
questions.explanation: Metrics represent aggregated numerical data over intervals (like request rates or error counts), while traces track the causal path and latency of individual requests as they propagate through distributed service boundaries.
questions.hint: Think about aggregated numerical values versus individual transaction paths.
questions.relatedConcept: Distributed tracing versus metrics aggregation
questions.interviewTip: This tests foundational knowledge of the three pillars of observability (logs, metrics, and traces).

questions.question: [Infosys • Test 1 • Q23] What is the primary security risk associated with using the `gets()` function in standard C, which led to its complete removal in the C11 standard?
options: It automatically strips the null terminator from the input string, causing out-of-bounds reads later.
It does not perform bounds checking on the input, leading to potential buffer overflow vulnerabilities.
It sends the read string over the network in plaintext if an active socket descriptor is open.
It allocates memory dynamically on the heap without providing a corresponding free mechanism, causing memory leaks.
