questions.interviewTip: Interviewers love asking about the async pipe to verify if candidates understand automatic resource management versus manual unsubscription patterns.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'AsyncPipe' to subscribe to an Observable in a template, what happens if the component is destroyed while the Observable is still 'cold' and waiting for an emission?
options: The Observable stream persists in memory until the browser tab is closed.
The AsyncPipe automatically unsubscribes, preventing a memory leak.
The Angular runtime throws an 'Uncaught Subscription Error' at the zone level.
The AsyncPipe keeps the subscription alive to ensure the last emitted value is cached for the next component instantiation.
questions.correctAnswer: The AsyncPipe automatically unsubscribes, preventing a memory leak.
questions.explanation: The AsyncPipe is specifically designed to manage the lifecycle of a subscription. When the component that uses the pipe is destroyed, the pipe's 'ngOnDestroy' method is invoked, which automatically calls 'unsubscribe()' on the internal subscription, thus preventing memory leaks without requiring manual management.
questions.hint: Consider the lifecycle management capabilities provided by built-in Angular pipes.
questions.relatedConcept: AsyncPipe lifecycle management
questions.interviewTip: Ask this to see if the candidate understands the benefit of built-in pipes over manual 'subscribe' calls.

questions.question: In an Angular application using the Default change detection strategy, which of the following scenarios will NOT trigger a re-check of the component's template by the ChangeDetectorRef during the digest cycle?
options: An Observable emitted from a service subscribed to using the AsyncPipe in the template.
A Promise resolved inside a @ViewChild-injected directive that does not call markForCheck().
An asynchronous event listener attached via Renderer2 inside the component.
A standard browser event (e.g., click) originating from within the component's DOM tree.
questions.correctAnswer: A Promise resolved inside a @ViewChild-injected directive that does not call markForCheck().
questions.explanation: Angular's Zone.js patches asynchronous browser APIs (setTimeout, click, etc.) to trigger change detection. AsyncPipe automatically calls markForCheck() when a new value arrives. However, a Promise resolution inside a directive that isn't connected to the component's own lifecycle or specifically marked for checking will not trigger a re-render of the component if it is OnPush, or simply lacks the signal to the ChangeDetectorRef.
questions.hint: Consider how Zone.js interacts with native browser events versus manually created asynchronous objects.
questions.relatedConcept: Zone.js and Change Detection lifecycle
questions.interviewTip: Distinguishing between Zone.js-triggered cycles and manual CD triggers is a hallmark of a senior Angular developer.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush' strategy, which of the following scenarios will successfully trigger a component re-render when a parent passes an object reference to an @Input property?
options: The component re-renders if the parent modifies a property of the existing object reference, such as 'this.data.value = 5'
The component re-renders if the parent replaces the object reference, such as 'this.data = {...this.data, value: 5}'
The component re-renders automatically because Angular performs a deep check on all @Input properties by default
The component will never re-render, even if the reference changes, because OnPush ignores @Input changes entirely
questions.correctAnswer: The component re-renders if the parent replaces the object reference, such as 'this.data = {...this.data, value: 5}'
questions.explanation: OnPush change detection strategy triggers only if the reference of an @Input property changes or if an event originates from within the component or its children. Modifying the properties of an object (mutation) does not change the reference, thus OnPush will not detect the change.
questions.hint: Consider how JavaScript compares object references versus object values in the context of change detection cycles.
questions.relatedConcept: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush and Reference checking
questions.interviewTip: Understanding OnPush is critical for performance tuning in large-scale Angular applications; candidates who know why reference checking matters demonstrate senior-level architectural awareness.

questions.question: In an Angular application using Zone.js, what is the consequence of calling a third-party library method that triggers an asynchronous task via 'requestAnimationFrame' inside an 'ngZone.runOutsideAngular' block?
options: The component view will be updated immediately because requestAnimationFrame is patched by Zone.js and triggers change detection regardless of the runOutsideAngular wrapper.
The component view will not be automatically updated, even if the ChangeDetectionStrategy is Default.
The application will throw a 'ZoneAwareError' because the task was initiated outside the Angular zone.
The data update will only reflect in the view if the user interacts with the application, triggering a new macro-task in the Angular zone.
questions.correctAnswer: The component view will not be automatically updated, even if the ChangeDetectionStrategy is Default.
questions.explanation: Zone.js patches browser APIs, including 'requestAnimationFrame'. However, 'runOutsideAngular' specifically removes the execution context from the Angular zone. Tasks scheduled within this block do not trigger Angular's change detection mechanism upon completion, meaning the 'data' property change will not be reflected in the UI unless manual detection is triggered.
questions.hint: Consider how Zone.js tracks asynchronous tasks to trigger change detection and what runOutsideAngular prevents.
questions.relatedConcept: Zone.js and Change Detection triggering
questions.interviewTip: This tests deep knowledge of how Angular reconciles asynchronous browser events with its internal change detection tree, essential for performance optimization.

questions.question: In Angular 14+, consider the following component code. What is the precise reason the view does not update with the new 'value' under the default change detection strategy, even though 'value' is assigned a new string reference inside the NgZone?
options: String primitives are compared by value in OnPush mode, so since 'updated' is a primitive, Angular skips CD to optimize performance.

OnPush change detection requires the component's inputs to be immutable and passed from a parent; it does not trigger CD for internal state changes unless an input binding changes or an event handler is attached to the element.
NgZone.run() must be nested inside ngAfterViewInit to properly queue the change detection tick for the current component instance.
setTimeout callbacks are executed in a Web Worker by default, isolating them from the main thread's NgZone and preventing CD from running.
questions.correctAnswer: OnPush change detection requires the component's inputs to be immutable and passed from a parent; it does not trigger CD for internal state changes unless an input binding changes or an event handler is attached to the element.
questions.explanation: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush instructs Angular to skip a component's view during change detection unless: (1) a reference equality check of an @Input() property changes, (2) an event handler defined within the component's template is fired, or (3) the component or one of its children manually calls markForCheck(). Assigning a new value to a local property (even inside zone.run) does not satisfy these conditions. Option B is wrong because OnPush uses reference equality, not deep value comparison, and primitives are passed by value but still trigger CD if they are inputs. Option C is incorrect because ngAfterViewInit is for initialization, not for CD timing. Option D is factually wrong as setTimeout runs on the main thread, not a Web Worker.
questions.hint: Review the specific triggers that force an OnPush component to reevaluate its view.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular OnPush Change Detection Triggers
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to distinguish between developers who just know 'OnPush is faster' and those who understand the strict limitations of the strategy, which is critical for debugging performance issues vs. UI update bugs.

title: Angular - Test 2: Technical Assessment
description: Test 2 for Angular. Every question is unique against the whole question database — no repeats, no renumbered or reworded variants of an existing question.

questions.question: What is the primary runtime performance advantage of Angular's new signal-based reactivity model over traditional Zone.js-based change detection?
options: It entirely prevents JavaScript garbage collection by pre-allocating memory blocks for all component state variables during bootstrap.
It eliminates the need to run change detection over the entire component tree by targeting updates directly to the affected DOM nodes or dependent computations.
It completely bypasses the browser's main thread by executing all reactive graph evaluations inside Web Workers.
It automatically converts all RxJS Observables into native Promise chains to reduce microtask queue contention.
questions.correctAnswer: It eliminates the need to run change detection over the entire component tree by targeting updates directly to the affected DOM nodes or dependent computations.
questions.explanation: Signals provide fine-grained reactivity, allowing Angular to know precisely which components or template bindings depend on a specific value. Consequently, when a signal changes, Angular only re-evaluates the exact dependent nodes rather than traversing and checking the entire component subtree as Zone.js does.
questions.hint: Think about what Zone.js forces Angular to do globally versus what fine-grained reactive primitives know about their consumers.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular signal fine-grained reactivity performance trade-offs
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if the candidate understands the fundamental shift in Angular's rendering architecture from coarse-grained component tree traversal to fine-grained dependency graphs.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'ViewChild' decorator to query a component or directive, what is the impact of setting the 'static' option to 'true' vs 'false'?
options: If set to 'true', the element is updated automatically during every change detection cycle; if 'false', it is updated only once.
If set to 'true', the element is available in 'ngOnInit'; if 'false', it is only available in 'ngAfterViewInit'.
If set to 'true', the query ignores any elements inside *ngIf or *ngFor blocks; if 'false', it includes them.
If set to 'true', the query is performed asynchronously; if 'false', it is performed synchronously at compile time.
questions.correctAnswer: If set to 'true', the element is available in 'ngOnInit'; if 'false', it is only available in 'ngAfterViewInit'.
questions.explanation: Setting 'static: true' instructs Angular to resolve the query before change detection runs, making it available in 'ngOnInit'. Setting it to 'false' (the default for many cases) waits until change detection completes, requiring 'ngAfterViewInit' to access the element safely.
questions.hint: Think about the lifecycle hooks and when the DOM is guaranteed to be rendered.
questions.relatedConcept: ViewChild static resolution
questions.codeSnippet: @ViewChild('target', { static: false }) element!: ElementRef;
questions.interviewTip: Candidates often struggle with 'ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError' which is frequently caused by incorrect static resolution settings.

questions.question: When defining an Angular Provider using the 'useFactory' property, what is the primary purpose of the 'deps' (dependencies) array?
options: To define the order in which services are instantiated across the entire application module tree.
To register the service in the DI container so it can be tree-shaken by the Angular compiler.
To explicitly list the injection tokens required by the factory function for dependency injection.
To perform a lazy-loading check on the provided dependencies before the factory is executed.
questions.correctAnswer: To explicitly list the injection tokens required by the factory function for dependency injection.
questions.explanation: The 'deps' array tells the Dependency Injection system which services or tokens to inject into the factory function as arguments. Without this, the DI container would not know which instances to pass to the factory function.
questions.hint: The factory function needs to receive its arguments from somewhere.
questions.relatedConcept: Dependency Injection Factory Providers
questions.codeSnippet: { provide: ServiceA, useFactory: (s: ServiceB) => new ServiceA(s), deps: [ServiceB] }
questions.interviewTip: Understanding factory providers is crucial for advanced DI scenarios, like conditional service instantiation or configuring third-party libraries.

questions.question: When utilizing the `ViewContainerRef.createEmbeddedView()` method to instantiate a template, what happens to the template's internal state if the host component is destroyed before the view is detached?
options: The view remains in the DOM until manually removed by the parent component.
The view triggers a 'detached' lifecycle hook on the component.
The view remains as a memory leak until the browser process terminates.
The view is automatically destroyed and its associated nodes are removed from the DOM.
questions.correctAnswer: The view is automatically destroyed and its associated nodes are removed from the DOM.
questions.explanation: Angular's ViewContainerRef manages the lifecycle of views it creates. When the host component is destroyed, Angular recursively destroys all embedded views attached to its ViewContainerRef, ensuring that DOM nodes are cleaned up and memory is released.
questions.hint: Consider the relationship between a component's lifecycle and its child view containers.
questions.relatedConcept: Component and View lifecycle management
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how Angular handles child view clean-up is crucial for avoiding memory leaks in dynamic UI components.

questions.question: In a scenario where a child component uses the 'OnPush' change detection strategy, what is the specific effect on change detection if a parent component uses a 'ChangeDetectorRef.detectChanges()' call within an event listener?
options: It triggers change detection for the parent and its children, even if the child's input properties remain unchanged.
It triggers change detection only for the parent component, skipping OnPush children entirely.
It force-updates the child component regardless of its own OnPush configuration, but only if they share the same change detection tree.
It throws a runtime error because ChangeDetectorRef.detectChanges() is forbidden on OnPush components.
questions.correctAnswer: It triggers change detection for the parent and its children, even if the child's input properties remain unchanged.
questions.explanation: Calling detectChanges() explicitly on a component tells Angular to run change detection starting from that component downwards. This bypasses the typical OnPush 'check-only-on-input-change' restriction, forcing all child components in that subtree to undergo change detection.
questions.hint: Think about the scope of the ChangeDetectorRef methods.
questions.relatedConcept: Change detection propagation and force-checking
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate about the performance implications of manual change detection versus using AsyncPipe.

questions.question: In Angular, when utilizing the 'defer' block with the 'on viewport' trigger, which intersection observer property determines whether the deferred content is swapped back to the placeholder if the element leaves the screen?
options: The browser's native intersection ratio threshold setting specified in the defer config.
The viewport trigger behavior is strictly 'lazy-load once'; the content remains rendered once instantiated.
It is determined by the 'on idle' configuration if paired with the viewport trigger.
The internal 'isIntersecting' flag requires manual cleanup via a custom directive to revert to placeholder.
questions.correctAnswer: The viewport trigger behavior is strictly 'lazy-load once'; the content remains rendered once instantiated.
questions.explanation: The Angular @defer block with the 'on viewport' trigger is designed for lazy loading. Once the deferred block is loaded and rendered, the placeholder is removed permanently. It does not natively toggle back to the placeholder when the element leaves the viewport.
questions.hint: Think about the lifecycle of lazy-loaded components in the defer block.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Deferrable Views
questions.codeSnippet: @defer (on viewport) { <large-component /> } @placeholder { <loader /> }
questions.interviewTip: Assess if the candidate understands that deferrable views are for optimization (loading performance), not for dynamic visibility toggling.

questions.question: When using 'ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush', which specific action results in the component NOT being marked for check by the Angular change detector?
options: Updating the reference of a deep property inside an object passed as an Input.
Triggering a DOM event bound via (@event) inside the component template.
Executing an asynchronous 'setTimeout' that updates a class member property.
Invoking 'ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck()' from within a service subscription.
questions.correctAnswer: Executing an asynchronous 'setTimeout' that updates a class member property.
questions.explanation: OnPush only marks a component for check on: Input reference changes, AsyncPipe emissions, or explicit detector triggers. A standard 'setTimeout' callback does not notify the detector unless manually triggered, unlike DOM events which are intercepted by Zone.js.
questions.hint: Remember that Zone.js wraps browser events, but doesn't track arbitrary timer callbacks automatically for OnPush components.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Change Detection Strategy
questions.codeSnippet: @Component({ changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush }) class DataComponent { @Input() data: any; }
questions.interviewTip: Distinguish between Zone.js event patching and the internal behavior of the OnPush change detection mechanism.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush' strategy, which specific lifecycle hook or event triggers a check if the component's input reference has not changed?
options: The component is automatically checked after every microtask completion regardless of event sources.
The component is checked every time the parent component's ngDoCheck runs, regardless of input state.
The component is checked only when the 'ngAfterContentChecked' hook is invoked by the renderer.
The component is only checked when an Input reference changes, an event originated from the component/children occurs, or markForCheck() is called.
questions.correctAnswer: The component is only checked when an Input reference changes, an event originated from the component/children occurs, or markForCheck() is called.
questions.explanation: OnPush strategy disables automatic check-on-every-event, restricting the change detection cycle to: Input reference changes, event listeners attached to the template, or manual signals like markForCheck().
questions.hint: Think about the mechanism that forces a check in a strategy designed for performance optimization.
questions.relatedConcept: OnPush Change Detection triggers
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands performance optimization boundaries in Angular.

questions.question: In the context of Angular Dependency Injection, what is the primary behavior difference between 'viewProviders' and 'providers' within a component's decorator?
options: Services defined in 'viewProviders' are inaccessible to projected content (ng-content), whereas 'providers' are accessible to all children.
Services in 'viewProviders' are singleton-scoped, while 'providers' are prototype-scoped per component instance.
There is no difference in runtime behavior; 'viewProviders' is merely a deprecated alias for 'providers'.
Services in 'viewProviders' are automatically destroyed when the view is detached, while 'providers' persist until the component is destroyed.
questions.correctAnswer: Services defined in 'viewProviders' are inaccessible to projected content (ng-content), whereas 'providers' are accessible to all children.
questions.explanation: viewProviders scope services specifically to the component's internal view tree, excluding components injected via ng-content, which is a common pattern for encapsulation.
questions.hint: Consider how Dependency Injection interacts with Content Projection.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Dependency Injection Scoping
questions.interviewTip: Ask this to see if the candidate knows how to handle injection scope for reusable components with templates.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the `DestroyRef` injection token in a standalone component or service, what is the primary advantage of calling `destroyRef.onDestroy()` versus manually implementing the `OnDestroy` lifecycle hook?
options: It forces an immediate garbage collection of all injected dependencies associated with the instance.
It decouples cleanup logic from the component class, allowing it to be encapsulated within reusable providers or helper functions.
It provides a mechanism to prevent the component from being destroyed until a specific asynchronous task finishes.
It significantly improves the performance of the Change Detection cycle by bypassing the standard lifecycle queue.
questions.correctAnswer: It decouples cleanup logic from the component class, allowing it to be encapsulated within reusable providers or helper functions.
questions.explanation: DestroyRef allows for registering teardown logic outside of the class itself, facilitating better composition and reuse, whereas OnDestroy is strictly bound to the class instance.
questions.hint: Consider modularity and whether the logic needs to live inside the component class definition.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Dependency Injection and DestroyRef lifecycle management
questions.interviewTip: Ask about this to check if the candidate understands modern Angular composition patterns vs legacy class-based hooks.

questions.question: When utilizing `ChangeDetectorRef.detach()` in an Angular component, what is the specific consequence regarding the component's interaction with the global Zone.js monkey-patched events?
options: The component will immediately stop receiving event emissions from internal @Output emitters.
The component remains responsive to all browser events, but will only update the DOM if the parent component is marked as Dirty.
The component is excluded from automatic change detection cycles initiated by Zone.js, meaning it will not re-render unless explicitly triggered.
The component forces an immediate transition to an OnPush detection strategy regardless of the component's declared strategy.
questions.correctAnswer: The component is excluded from automatic change detection cycles initiated by Zone.js, meaning it will not re-render unless explicitly triggered.
questions.explanation: Detaching the change detector removes it from the tree that Angular traverses during change detection, effectively silencing automatic updates until reattached or manually triggered.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the change detection tree when a node is detached.
questions.relatedConcept: Manual Change Detection control
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands the boundaries of Zone.js and manual performance optimizations.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'defer' block with the 'on idle' trigger, what determines the timing of the content rendering?
options: The content renders immediately after the component's ngOnInit cycle completes.
The content renders only when the user scrolls the defer element into the viewport.
The content renders after a hardcoded 500ms delay to ensure main thread stability.
The content renders after the browser's requestIdleCallback is invoked.
questions.correctAnswer: The content renders after the browser's requestIdleCallback is invoked.
questions.explanation: The 'on idle' trigger leverages the browser's native requestIdleCallback API, which schedules the defer block's content to load when the main thread is not heavily utilized, optimizing perceived performance. Option 2 is incorrect because it relates to component lifecycle, not idle-time scheduling.
questions.hint: Think about how modern browsers schedule non-urgent tasks during quiet periods.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Deferrable Views
questions.codeSnippet: @defer (on idle) { <heavy-component /> }
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate how deferrable views impact Core Web Vitals to assess their architectural knowledge.

questions.question: What is the consequence of modifying a Signal's value during the 'effect' execution phase when 'allowSignalWrites' is not explicitly enabled?
options: Angular throws a runtime error preventing circular dependencies and infinite feedback loops.
The effect executes silently but the change is batched until the next microtask.
The signal update triggers a nested change detection cycle that updates the DOM synchronously.
The effect is automatically converted into a computed property to maintain state consistency.
questions.correctAnswer: Angular throws a runtime error preventing circular dependencies and infinite feedback loops.
questions.explanation: Angular's 'effect' function is designed to prevent side effects that create infinite loops. Writing to a signal inside an effect that is subscribed to that same signal without explicit 'allowSignalWrites: true' triggers a runtime error. Option 1 is incorrect because Angular prevents this by design, it does not batch or convert it.
questions.hint: Consider the relationship between change detection cycles and circular reactivity.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Signals and Side Effects
questions.codeSnippet: effect(() => { count.set(count() + 1); });
questions.interviewTip: Use this to see if the candidate understands the difference between reactive triggers and side-effect management in Angular.

questions.question: In an Angular application, when a component implements the 'AfterContentChecked' lifecycle hook, why might you observe unexpected template flickering or 'ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError' when updating a parent-provided property within that hook?
options: The hook is intended to be synchronous, but the DOM rendering engine treats any property assignment inside it as an asynchronous microtask.
The hook runs after the change detection cycle has already verified the view, and modifying state here triggers a new verification cycle that conflicts with the previous one.
The 'AfterContentChecked' hook only fires when the parent component explicitly invokes a manual change detection update via ChangeDetectorRef.
The hook does not have access to the component's internal state unless the component is decorated with the @Injectable decorator.
questions.correctAnswer: The hook runs after the change detection cycle has already verified the view, and modifying state here triggers a new verification cycle that conflicts with the previous one.
questions.explanation: AfterContentChecked runs after the change detection run for the component's content has completed. Changing state here modifies the view model after it has been checked, violating the unidirectional data flow principle and causing the runtime error in development mode.
questions.hint: Consider the order of operations in the Angular change detection cycle and the unidirectional data flow requirement.
questions.relatedConcept: Lifecycle hook execution timing and change detection constraints
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands that lifecycle hooks are not just event triggers, but have specific implications for Angular's internal state reconciliation.

questions.question: When utilizing the 'provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()' configuration in Angular 18+, what is the fundamental impact on how the application handles template updates compared to the traditional Zone.js approach?
options: The entire component tree is automatically checked every 16ms to ensure synchronization without needing Zone.js hooks.
Angular reverts to a polling mechanism that inspects the DOM for changes rather than tracking object state mutations.
Template updates only occur when Signals used in the template are updated or when markForCheck() is manually called.
Change detection becomes strictly reactive, forcing all templates to be wrapped in an 'Observable' wrapper or they will fail to compile.
questions.correctAnswer: Template updates only occur when Signals used in the template are updated or when markForCheck() is manually called.
questions.explanation: Zoneless change detection removes the reliance on monkey-patching asynchronous APIs (Zone.js). Instead, it relies on explicit signals or manual marking of components as dirty, leading to more predictable performance and smaller bundle sizes.
questions.hint: Think about what replaces the 'global' notification system that Zone.js provided.
questions.relatedConcept: Zoneless Angular architecture and Signal-based reactivity
questions.interviewTip: Zoneless is the modern direction of Angular. Expect senior developers to know that it shifts the responsibility of change detection from the framework's global monkey-patching to local signal notification.

questions.question: When utilizing the 'inject()' function in Angular outside of a constructor or field initializer, specifically within a lifecycle hook like 'ngOnInit', what is the expected outcome?
options: The injection succeeds normally, as 'inject()' is designed to be called at any point in the component lifecycle.
The injection succeeds, but the 'DataService' instance is only available until 'ngOnInit' completes.
The 'inject()' call results in a compile-time error, as the function is restricted to constructor usage only.
The injection fails and throws an error because 'inject()' can only be called during the instantiation phase of an injection context.
questions.correctAnswer: The injection fails and throws an error because 'inject()' can only be called during the instantiation phase of an injection context.
questions.explanation: The 'inject()' function relies on the active injection context, which is only available during the component's construction phase. Calling it in 'ngOnInit' or other lifecycle hooks occurs after the injection context has been cleared, resulting in a runtime error.
questions.hint: Consider the lifecycle of the dependency injection context versus the lifecycle of an Angular component.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Injection Context limitations
questions.interviewTip: Understanding DI limitations prevents runtime errors when transitioning from constructor-based DI to functional injection.

questions.question: What is the primary technical consequence of using 'ChangeDetectorRef.detach()' on an Angular component that is part of a parent component utilizing the 'Default' change detection strategy?
options: The component is removed from the change detection tree, meaning its own 'check' and all child checks are skipped until 'detectChanges()' is called manually.
The component remains in the change detection tree but its template is never re-rendered.
The component remains in the tree, but input properties (via @Input) will no longer trigger automatic updates in the component template.
The component is destroyed, and all of its current state and references are wiped from the DOM immediately.
questions.correctAnswer: The component is removed from the change detection tree, meaning its own 'check' and all child checks are skipped until 'detectChanges()' is called manually.
questions.explanation: Detaching a component removes it from the change detection tree. Angular's change detection mechanism will skip that component subtree during subsequent cycles, requiring manual triggering via 'detectChanges()' to update the view.
questions.hint: Think about how detach() affects the propagation of the change detection tree.
questions.relatedConcept: Manual Change Detection control
questions.interviewTip: This is a critical concept for performance optimization in high-frequency update scenarios.

questions.question: In an Angular application using the 'OnPush' change detection strategy, which of the following scenarios will force a component to perform change detection without an explicit call to 'ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck()'?
options: An asynchronous event triggered by a standard DOM listener (e.g., 'window.resize') that is not wrapped in a Zone.js task.
An event originating from a template-bound event listener, such as a '(click)' handler.
An update to an 'Input()' property where the reference remains identical but the internal state of the object changes.
A timer created using the native 'window.setTimeout' function outside of the Angular Zone.
questions.correctAnswer: An event originating from a template-bound event listener, such as a '(click)' handler.
questions.explanation: Angular's Zone.js patches asynchronous browser events. When an event listener is defined in a template (like '(click)'), the event is executed within the Angular Zone, which automatically triggers change detection across the component tree, even for OnPush components. Option 3 is correct because it is the standard way to trigger detection. Options 1 and 4 do not trigger detection unless they are inside the NgZone, and Option 2 is incorrect because OnPush only reacts to reference changes in @Input properties.
questions.hint: Consider which asynchronous triggers are automatically patched by Angular's Zone.js.
questions.relatedConcept: OnPush Change Detection and Zone.js
questions.interviewTip: Understand that OnPush components are not 'isolated'—they are just skipped during default change detection cycles unless specific conditions (input ref change, event listener, or explicit marking) are met.

questions.question: When utilizing the 'provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()' provider in an Angular application, how does the framework determine when to initiate a view refresh?
options: It polls the application state at a fixed 16ms interval regardless of component activity.
It requires a global 'EventEmitter' to be manually broadcasted after every service method call.
It relies on Angular's internal Signal graph to automatically schedule updates when a dependent signal value changes.
It reverts to checking every component in the DOM tree every time a 'Promise' resolves.
questions.correctAnswer: It relies on Angular's internal Signal graph to automatically schedule updates when a dependent signal value changes.
questions.explanation: In zoneless mode, Angular moves away from Zone.js-based global change detection. Instead, it leverages the reactivity provided by Signals. When a Signal value used in a template is updated, the framework is notified and schedules a targeted change detection pass for the affected components only.
questions.hint: Think about the relationship between Signals and the Angular rendering engine.
questions.relatedConcept: Zoneless Change Detection
questions.interviewTip: Zoneless architecture is the future of Angular performance. Differentiate between 'push-based' signal reactivity and 'pull-based' zone-driven detection.

questions.question: When utilizing the Angular 'TestBed.overrideComponent' method to replace a dependency in a component's provider array during unit testing, what is the primary prerequisite for this override to take effect?
options: The component must be re-compiled using 'TestBed.compileComponents()' after the override
The component's 'providers' array must be empty in the original component decorator
The override must be performed before 'TestBed.configureTestingModule' is called
The component must be defined in the 'declarations' array of the testing module
questions.correctAnswer: The component must be defined in the 'declarations' array of the testing module
questions.explanation: TestBed operations that modify metadata, such as overrideComponent, require the component to be registered in the testing module's declarations to be successfully identified and patched by the test framework.
questions.hint: Think about how TestBed resolves component metadata versus module declarations.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Unit Testing infrastructure
questions.codeSnippet:
TestBed.configureTestingModule({ declarations: [MyComp] });
TestBed.overrideComponent(MyComp, { set: { providers: [{ provide: Logger, useValue: mockLogger }] } });
questions.interviewTip: Testing complex components often requires dependency mocking; understanding how TestBed patches metadata is a key differentiator between junior and mid-level developers.

questions.question: When diagnosing a memory leak in an Angular application caused by hanging RxJS subscriptions, which mechanism in the 'takeUntil' pattern ensures the subscription is cleaned up when a component is destroyed?
options: The 'destroy$.next()' call triggers the emission that causes 'takeUntil' to complete the source observable
The Angular DI container automatically tracks and unsubscribes from all observables injected into components
The 'takeUntil' operator internally executes the 'ngOnDestroy' lifecycle hook of the component
The RxJS library automatically monitors the component's garbage collection state to invoke 'unsubscribe'
questions.correctAnswer: The 'destroy$.next()' call triggers the emission that causes 'takeUntil' to complete the source observable
questions.explanation: When the component is destroyed, calling .next() on the subject causes 'takeUntil' to catch the emission and terminate the stream, effectively unsubscribing from the source.
questions.hint: Consider the reactive flow triggered by an emission from a notifier subject.
questions.relatedConcept: Observability and Resource Management
questions.codeSnippet:
private destroy$ = new Subject<void>();
ngOnDestroy() { this.destroy$.next(); this.destroy$.complete(); }
questions.interviewTip: Memory leaks are a common production issue in Angular; verifying that candidates understand the manual lifecycle management of RxJS is crucial.

questions.question: When using `DomSanitizer` in an Angular application, which scenario demonstrates a security vulnerability resulting from improper usage of 'bypassSecurityTrust' methods?
options: The application will throw a runtime error because DomSanitizer cannot process untrusted dynamic strings.
The application is now vulnerable to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) because the input bypasses Angular's context-aware sanitization.
The application will automatically re-sanitize the output during the rendering phase, rendering the bypass ineffective.
The code is safe because Angular's template binding engine automatically validates the trust level of the injected string.
questions.correctAnswer: The application is now vulnerable to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) because the input bypasses Angular's context-aware sanitization.
questions.explanation: The bypassSecurityTrust methods explicitly instruct Angular to treat the input as safe, effectively disabling the built-in sanitization mechanism. Using it on raw user input allows malicious scripts (like ) to execute in the DOM.
questions.hint: Consider what the 'bypass' prefix signifies regarding Angular's internal security architecture.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular DomSanitizer security implications
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate how they would safely render user-provided HTML instead of using the bypass methods.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the risk of using 'ViewEncapsulation.None' in a shared UI library component?
options: The component's templates will fail to render because the CSS-in-JS compilation step requires scoped encapsulation.
Angular will disable Shadow DOM emulation for the entire application, reverting to standard HTML rendering.
Styles defined within the component will leak into the global scope and may unintentionally affect other parts of the application.
It prevents the component from inheriting global styles defined in the 'styles.css' file.
questions.correctAnswer: Styles defined within the component will leak into the global scope and may unintentionally affect other parts of the application.
questions.explanation: ViewEncapsulation.None removes the attribute-based scoping that Angular applies to styles. Consequently, CSS rules inside that component are treated as global, making them liable to collide with or override styles in unrelated parts of the app.
questions.hint: Focus on the scoping mechanism of CSS in Angular components.
questions.relatedConcept: ViewEncapsulation scope collision
questions.interviewTip: Follow up by asking how to style specific child components safely while still using ViewEncapsulation.None (e.g., host-context or global scoped classes).

questions.question: In Angular's dependency injection system, what is the specific effect of using the `self` decorator on an injection token in a component that provides that same token in its own `providers` array?
options: The component will throw a 'NullInjectorError' because @Self prevents looking at the component's own providers.
The component will ignore the local provider and look for the token in the parent component's injector.
The injection will result in 'undefined' because the provider is instantiated after the constructor execution.
The component will successfully inject the value 'Child' provided in its own array.
questions.correctAnswer: The component will successfully inject the value 'Child' provided in its own array.
questions.explanation: The @Self decorator restricts the injection search to the element's own injector. Since the component defines the token in its own providers array, it is visible to @Self. The common misconception is that @Self forces a skip of the local injector, but it actually forces the search to start AND end within the local injector.
questions.hint: Check the scope of the injector that @Self targets.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Dependency Injection Scope
questions.interviewTip: Understanding DI scopes is critical for architecting modular components that shouldn't leak or over-consume global services.

questions.question: When utilizing Angular Signals in a template, what happens to the view update cycle if a computed signal is derived from another signal that is updated synchronously multiple times within the same task?
options: The template will re-render exactly once after the task completes, reflecting the value derived from the final state.
The template will re-render three times, once for each call to count.set().
The computed signal will throw a 'CircularDependencyError' due to rapid synchronous updates.
The view will not update until an explicit 'ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck()' is called.
questions.correctAnswer: The template will re-render exactly once after the task completes, reflecting the value derived from the final state.
questions.explanation: Angular Signals are designed to be glitch-free. When a source signal is updated multiple times synchronously, the derived computed signal (and consequently the DOM) only reacts to the final state once the synchronous execution block has completed, preventing unnecessary intermediate re-renders.
questions.hint: Consider the reactive 'glitch-free' guarantee of the Signals library.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Signals Reactivity
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate how Signals differ from RxJS BehaviorSubjects regarding batching and performance.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'ViewChild' decorator with 'read: ElementRef', what specific lifecycle hook is the earliest point at which the element reference is guaranteed to be populated and queryable?
options: ngOnInit
ngAfterViewInit
ngAfterContentInit
constructor
questions.correctAnswer: ngAfterViewInit
questions.explanation: ViewChild queries are resolved after the view is initialized. 'ngOnInit' is too early because the component's template has not been rendered yet. 'ngAfterContentInit' relates to projected content (ng-content), not the component's own template view.
questions.hint: Consider the timing of template rendering versus content projection.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Lifecycle Hooks and ViewChild resolution
questions.codeSnippet: @ViewChild('myEl', {read: ElementRef}) myElement!: ElementRef;
questions.interviewTip: Understanding the DOM lifecycle is crucial for avoiding 'undefined' errors when manipulating DOM elements directly.

questions.question: When utilizing the 'provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection' provider in an Angular application, how does the framework determine when to run change detection?
options: Change detection continues to run on every microtask, just like Zone.js, but without the zone wrapping.
Change detection is triggered by a polling mechanism that checks for state differences every 100ms.
Change detection is triggered only by signal updates or manual request via ChangeDetectorRef.
Change detection is disabled entirely and must be handled by external browser events.
questions.correctAnswer: Change detection is triggered only by signal updates or manual request via ChangeDetectorRef.
questions.explanation: Zoneless change detection relies on reactive primitives (Signals) and explicit triggers (like markForCheck) rather than monkey-patching asynchronous browser APIs to trigger global cycles automatically.
questions.hint: Zoneless architecture shifts away from global event monkey-patching.
questions.relatedConcept: Zoneless Change Detection mechanism
questions.interviewTip: This is a forward-looking question testing awareness of Angular's evolution away from Zone.js dependency.

questions.question: In Angular, what is the specific consequence of defining an injection token with `providedIn: 'root'` while simultaneously including that same service in the `providers` array of a lazy-loaded feature module?
options: Angular will throw a runtime error indicating a circular dependency during the lazy-loading process.
The application will override the root provider, causing the service to be destroyed and re-initialized as a module-scoped singleton.
The root provider will continue to be used as a singleton across the entire application, and the provider in the lazy-loaded module will be ignored.
The lazy-loaded module will instantiate its own separate instance of the service, effectively creating a singleton for that module hierarchy.
questions.correctAnswer: The lazy-loaded module will instantiate its own separate instance of the service, effectively creating a singleton for that module hierarchy.
questions.explanation: Angular's dependency injection system treats providers defined in a module's 'providers' array as a new, local injection scope. Even if the service is marked 'providedIn: root', adding it to a 'providers' array in a module causes the DI system to create a new instance local to that injector, effectively breaking the singleton pattern.
questions.hint: Think about how Angular resolves providers when they exist in multiple scopes.
questions.relatedConcept: Dependency Injection Scope and Singleton Pattern violations
questions.interviewTip: This tests if a candidate understands the hierarchical nature of Angular's DI system versus the newer tree-shakable provider syntax.

questions.question: When utilizing `ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck()` inside a component using `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`, what exactly is the effect on the component's child components?
options: It marks the entire component sub-tree, starting from the current component, as dirty, forcing change detection on all descendants regardless of their strategy.
It only forces a change detection check on the current component itself; children are only checked if they have their own inputs modified.
It effectively converts the component and all children to the 'Default' change detection strategy for the remainder of the application lifecycle.
It clears the component's internal state and forces a complete re-render of the DOM nodes associated with the component's template.
questions.correctAnswer: It marks the entire component sub-tree, starting from the current component, as dirty, forcing change detection on all descendants regardless of their strategy.
questions.explanation: Calling 'markForCheck()' tells Angular's change detection mechanism that the component (and its entire sub-tree) needs to be checked during the next cycle, effectively bypassing the 'OnPush' optimization for the current cycle until the process reaches the component.
questions.hint: Consider the propagation behavior of the change detection tree in Angular.
questions.relatedConcept: Change Detection propagation under OnPush strategy
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how OnPush interacts with the component tree is critical for performance tuning; this differentiates developers who know the syntax from those who understand the framework internals.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush' component strategy, what is the specific consequence of directly mutating an object property bound in the template (e.g., 'this.user.name = "New"') compared to replacing the object (e.g., 'this.user = { ...this.user, name: "New" }')?
options: The template will update only if the parent component also uses OnPush.
The template will not update because the component reference check fails to detect the mutation.
The change is automatically reflected because Angular performs deep object comparison by default.
The template will update because Angular instruments all object property assignments in the constructor.
questions.correctAnswer: The template will not update because the component reference check fails to detect the mutation.
questions.explanation: OnPush strategy relies on reference checking (referential equality) rather than deep-tree traversal. If an object is mutated, its reference remains identical, so Angular's check returns false, and the view is not updated. Replacing the object reference triggers the check.
questions.hint: Consider how Angular determines whether to trigger change detection in OnPush components.
questions.relatedConcept: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush and Reference Equality
questions.interviewTip: Understanding OnPush is critical for performance tuning; ensure the candidate knows why deep-mutating objects breaks reactive UI updates.

questions.question: In Angular, what is the precise runtime lifecycle order when an injection token is resolved via `inject()` inside a component's field initializer compared to constructor injection?
options: Constructor injection executes before field initializers because TypeScript compiles constructor parameters first.
Field initializers using inject() execute before the constructor body, but both occur during the component instantiation phase before ngOnInit.
Field initializers using inject() execute after the constructor body completes.
inject() can only be called inside the constructor; calling it in a field initializer throws a runtime dependency injection context error.
questions.correctAnswer: Field initializers using inject() execute before the constructor body, but both occur during the component instantiation phase before ngOnInit.
questions.explanation: Field initializers in TypeScript classes are evaluated in the order they are written in the class body, which happens during the instantiation of the class instance, prior to the execution of the constructor body. The inject() function relies on the active injection context established when the component factory instantiates the class, which is active during both field initialization and constructor execution.
questions.hint: Think about TypeScript class property initialization order relative to the constructor.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular inject() function initialization lifecycle context
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates truly understand TypeScript class compilation semantics combined with Angular's reactive injection context.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'OnPush' change detection strategy, which of the following scenarios will trigger a change detection check for a component?
options: A public property of the component class is updated directly from within a standard 'setTimeout' callback.
An @Input property value changes when passed via an Observable using the 'async' pipe.
A nested child component's internal state changes due to a user event, if the child uses the default change detection strategy.
A global service variable injected into the component is mutated directly from another component.
questions.correctAnswer: An @Input property value changes when passed via an Observable using the 'async' pipe.
questions.explanation: The OnPush strategy disables automatic change detection for the component unless an @Input reference changes, an event originates from within the component (or its children), or an Observable marked with the async pipe emits a new value. Simply changing a local property via setTimeout or a service mutation will not trigger re-rendering in OnPush components without manual intervention (ChangeDetectorRef).
questions.hint: Consider how the async pipe interacts with the component's change detection cycle under OnPush.
questions.relatedConcept: OnPush Change Detection Strategy
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate how they would force an update in an OnPush component if the input reference does not change.

questions.question: When using the Angular 'AsyncPipe' in a template with an Observable, what is the precise behavior of the pipe when the component is destroyed?
options: The AsyncPipe keeps the subscription active until the browser session ends.
The AsyncPipe automatically unsubscribes from the Observable, preventing memory leaks.
The AsyncPipe throws an error because manual unsubscription is required via OnDestroy.
The AsyncPipe detaches the change detector but maintains the subscription.
questions.correctAnswer: The AsyncPipe automatically unsubscribes from the Observable, preventing memory leaks.
questions.explanation: The AsyncPipe is designed to manage the subscription lifecycle automatically. When the component or directive is destroyed, the AsyncPipe performs an internal cleanup by unsubscribing from the source Observable, which is a key advantage over manual subscription management.
questions.hint: Think about how Angular manages the lifecycle of subscriptions declared directly in templates.
questions.relatedConcept: AsyncPipe Lifecycle Management
questions.codeSnippet: {{ data$ | async }}
questions.interviewTip: This tests if a candidate understands Angular's built-in memory management patterns versus manual subscription handling.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'async' pipe with an Observable, what happens to the subscription if the component containing the pipe is destroyed?
options: The subscription remains active unless manually unsubscribed in ngOnDestroy.
The async pipe automatically unsubscribes, preventing memory leaks.
The subscription is paused but remains active until the application terminates.
The observable is completed, but the subscription is not destroyed.
questions.correctAnswer: The async pipe automatically unsubscribes, preventing memory leaks.
questions.explanation: The 'async' pipe is specifically designed to manage the lifecycle of the subscription for the provided Observable or Promise. It automatically subscribes when the component is initialized and unsubscribes when the component is destroyed, making it a best practice for preventing memory leaks.
questions.hint: Think about the lifecycle management responsibilities of Angular's built-in pipes.
questions.relatedConcept: Async Pipe Lifecycle
questions.codeSnippet: {{ data$ | async }}
questions.interviewTip: This question tests if the candidate understands automated resource management in Angular versus manual subscription handling.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'OnPush' change detection strategy, which of the following scenarios will trigger a change detection cycle for that component?
options: An asynchronous event outside of the component, such as a setTimeout, completes.
An Observable input bound to the component emits a new value.
A property on a nested object within the component's state is mutated directly.
An event is triggered by a child component that does not propagate to the parent.
questions.correctAnswer: An Observable input bound to the component emits a new value.
questions.explanation: With OnPush, Angular only checks the component if an @Input reference changes, an event originated from the component or its children, or an AsyncPipe emits a new value. Option 0 covers the Input reference change. Option 1 is incorrect because OnPush ignores global async tasks unless they are inside the component's view. Option 2 is incorrect because Angular does not track nested object mutations in OnPush. Option 3 is incorrect because standard bubbling does not necessarily trigger change detection for the parent unless specifically handled.
questions.hint: Focus on the triggers that Angular's change detector watches when OnPush is enabled.
questions.relatedConcept: OnPush Change Detection Strategy
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands the performance implications and specific triggers of Angular's optimized change detection mechanism.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'async' pipe with an Observable, what happens to the subscription if the component containing the pipe is destroyed?
options: The subscription remains active, requiring manual unsubscription in ngOnDestroy.
The async pipe automatically unsubscribes, preventing memory leaks.
The async pipe does not create a subscription until the component is initialized.
The subscription is transferred to the parent component automatically.
questions.correctAnswer: The async pipe automatically unsubscribes, preventing memory leaks.
questions.explanation: The 'async' pipe is specifically designed to manage the lifecycle of Observables. It automatically subscribes when the component is initialized and unsubscribes when the component is destroyed, eliminating the need for boilerplate cleanup logic.
questions.hint: Consider the primary benefit of using built-in pipes over manual subscriptions in components.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Pipe Lifecycle and Observable management
questions.codeSnippet: {{ data$ | async }}
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands how Angular handles reactive patterns and resource management, which is crucial for preventing memory leaks in large applications.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush' strategy, which of the following scenarios will trigger a re-run of change detection for that component?
options: A property of an object passed as an @Input() is modified directly (e.g., this.data.value = 5).
An Observable input property emits a new value, provided the component uses the AsyncPipe in its template.
A global timer (setTimeout) fires within the component instance without utilizing the AsyncPipe or explicit ChangeDetectorRef calls.
The component's parent component triggers change detection, regardless of the input data state.
questions.correctAnswer: An Observable input property emits a new value, provided the component uses the AsyncPipe in its template.
questions.explanation: With OnPush, Angular only checks the component if an @Input reference changes, an event originated from the component/children, or an AsyncPipe emits a new value. Since AsyncPipe internally calls markForCheck(), it correctly triggers the check even if the object reference itself is the same. Mutating an object property does not change the reference, so it does not trigger a check.
questions.hint: Consider how the AsyncPipe interacts with the component's change detection cycle.
questions.relatedConcept: OnPush Change Detection Strategy
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands the difference between reference-based input changes and reactive stream updates in Angular.

questions.question: In Angular's dependency injection system, when a service is provided in a feature module's 'providers' array while that module is loaded via 'loadChildren' (lazy loading), what is the impact on service instance scoping?
options: The service is automatically promoted to the root application injector to ensure consistency.
The service becomes a child-injector singleton, distinct from the root-injector singleton.
The service will fail to inject unless it is also listed in the main AppModule providers.
The service behaves as a global singleton across the entire application once loaded.
questions.correctAnswer: The service becomes a child-injector singleton, distinct from the root-injector singleton.
questions.explanation: When a module is lazy-loaded, Angular creates a child injector for that module. Services provided in the 'providers' array of a lazy-loaded module are scoped to that child injector, meaning they are separate instances from any services provided in the root application injector.
questions.hint: Consider the relationship between lazy loading and Angular's hierarchical dependency injection system.
questions.relatedConcept: Hierarchical Dependency Injection
questions.interviewTip: Understanding DI hierarchy is crucial for senior roles; it distinguishes candidates who understand Angular's architecture from those who only know the basics.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush' strategy, which of the following scenarios will trigger a view update for the component?
options: An asynchronous event (like a setTimeout) triggers inside the component's class.
An Observable input property emits a new value, and the component subscribes to it using the 'async' pipe.
An object passed as an @Input is mutated internally (e.g., this.user.name = 'New Name').
A service injected into the component emits a value via a Subject that is not bound to an @Input.
questions.correctAnswer: An Observable input property emits a new value, and the component subscribes to it using the 'async' pipe.
questions.explanation: OnPush strategy only checks for changes if an @Input reference changes, an event originated from the component or its children occurs, or an Observable marked with the async pipe emits. Mutation of an object reference does not trigger change detection because the reference itself has not changed. A service emission does not trigger change detection unless an event listener or the async pipe is involved.
questions.hint: OnPush change detection focuses on input reference changes and the async pipe.
questions.relatedConcept: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush
questions.interviewTip: Ask this to ensure the candidate understands the performance implications and the specific contract of OnPush change detection.

questions.question: In Angular, setting a component's `changeDetection` property to `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush` changes the default change detection behavior. Which of the following statements best describes this effect?
options: The component's change detection is completely disabled, and the view will never update.
The component is checked only when one of its @Input properties receives a new object reference or when an event originated inside the component triggers change detection.
The component is checked on every browser repaint, regardless of input changes or events.
The component will be checked only after the developer manually calls `ChangeDetectorRef.detectChanges()`.
questions.correctAnswer: The component is checked only when one of its @Input properties receives a new object reference or when an event originated inside the component triggers change detection.
questions.explanation: OnPush tells Angular to run change detection for that component only when its input bindings change by reference, when an event originates inside the component, or when an observable bound with the async pipe emits. It does not disable detection, nor does it run on every repaint. Manual detection is optional but not required for typical OnPush usage.
questions.hint: Consider what Angular monitors to decide a component needs checking under OnPush.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Change Detection Strategies
questions.interviewTip: Helps gauge the candidate's understanding of performance optimizations and when to use OnPush.

questions.question: What is the primary difference in behavior between Angular's `HostBinding` decorator and standard element property binding within a component template?
options: HostBinding operates asynchronously via microtasks, while template bindings update synchronously during the change detection cycle.
HostBinding binds properties on the host element of the directive or component, whereas template binding targets elements inside the component's own template.
HostBinding can only bind to standard HTML attributes, whereas template binding supports custom component inputs.
HostBinding automatically sanitizes all CSS values, whereas template binding bypasses the DOM sanitizer for style properties.
questions.correctAnswer: HostBinding binds properties on the host element of the directive or component, whereas template binding targets elements inside the component's own template.
questions.explanation: The @HostBinding decorator allows a directive or component to bind properties, attributes, or styles directly to its own host element (the element on which the directive/component is placed). Standard template bindings, conversely, apply to elements contained within the component's HTML template.
questions.hint: Think about where the target element resides relative to the directive or component containing the decorator.
questions.relatedConcept: HostBinding decorator mechanics
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check your understanding of host elements versus encapsulated component templates in Angular directives.

questions.question: When using Angular's reactive forms, what is the precise operational difference between using 'setValue()' versus 'patchValue()' on a FormGroup?
options: patchValue() triggers valueChanges events recursively down the tree while setValue() silently updates values without triggering events.
setValue() requires every control in the model to be defined and throws an error if any are missing, whereas patchValue() allows updating a subset of controls without strict checking.
setValue() automatically sanitizes input strings against XSS attacks, whereas patchValue() accepts raw unescaped strings.
patchValue() updates form control states asynchronously, whereas setValue() executes all validations synchronously on the main thread.
questions.correctAnswer: setValue() requires every control in the model to be defined and throws an error if any are missing, whereas patchValue() allows updating a subset of controls without strict checking.
questions.explanation: setValue() enforces that the object passed must match the exact structure of the FormGroup, throwing an error if any control is missing or extra. patchValue() allows updating a subset of properties within the form model, gracefully ignoring missing controls.
questions.hint: Think about strictness and structural completeness when updating form group states.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular Reactive Forms setValue vs patchValue
questions.codeSnippet: this.formGroup.patchValue({ firstName: 'Alice' });
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers frequently ask this to ensure developers know how to safely and partially update form models without triggering runtime structural errors.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'AsyncPipe' on an Observable, which of the following lifecycle behaviors correctly describes how the subscription is handled?
options: The pipe creates a new subscription every time the change detection cycle marks the component for check.
The pipe subscribes to the Observable when the component is initialized and automatically unsubscribes when the component is destroyed.
The pipe manually manages the subscription, requiring the developer to call 'unsubscribe()' in the 'ngOnDestroy' lifecycle hook.
The pipe keeps the subscription alive until the Observable emits a 'complete' notification, ignoring the component lifecycle.
questions.correctAnswer: The pipe subscribes to the Observable when the component is initialized and automatically unsubscribes when the component is destroyed.
questions.explanation: The AsyncPipe is specifically designed to handle the subscription lifecycle automatically. It subscribes to the passed observable (or promise) when the component is initialized or the pipe is created, and it performs an automatic unsubscription when the component is destroyed, preventing memory leaks.
questions.hint: Consider the primary benefit of using AsyncPipe over manual subscribe() calls.
questions.relatedConcept: AsyncPipe Lifecycle Management
questions.interviewTip: This tests the candidate's understanding of memory management and their knowledge of built-in Angular tools that simplify common architectural patterns.

questions.question: In an Angular component using OnPush change detection, which of the following scenarios will trigger a re-render of the component template?
options: The parent component modifies a property of the 'user' object (e.g., user.name = 'New').
The parent component updates the 'user' input reference with a new object.
A service injected into the component emits a value via a Subject, without updating the 'user' reference.
The component calls its own 'ChangeDetectorRef.detectChanges()' method within a 'setTimeout' block.
questions.correctAnswer: The parent component updates the 'user' input reference with a new object.
questions.explanation: OnPush change detection in Angular is triggered primarily by input property reference changes (using strict equality check), events originating from the component template, or manual markForCheck calls. Modifying the property of an existing object (mutating) does not trigger a change detection cycle because the object reference remains the same. Manual detection changes (like detectChanges) typically happen inside the component's own lifecycle or event handlers; however, referencing the 'user' input object change is the primary structural mechanism defined by Angular's OnPush strategy.
questions.hint: OnPush change detection relies on shallow reference equality checks for @Input properties.
questions.relatedConcept: OnPush Change Detection Strategy
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate how they would force an update in an OnPush component if the underlying object reference must remain constant.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'AsyncPipe' with an Observable in a template, what happens to the subscription if the component is destroyed?
options: The component must manually unsubscribe in the 'ngOnDestroy' lifecycle hook to avoid memory leaks.
The AsyncPipe automatically unsubscribes from the Observable, preventing memory leaks.
The subscription remains active until the entire application is reloaded or the browser tab is closed.
The Observable is converted to a Promise, and the subscription is automatically handled by the browser's Garbage Collector.
questions.correctAnswer: The AsyncPipe automatically unsubscribes from the Observable, preventing memory leaks.
questions.explanation: The AsyncPipe is designed to manage the lifecycle of the subscription automatically. It subscribes to the Observable when the component is initialized and automatically calls .unsubscribe() when the component is destroyed, which is a best practice for avoiding memory leaks.
questions.hint: Think about how Angular manages the lifecycle of pipes tied to component views.
questions.relatedConcept: AsyncPipe lifecycle management
questions.codeSnippet: {{ data }}
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how the AsyncPipe handles subscriptions is crucial for demonstrating knowledge of memory management and cleaner code in Angular applications.

questions.question: In Angular, when using the 'ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush' setting on a component, what is the specific condition under which Angular will skip the change detection check for that component during a tick?
options: The component does not implement the OnInit lifecycle hook.
The component's input references remain unchanged and no event originating from the component or its children triggers the check.
The component's internal state variables have been modified directly, but the parent component has not triggered a change detection cycle.
The component is currently hidden using CSS 'display: none'.
questions.correctAnswer: The component's input references remain unchanged and no event originating from the component or its children triggers the check.
questions.explanation: OnPush strategy optimizes performance by skipping change detection for a component unless an @Input reference changes, an event originated from the component/children, or an Observable marked with the 'async' pipe emits a new value. Simply changing internal state or DOM visibility does not trigger the check.
questions.hint: Think about how Angular decides when to traverse the component tree during change detection.
questions.relatedConcept: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush internals
questions.interviewTip: Use this to evaluate if the candidate understands the performance implications of Angular's zone-based change detection and how to manually signal intent for updates.

questions.question: In Angular, a component is declared with `changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`. Which of the following statements correctly describes when this component's view will be checked for updates?
options: Whenever any change occurs anywhere in the application, just like the default strategy.
Only when one of its @Input properties receives a new reference value, when it emits an event, or when an observable bound in the template emits a new value.
Never, the component's view will not be checked after the initial rendering.
Only when a global timer (e.g., setInterval) triggers change detection manually.
questions.correctAnswer: Only when one of its @Input properties receives a new reference value, when it emits an event, or when an observable bound in the template emits a new value.
questions.explanation: OnPush tells Angular to skip this component during the regular change‑detection run unless one of the listed conditions occurs: a changed @Input reference, an event originated from the component, or an async pipe/observable in the template emits. The other options describe the default strategy, a non‑functional behavior, or a specific manual trigger, which are incorrect.
questions.hint: Think about what triggers change detection for OnPush components.
questions.relatedConcept: Angular change detection strategies (OnPush vs Default)
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to see if candidates understand performance‑optimizing patterns and the mechanics behind Angular's change detection.

title: AutoCAD - Test 1: Core Fundamentals & Patterns
