questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates understand that `React.memo` only prevents re-renders if prop references remain strictly identical, and that inline closures defeat prop stability.

questions.question: [React • Test 1 • Q28] Why does calling `ReactDOM.unmountComponentAtNode` or returning a cleanup function from `useEffect` that updates state on an unmounted component cause a memory leak warning in modern React?
options: The asynchronous callback retains a closure reference to the component fiber, preventing garbage collection of the entire unmounted tree until the promise settles and state updates.
React's internal scheduler continuously polls unmounted components to check if their state setters have been invoked.
JavaScript engines reserve permanent stack memory for any function that calls a React state updater.
The browser's event loop locks the thread indefinitely waiting for the unmounted component to re-attach.
questions.correctAnswer: The asynchronous callback retains a closure reference to the component fiber, preventing garbage collection of the entire unmounted tree until the promise settles and state updates.
questions.explanation: When an async operation holds a reference to a state setter inside its closure, the garbage collector cannot reclaim the component fiber and associated DOM nodes until the async task completes and the state update executes on an unmounted component, triggering React's warning.
questions.hint: Think about closures holding onto component scope references while waiting for an asynchronous task to finish.
questions.relatedConcept: Asynchronous state updates on unmounted components and closure memory retention
questions.interviewTip: Often asked to evaluate a candidate's practical experience with asynchronous side effects and cleanup patterns in React hooks.

questions.question: [React • Test 1 • Q29] What is the primary architectural reason that performing state updates directly inside a React component's render phase (rather than inside an effect or event handler) causes performance bottlenecks or infinite loops?
options: It immediately flushes synchronous DOM mutations, bypassing React's fiber reconciliation and triggering rapid browser repaints.
It invalidates the virtual DOM tree and forces React to repeatedly abort and restart the render pass until the trigger condition ceases, which can lock the main thread.
It permanently leaks memory in the React Fiber reconciler by creating uncollected component instance descriptors.
It disables concurrent rendering optimizations permanently for the entire React root subtree.
questions.correctAnswer: It invalidates the virtual DOM tree and forces React to repeatedly abort and restart the render pass until the trigger condition ceases, which can lock the main thread.
questions.explanation: State updates schedule a new render pass. If called unconditionally during render, each pass triggers another update immediately, leading to an infinite cascade where React repeatedly invalidates the current render frame and exhausts the main JavaScript call stack or traps the thread.
questions.hint: Think about what a state setter does when invoked and how React handles re-triggering renders.
questions.relatedConcept: React Render Phase Side Effects and Infinite Render Loops
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates understand React's lifecycle phases and why side effects must be isolated from pure render execution.

questions.question: [React • Test 1 • Q30] When utilizing React 18's 'useTransition' hook for a non-urgent state update, how does React manage the priority and scheduling of the rendering work compared to concurrent urgent updates?
options: React completely defers execution of the transition callback until the network is idle and all useEffect hooks have finished resolving.
React executes the transition update in a separate Web Worker thread to keep the main UI thread completely free of computations.
React marks the state update inside 'startTransition' with low priority, allowing urgent updates (like typing or clicks) to interrupt or preempt the background render work.
React automatically debounces the transition state update by a fixed 300ms window before queuing it in the microtask queue.
questions.correctAnswer: React marks the state update inside 'startTransition' with low priority, allowing urgent updates (like typing or clicks) to interrupt or preempt the background render work.
questions.explanation: Concurrent React uses priorities to interrupt low-priority rendering (transitions) when higher-priority updates (user input, animations) occur, ensuring the UI remains responsive without dropping frames.
questions.hint: Consider how concurrent mode handles interruption between different types of state updates.
questions.relatedConcept: React 18 Concurrent Rendering and useTransition Priority
questions.interviewTip: Expect this question when discussing modern React performance optimization techniques and concurrent features.

questions.question: What is the primary risk or behavioral side effect of invoking `ReactDOM.render` (or `createRoot().render`) multiple times targeting the same container element throughout a React application's lifecycle, rather than utilizing state updates within a root component?
options: It throws a fatal hydration mismatch error if the root container was previously populated by server-side rendering.
It tears down the existing React tree, unmounting all components, destroys their local state, and reconstructs the DOM nodes from scratch.
It automatically merges the newly rendered tree with the existing virtual DOM without losing component state.
It queues an asynchronous reconciliation pass that batches updates from both roots into a single commit phase.
questions.correctAnswer: It tears down the existing React tree, unmounting all components, destroys their local state, and reconstructs the DOM nodes from scratch.
questions.explanation: Calling render multiple times on the same root container without using createRoot's proper update mechanisms or root re-hydration will cause React to unmount the entire old tree, destroying all component state and rebuilding the DOM tree anew, which defeats the purpose of the virtual DOM reconciliation algorithm.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the existing component instances and their states when a fresh render call is made to an already initialized container.
questions.relatedConcept: React DOM Root Lifecycle and Mounting Semantics
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of how React bridges the virtual DOM to real DOM containers at the very top level.

questions.question: In React, when using the 'useMemo' hook to optimize heavy computations, which of the following scenarios describes the correct behavior regarding cache invalidation and component re-renders?
options: The function 'computeExpensiveValue' re-executes if the reference of 'b' changes, even if 'a' remains the same.
The function 'computeExpensiveValue' only re-executes if the shallow equality check fails for any primitive value in the dependency array [a].
The memoized value is guaranteed to persist across component unmounts and remounts within the same session.
The function 'computeExpensiveValue' is executed during every render to determine if the result has changed compared to the previous state.
questions.correctAnswer: The function 'computeExpensiveValue' only re-executes if the shallow equality check fails for any primitive value in the dependency array [a].
questions.explanation: useMemo uses a shallow comparison (Object.is) for each item in the dependency array. If any item (in this case, 'a') has a different value based on shallow equality, the function re-runs. If 'b' changes but is not in the array, it does not trigger a re-run. Option 0 is wrong because 'b' is ignored. Option 2 is wrong because useMemo is tied to the component lifecycle. Option 3 is wrong because the function is only executed when dependencies change, not on every render.
questions.hint: Focus on how the dependency array triggers updates vs. the internal logic of the hook.
questions.relatedConcept: React Hooks Dependency Array Semantics
questions.codeSnippet: const memoizedValue = useMemo(() => computeExpensiveValue(a, b), [a]);
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how React's dependency checking works is crucial for performance optimization and avoiding common bugs like stale closures.

questions.question: In React, when using the 'useMemo' hook, what determines the cache invalidation strategy for the returned value?
options: The hook performs a deep recursive equality check on every property within the dependency array objects.
The hook performs a shallow comparison of each element in the dependency array via Object.is().
The hook re-runs the computation if the function reference itself changes, regardless of the dependency array content.
The hook evaluates the truthiness of the dependency array; if any item is falsy, the value is recomputed.
questions.correctAnswer: The hook performs a shallow comparison of each element in the dependency array via Object.is().
questions.explanation: React's useMemo (and useEffect/useCallback) internally uses Object.is() to compare each item in the dependency array with its previous value from the last render. A shallow comparison is performed; it does not perform deep equality checks for objects or arrays.
questions.hint: Think about how React determines if an item in the dependency array has 'changed' between renders.
questions.relatedConcept: Hooks Dependency Comparison
questions.codeSnippet: const memoizedValue = useMemo(() => computeExpensiveValue(a, b), [a, b]);
questions.interviewTip: Understanding the shallow comparison rule is critical for preventing unnecessary re-renders and debugging performance issues in complex React apps.

questions.question: In React, when using the 'useMemo' hook, what determines whether the cached calculation function is re-executed during a re-render?
options: The deep equality comparison of the return value of the function against its previous result.
The shallow comparison (Object.is) of every value in the dependency array against its previous state.
Whether the function reference itself has changed in memory since the last render cycle.
The execution of the component's parent lifecycle methods regardless of the dependency values.
questions.correctAnswer: The shallow comparison (Object.is) of every value in the dependency array against its previous state.
questions.explanation: React implements 'useMemo' by performing a shallow comparison (specifically Object.is) of each element in the dependency array provided. If all elements are reference-equal to their counterparts from the previous render, it returns the memoized value; otherwise, it re-runs the calculation. It does not perform deep equality, nor does it track the internal function reference.
questions.hint: Focus on how React compares the array items provided in the dependency list.
questions.relatedConcept: Memoization and dependency comparison mechanics in React hooks.
questions.codeSnippet: const memoizedValue = useMemo(() => compute(a, b), [a, b]);
questions.interviewTip: Understanding that React relies on shallow comparison is crucial for debugging performance issues, as it explains why passing new object/array literals as dependencies causes unnecessary re-renders.

questions.question: What happens when you invoke `setState` inside a React component's render phase (i.e., directly in the component body outside of an effect or event handler)?
options: React optimizes the update into a single render pass, avoiding any infinite loops automatically.
React catches the infinite update loop and throws a runtime error after exceeding the maximum update depth.
The component renders successfully once with the updated count and skips further re-renders.
JavaScript throws a Stack Overflow error immediately before React can even process the state update.
questions.correctAnswer: React catches the infinite update loop and throws a runtime error after exceeding the maximum update depth.
questions.explanation: Calling `setState` directly during the render phase causes an infinite re-render loop because every render triggers a state update, which in turn triggers another render. React detects this pattern and halts execution by throwing a 'Maximum update depth exceeded' error.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when rendering triggers another render continuously.
questions.relatedConcept: React Render Phase Side-Effects and Infinite Loops
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify if the candidate understands React's rendering lifecycle and where side-effects like state updates are legally allowed to execute.

questions.question: What happens when you pass a function to 'setState' in React, such as 'setCount(prevCount => prevCount + 1)', as opposed to passing a direct value?
options: It forces React to execute the state update synchronously on the main thread, bypassing the reconciliation queue.
It guarantees that state updates are based on the most current state value, even when updates are batched or asynchronous.
It automatically memoizes the callback function to prevent unnecessary child component re-renders.
It converts the local component state into a global shared state accessible by context providers.
questions.correctAnswer: It guarantees that state updates are based on the most current state value, even when updates are batched or asynchronous.
questions.explanation: Passing an updater function to a state setter provides access to the pending state snapshot (the accumulator of queued updates), preventing race conditions during asynchronous or batched state transitions.
questions.hint: Think about asynchronous batching and how multiple rapid state updates access prior values.
questions.relatedConcept: functional updates in useState
questions.interviewTip: Interweaves state batching mechanisms with functional programming patterns in React.

questions.question: What is the primary operational consequence when a React component's custom hook updates state immediately inside the hook body during render without any conditional guard or effect wrapping?
options: The state update is automatically batched and defers execution to the next commit phase.
React catches the infinite render loop and throws a 'Maximum update depth exceeded' error.
React bypasses the render cycle entirely and freezes the component DOM tree.
The hook safely computes the memoized value on the initial pass and skips subsequent renders.
questions.correctAnswer: React catches the infinite render loop and throws a 'Maximum update depth exceeded' error.
questions.explanation: Calling a state setter directly during the render phase causes an infinite loop because each render triggers the state update, which in turn schedules another render. React detects this excessive recursion and throws a maximum update depth error.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when a component keeps scheduling renders during its own evaluation.
questions.relatedConcept: Render-phase state updates and infinite loops
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates understand React's render lifecycle rules and where side effects or state updates are legally permitted.

questions.question: In React, consider a scenario where you pass an object literal as a prop: <Component data={{ id: 1 }} />. Why is this generally discouraged in a production environment where <Component /> is wrapped in React.memo()?
options: It triggers a reconciliation error because object literals are not valid props for memoized components.
It causes the component to re-render on every parent update because the object reference changes every render.
It prevents the parent component from updating its own state during the same event loop cycle.
It causes the React runtime to throw a warning about prop pollution in the virtual DOM.
questions.correctAnswer: It causes the component to re-render on every parent update because the object reference changes every render.
questions.explanation: When an object literal is defined inside the JSX, a new object reference is created on every render. Even if the content of the object remains identical, the shallow comparison performed by React.memo() will see it as a new prop, causing the child component to re-render unnecessarily.
questions.hint: Think about reference equality in JavaScript objects and how React.memo works.
questions.relatedConcept: Referential Equality and Memoization
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands the performance implications of object references in JSX, which is crucial for optimizing large React trees.

questions.question: In React, when using the 'useMemo' hook, what determines whether the cached value is recomputed during a render cycle?
options: The change in the identity of the function passed as the first argument to useMemo
The equality of each item in the dependency array compared to its previous value using Object.is()
Whether the component's parent has re-rendered, regardless of the dependency array values
A shallow comparison of the entire dependency array as a single object reference
questions.correctAnswer: The equality of each item in the dependency array compared to its previous value using Object.is()
questions.explanation: React uses Object.is() comparison (with the exception of some legacy differences) to determine if any element in the dependency array has changed since the last render. If any element differs, the memoized function is executed.
questions.hint: Think about how React decides if a dependency has 'changed'.
questions.relatedConcept: useMemo dependency equality check
questions.codeSnippet: const memoizedValue = useMemo(() => computeExpensiveValue(a, b), [a, b]);
questions.interviewTip: Understanding the shallow comparison mechanism of hooks is crucial for debugging performance issues and infinite loops in React.

options: `React.memo` blocks re‑renders when `step` changes, so the component never sees the new prop.
The `useCallback` dependency array is empty, so `step` is captured with its initial value and never updates.
`useState` should be initialized with `step` so that the state reflects the prop value.
The `increment` function must be defined outside the component to access the latest `step`.
questions.correctAnswer: The `useCallback` dependency array is empty, so `step` is captured with its initial value and never updates.
questions.explanation: Because the dependency array of `useCallback` is empty, the callback closes over the `step` value from the first render. Subsequent updates to the `step` prop do not cause the callback to be recreated, so it always adds the stale initial step. Adding `step` to the dependency array fixes the issue. The other options misunderstand how `React.memo`, `useState`, and function placement work.
questions.hint: Consider what values a closure captures when the dependency array is empty.
questions.relatedConcept: React Hook dependency arrays and stale closures
questions.interviewTip: This question reveals whether the candidate understands how hooks capture values and the pitfalls of missing dependencies.

questions.question: In React 18+, when a component re-renders and passes a new object literal as a prop to a child wrapped in `React.memo`, what is the definitive condition for the child to skip re-rendering?
options: The child skips re-rendering if the JSON stringification of the object matches the previous render.
The child re-renders because the object literal creates a new reference identity, causing `Object.is` comparison in `React.memo` to fail.
The child skips re-rendering if the object's property values are identical to the previous render, regardless of reference.
The child skips re-rendering if it has not been explicitly updated via a state change within its own scope.
questions.correctAnswer: The child re-renders because the object literal creates a new reference identity, causing `Object.is` comparison in `React.memo` to fail.
questions.explanation: React.memo performs a shallow comparison using `Object.is` (similar to `===`) by default. Since an object literal `{ label: "Hi" }` creates a new reference in memory on every render of `Parent`, the comparison `prevConfig === nextConfig` evaluates to false. Consequently, `React.memo` determines the props have changed and triggers a re-render. Option B is a common misconception confusing deep equality with React's default shallow check. Option A suggests a deep equality check which is not the default behavior.
questions.hint: Consider how JavaScript handles reference types during comparison operators.
questions.relatedConcept: React.memo shallow comparison semantics and reference identity
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to verify if candidates understand that `React.memo` is not a 'deep' cache but a shallow reference check, a critical distinction for optimizing components receiving object/prop data.

title: React - Test 2: Technical Assessment
description: Test 2 for React. Every question is unique against the whole question database — no repeats, no renumbered or reworded variants of an existing question.

questions.question: What is the key functional difference between a React component that returns a custom object implementing the iterable protocol versus standard JSX elements?
options: React Fiber natively iterates over any object returning an iterator yielding JSX nodes directly from a component return value.
React considers any object without a $$typeof property as invalid, throwing an error regardless of whether it implements the iterable protocol.
React automatically flattens iterables returned directly by components into fragment-like children.
React converts the iterable into an array via Array.from during the commit phase.
questions.correctAnswer: React considers any object without a $$typeof property as invalid, throwing an error regardless of whether it implements the iterable protocol.
questions.explanation: React components must return valid React elements (which have a specific $$typeof property, e.g., Symbol.for('react.element')) or null/booleans/numbers/strings. Returning a raw iterable object directly from a component function causes React to throw an invariant/render error because it does not recognize the object as a valid renderable node.
questions.hint: Think about what React expects component return values to look like under the hood (specifically regarding internal element identifiers).
questions.relatedConcept: React component return value validation and element identification
questions.interviewTip: Use this to gauge whether the candidate understands React's internal element representation versus standard JavaScript data structures.

questions.question: When utilizing React portals (`ReactDOM.createPortal`), how does the React SyntheticEvent bubbling mechanism behave across the portal boundary?
options: Events do not bubble at all because the DOM tree hierarchy is broken.
Events bubble according to the DOM tree hierarchy (where modal-root is placed in the DOM).
Events bubble according to the React tree hierarchy (the React parent), not the DOM tree hierarchy.
Events bubble twice: once through the DOM tree and once through the React tree.
questions.correctAnswer: Events bubble according to the React tree hierarchy (the React parent), not the DOM tree hierarchy.
questions.explanation: Even though a portal child is mounted to a completely different DOM node outside the parent DOM hierarchy, React synthetic events bubble up through the React tree structure (i.e., the component tree where PortalParent is defined), not the physical DOM tree.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between the physical DOM tree and the virtual React component tree when dealing with portals.
questions.relatedConcept: React Portals and SyntheticEvent propagation behavior
questions.interviewTip: Crucial question for mid-to-senior levels when evaluating event management in complex applications involving modals and tooltips.

questions.question: What happens when an error is thrown during the rendering phase of a React component tree, and no Error Boundary component exists higher up in the hierarchy?
options: React catches the error internally and retries rendering the subtree indefinitely.
React logs the error to the console but continues rendering the remaining sibling components normally.
The browser crashes with a stack overflow due to unhandled promise rejections.
React unmounts the entire root application tree, resulting in a completely blank screen.
questions.correctAnswer: React unmounts the entire root application tree, resulting in a completely blank screen.
questions.explanation: Starting from React 16, if an error is thrown during rendering and there is no Error Boundary to catch it, React unmounts the entire component tree to prevent leaving the UI in an inconsistent or corrupted state.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the whole application when an uncaught rendering error occurs.
questions.relatedConcept: Error Boundary unmounting behavior
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of resilient UI architecture and React's failure recovery mechanisms.

questions.question: Why does calling `ReactDOM.unstable_batchedUpdates` or relying on React's automatic batching fail to batch state updates when they are triggered inside a native browser event listener or an async `setTimeout` callback in older React versions?
options: Because React only hooks into its own synthetic event system and commit phase lifecycle loops to batch updates automatically.
Because asynchronous code executes on a separate worker thread that cannot communicate with the React fiber reconciler.
Because native events bypass the JavaScript event loop entirely, preventing any synchronous code execution.
Because the V8 engine explicitly blocks state batching outside of strict React component methods.
questions.correctAnswer: Because React only hooks into its own synthetic event system and commit phase lifecycle loops to batch updates automatically.
questions.explanation: React's batching mechanism historically relied on wrapping event handlers within its own synthetic event dispatch wrapper. Outside of React-controlled event loops or lifecycles (like setTimeout or native addEventListener), updates executed synchronously one after another unless wrapped explicitly.
questions.hint: Consider how React tracks the lifecycle of event propagation versus standard browser APIs.
questions.relatedConcept: React batching mechanism and event loops
questions.interviewTip: This distinguishes candidates who deeply understand React internals and scheduling from those who only know basic hooks.

questions.question: What is the primary performance risk when using object spread syntax (`{ ...prev, [field]: value }`) to update deeply nested or high-frequency state objects in React?
options: It mutates the original state object directly in place, bypassing React's immutability checks entirely and preventing rerenders.
It creates shallow copies of intermediate parent objects along the path, generating unnecessary garbage collection pressure and breaking referential equality for child components.
It invokes a deep recursive clone of the entire state tree synchronously, causing main thread blocking for large state graphs.
It automatically memoizes all resulting child properties, which can lead to stale closures if not explicitly reset.
questions.correctAnswer: It creates shallow copies of intermediate parent objects along the path, generating unnecessary garbage collection pressure and breaking referential equality for child components.
questions.explanation: Object spread creates a new reference at the top level and copies properties shallowly. When done frequently across deeply nested structures, it allocates multiple short-lived object wrappers, increasing garbage collection churn and invalidating memoization (React.memo) on child components because parent reference identity changes.
questions.hint: Think about what kind of copy object spread performs and how reference equality affects component memoization.
questions.relatedConcept: State immutability performance trade-offs and reference equality in React
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates understand the performance implications of immutable updates beyond just 'immutability is good for React'.

questions.question: How does lifting state up too high in a large React component tree negatively impact runtime rendering performance?
options: It causes React to store the state in global window scope, violating encapsulation and leading to memory leaks.
It automatically shifts all child components from concurrent mode rendering back to legacy blocking synchronous rendering.
It forces the common ancestor and all its descending subtree components to re-evaluate on every state change, unless explicit memoization boundaries are established.
It prevents fiber nodes from being garbage collected when components unmount, causing persistent memory bloat.
questions.correctAnswer: It forces the common ancestor and all its descending subtree components to re-evaluate on every state change, unless explicit memoization boundaries are established.
questions.explanation: When state is placed higher in the component tree, any update to that state causes React to re-render the component owning the state and everything beneath it. Without strategic use of `React.memo`, `useMemo`, or composition patterns like children passing, this leads to wasted reconciliation cycles across unrelated sibling components.
questions.hint: Consider the scope of React's default reconciliation process when a component higher up updates its state.
questions.relatedConcept: Component tree restructuring and reconciliation overhead
questions.interviewTip: Great architects know that while lifting state up solves data-flow problems, doing it carelessly ruins rendering performance. Interviewers want to hear about mitigation strategies.

questions.question: Why is conditionally invoking a React hook (such as placing a 'useState' call inside an 'if' statement or loop) flagged during code review?
options: Conditional hooks cause memory leaks because uncalled hooks release their internal DOM nodes prematurely.
The JavaScript engine throws a ReferenceError because conditionally declared variables cannot be hoisted.
React's JSX compiler explicitly strips out any hooks placed inside control flow statements during bundling.
React relies on the absolute invocation order of hooks on every render to map state variables to their corresponding internal fibers.
questions.correctAnswer: React relies on the absolute invocation order of hooks on every render to map state variables to their corresponding internal fibers.
questions.explanation: React maintains hook state in a linked list per component fiber. It identifies each hook strictly by its call order across renders. Conditional execution alters this order, causing subsequent hooks to mismatch with previously stored state data.
questions.hint: Think about how React keeps track of multiple state calls inside a single component without explicit keys.
questions.relatedConcept: Rules of Hooks and Fiber state index alignment
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates understand the underlying data structures (linked lists/fibers) of React rather than just memorizing rules.

questions.question: What is the primary code review concern when an effect hook modifies a reactive value without including that value in its dependency array?
options: It creates a stale closure where 'count' remains permanently frozen at its initial value from the initial render.
React will automatically throw a runtime exception and unmount the component to prevent infinite loops.
The browser's JavaScript garbage collector will immediately purge the component's fiber node.
It causes the effect to re-run on every single render cycle, rendering the dependency array obsolete.
questions.correctAnswer: It creates a stale closure where 'count' remains permanently frozen at its initial value from the initial render.
questions.explanation: Because the effect callback closes over the lexical scope of the initial render, omitting 'count' from dependencies locks its reference to the initial value (0), leading to stale state updates unless functional updates (e.g., setCount(c => c + 1)) are used.
questions.hint: Consider how lexical scoping and closures retain references to variables from the exact render pass where the effect was created.
questions.relatedConcept: Stale closures and useEffect dependency management
questions.interviewTip: This checks if the candidate understands JavaScript lexical scope interaction with React rendering lifecycles.

questions.question: What happens regarding memory and garbage collection when a React component unmounts while an asynchronous operation (such as a 'fetch' request or a 'setTimeout') is still pending inside a 'useEffect' hook?
options: React automatically intercepts and cancels all pending promises and timers associated with the unmounted component, immediately freeing all allocated memory.

The asynchronous callback retains a closure reference to the component's scope and state setters, preventing garbage collection of the unmounted component instance until the promise settles or timer fires, which may trigger a memory leak warning if state is updated.
The JavaScript engine instantly terminates all pending asynchronous callbacks the moment the component's fiber node is detached from the DOM.
The component is garbage collected immediately because fiber unmounting clears all lexical environments and reference pointers instantly.
questions.correctAnswer: The asynchronous callback retains a closure reference to the component's scope and state setters, preventing garbage collection of the unmounted component instance until the promise settles or timer fires, which may trigger a memory leak warning if state is updated.
questions.explanation: When a component unmounts, any pending asynchronous operation holding a reference to local variables or state-setting functions via closures will keep those structures in memory until the operation completes. If the callback attempts to update state on an unmounted component, React logs a memory leak warning in development. Therefore, cleanup functions are required to cancel requests or clear timers.
questions.hint: Think about how JavaScript closures keep references alive in the event loop until execution finishes.
questions.relatedConcept: Garbage collection and memory retention in React effects via closures
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to check if candidates understand asynchronous lifecycle management and how closures impact memory retention.

questions.question: In React 18+, when utilizing `useSyncExternalStore` to subscribe to an external mutable data source, what specific problem does it solve regarding concurrent rendering and memory consistency?
options: It automatically memoizes the external data store in a persistent global cache to eliminate redundant memory allocations across component remounts.
It serializes all state updates into a single web worker thread to prevent main thread blocking and reduce peak memory usage.
It prevents 'Tearing', a visual inconsistency where different parts of the UI reflect states from different points in time due to high-priority interruptions during concurrent rendering.
It forces the garbage collector to immediately sweep unused store subscriptions as soon as the reading component unmounts.
questions.correctAnswer: It prevents 'Tearing', a visual inconsistency where different parts of the UI reflect states from different points in time due to high-priority interruptions during concurrent rendering.
questions.explanation: During concurrent rendering, React can pause and resume rendering work. If an external store is mutated while rendering is paused, different components might read different values from the store, leading to 'Tearing'. `useSyncExternalStore` forces synchronous reads of the store during render passes when concurrent updates happen, ensuring data consistency across the UI tree.
questions.hint: Consider what happens if a store changes values midway through a paused and resumed render pass in concurrent mode.
questions.relatedConcept: useSyncExternalStore and preventing tearing in concurrent React
questions.codeSnippet: const state = useSyncExternalStore(store.subscribe, store.getSnapshot);
questions.interviewTip: This tests deep knowledge of React 18's concurrency model and how external stores interact with fiber tree construction.

questions.question: What is the specific scheduling and execution behavior of a cleanup function returned by a `useEffect` hook when the component unmounts?
options: It is executed synchronously before the browser paints the screen, mirroring the timing of useLayoutEffect cleanups.
It is executed immediately on the microtask queue before React finishes committing the DOM updates.
It is deferred until the next browser idle callback or requestAnimationFrame tick.
It is executed asynchronously after the browser has painted, during the commit phase cleanup queue, after paint completes.
questions.correctAnswer: It is executed asynchronously after the browser has painted, during the commit phase cleanup queue, after paint completes.
questions.explanation: Effect cleanups and setup functions for `useEffect` are deferred and run asynchronously after the browser has painted, ensuring they do not block browser painting or user interactions. This contrasts with `useLayoutEffect`, whose cleanups run synchronously before paint.
questions.hint: Remember that standard useEffect doesn't block painting.
questions.relatedConcept: useEffect cleanup execution timing relative to browser paint
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify if the candidate understands React's commit phase vs browser paint timeline.

questions.question: When utilizing `useId` in React 18 for generating unique accessibility IDs across server-side rendering (SSR) and client hydration, how does React guarantee uniqueness and determinism between hydration passes?
options: It relies on an internal tree-traversal counter and prefix mechanism that tracks component nesting order rather than component render order.
It uses a cryptographically secure random number generator (Math.random) initialized identically on client and server.
It stores a globally incrementing integer counter in a shared module scope that resets on every root hydration.
It generates UUIDv4 tokens on the server and embeds them in window.__INITIAL_IDS__ for the client to parse.
questions.correctAnswer: It relies on an internal tree-traversal counter and prefix mechanism that tracks component nesting order rather than component render order.
questions.explanation: React's `useId` generates IDs based on the component's position within the React component tree (using a tree-walk counter and a server/client shared prefix like ':r:'), ensuring that as long as the tree structure matches between server and client, the generated IDs will be identical without relying on random tokens or global mutable state.
questions.hint: Think about how React identifies components structurally across tree renders.
questions.relatedConcept: useId deterministic generation mechanism for SSR hydration
questions.codeSnippet: const id = useId();
questions.interviewTip: Tests deep understanding of React 18 SSR primitives and how hydration mismatch on IDs is prevented.

questions.question: When developing a custom React hook that subscribes to an external mutable store using `useSyncExternalStore`, what symptom implies that you forgot to wrap your selector function with `useCallback` or memoize it outside the hook?
options: The component completely fails to re-render when the external store updates
An infinite loop or continuous re-rendering warning thrown by React due to a new selector instance being passed on every render
Memory leaks caused by dangling subscription listeners piling up in the store
Stale closure values being read from the store during concurrent transitions
questions.correctAnswer: An infinite loop or continuous re-rendering warning thrown by React due to a new selector instance being passed on every render
questions.explanation: If a selector function passed to useSyncExternalStore is recreated on every render without memoization, React considers it a new reference and triggers an immediate re-render check, leading to an infinite render loop if the selector's return value is a newly created object or array.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when React compares a newly allocated inline function reference on every render cycle.
questions.relatedConcept: useSyncExternalStore selector stability and infinite re-render symptoms
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test deep understanding of modern React 18 concurrent-safe external store integration hooks.

questions.question: If a React functional component renders correctly on initial mount but immediately loses its internal component state and unmounts/remounts its entire DOM subtree every time its parent re-renders, what architectural defect in the parent's render logic is most likely the cause?
options: Passing a state setter function directly down to the child component as a regular prop
Forgetting to wrap the child component in a `React.memo` higher-order component
Defining a child component function dynamically inside the parent component's body, creating a new component type reference on every render
Mutating a ref object property directly during the render phase instead of inside an effect
questions.correctAnswer: Defining a child component function dynamically inside the parent component's body, creating a new component type reference on every render
questions.explanation: Declaring a component inside another component creates a brand new component reference every time the parent renders. React uses referential equality to determine if an existing component tree should be preserved or destroyed, so a changing component type forces a full remount.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to React's reconciliation algorithm when the component tag/type itself changes on every parent render.
questions.relatedConcept: nested component definitions causing unintended remounts and state loss
questions.interviewTip: This is a classic React debugging scenario used to test whether candidates understand React's reconciliation and component identity rules.

questions.question: What occurs when a React custom Hook returns a state updater function that is subsequently invoked during the initial render phase of a consuming component?
options: The state update is silently ignored for the initial render pass to prevent infinite loops
The component immediately restarts its render pass with the updated state value
JavaScript throws a runtime TypeError because the setter is uninitialized
React catches the recursive update and throws a maximum update depth exceeded error
questions.correctAnswer: React catches the recursive update and throws a maximum update depth exceeded error
questions.explanation: Calling a state updater directly inside the render body causes an infinite render loop because every render triggers the updater, which schedules another render. React detects this excessive re-rendering and throws a 'Maximum update depth exceeded' error.
questions.hint: Think about what happens if a side-effect or state change is executed synchronously while calculating the JSX tree.
questions.relatedConcept: React render-phase state updates and infinite loop safeguards
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates understand pure rendering principles and where side-effects or state modifications are legally allowed.

questions.question: In React 18+, what is the exact execution behavior of cleanup functions returned by `useEffect` when a component is unmounted during an active concurrent transition?
options: Cleanups for unmounted trees execute immediately during the commit phase, regardless of concurrent priority
Cleanups are executed synchronously before the concurrent transition completes its commit phase
Cleanups are deferred and batched alongside passive garbage collection tasks
Cleanups are skipped entirely if the unmount was triggered by a low-priority transition interrupt
questions.correctAnswer: Cleanups for unmounted trees execute immediately during the commit phase, regardless of concurrent priority
questions.explanation: Even during concurrent rendering transitions, when a component is definitively unmounted from the active fiber tree, its effect cleanup functions run synchronously during the commit phase (specifically during passive effect unmounting) to release resources properly.
questions.hint: Consider whether memory cleanup can ever be safely bypassed or deferred indefinitely when a node is removed from the DOM.
questions.relatedConcept: Concurrent mode commit phase and effect cleanup lifecycle timing
questions.interviewTip: This distinguishes candidates who merely use hooks from those who understand React's fiber commit phase internals and garbage collection semantics.

questions.question: In React 18+ concurrent rendering, how does the behavior of Server-Side Rendering (SSR) streaming with Suspense differ when a component on the server throws a promise outside of a Suspense boundary compared to inside one?
options: Throwing outside a Suspense boundary automatically triggers client-side fallback hydration, while throwing inside it crashes the Node.js process.

Throwing outside a Suspense boundary aborts the entire server render with an error, whereas throwing inside a Suspense boundary allows the server to stream a fallback and catch up later once resolved.
There is no functional difference; React always catches the promise and streams the fallback regardless of the boundary presence.
Throwing outside a Suspense boundary converts the component into a Client Component, whereas inside it remains a Server Component.
questions.correctAnswer: Throwing outside a Suspense boundary aborts the entire server render with an error, whereas throwing inside a Suspense boundary allows the server to stream a fallback and catch up later once resolved.
questions.explanation: React's server-side suspense architecture requires promises thrown during rendering to be caught by a nearest <Suspense> boundary. If a promise escapes all boundaries, React treats it as an unhandled error during SSR, aborting the stream or falling back to client-side rendering entirely depending on the configuration.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to error propagation when no boundary is available to catch the asynchronous suspension.
questions.relatedConcept: React 18 SSR Suspense boundary fallback behavior and error boundaries
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates understand the architectural contract between React Server Components, Suspense boundaries, and SSR streaming recovery mechanics.

questions.question: What is the precise execution lifecycle difference between a callback ref assigned to a DOM element and a standard `useRef` object when the target element mounts or unmounts during a re-render?
options: A callback ref executes asynchronously during useEffect, while a `useRef` object updates synchronously before layout effects.
A callback ref only runs when the component first mounts, whereas `useRef` updates on every single render pass.

A callback ref is called with the DOM instance upon mounting and null upon unmounting immediately during commit, whereas a `useRef` current property is mutated without triggering any notification or callback.
There is no difference; both execute inside the passive effect phase after paint.
questions.correctAnswer: A callback ref is called with the DOM instance upon mounting and null upon unmounting immediately during commit, whereas a `useRef` current property is mutated without triggering any notification or callback.
questions.explanation: Callback refs provide a direct subscription to the node's lifecycle: React calls the function with the DOM element when it mounts and with `null` when it unmounts, synchronously during the commit phase. In contrast, `useRef` simply holds a mutable object whose `.current` property is updated silently without notifying the parent component.
questions.hint: Consider how you would know the exact moment an element is detached from the DOM tree without polling.
questions.relatedConcept: React callback refs vs useRef lifecycle notification
questions.interviewTip: Tested frequently when senior engineers discuss measuring DOM node dimensions or managing dynamic child attachments without extra state hooks.

questions.question: When building an Error Boundary component in React to catch runtime errors in child component trees, which lifecycle method or hook is specifically responsible for updating the component state so the fallback UI can be rendered on the next render pass?
options: componentDidCatch(error, info)
useErrorBoundary(error)
static getDerivedStateFromProps(props, state)
static getDerivedStateFromError(error)
questions.correctAnswer: static getDerivedStateFromError(error)
questions.explanation: static getDerivedStateFromError() is called during the 'render' phase when an error has been thrown by a descendant component, allowing the component to return a fallback state to update the UI. componentDidCatch() is called during the 'commit' phase and is intended for side effects like logging errors.
questions.hint: Think about which phase (render vs commit) state updates must happen in to affect the upcoming fallback UI render.
questions.relatedConcept: React Error Boundary lifecycle methods
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to verify if the candidate understands the distinction between commit-phase side effects (logging) and render-phase state mutations for error recovery.

questions.question: When utilizing React DevTools Profiler to diagnose performance issues in a production-like build, what specific configuration or build step is mandatory to ensure component display names and precise profiling metrics (such as render durations and 'why did this render' insights) are fully accurate?
options: Ensuring NODE_ENV is set to development and React modules are unminified/not stripped
Enabling strict mode globally via <React.StrictMode>
Bundling the application using Webpack's production optimization flags
Using the experimental concurrent root API explicitly in the entry file
questions.correctAnswer: Ensuring NODE_ENV is set to development and React modules are unminified/not stripped
questions.explanation: React's profiling tools and development features rely on development builds where performance profiling hooks and component display names are preserved. Production builds strip out much of this metadata and disable profiling hooks by default to optimize bundle size and execution speed.
questions.hint: Consider how minifiers and environment variables handle internal React warning and profiling flags.
questions.relatedConcept: React Profiler and production build profiling configuration
questions.interviewTip: This question tests practical debugging maturity, ensuring candidates know how to configure environments correctly when auditing rendering bottlenecks.

questions.question: What is the security risk of directly passing unsanitized location search parameters into React's useId hook or trusting user-controlled input for dynamic component keys?
options: It triggers a React Server Components hydration error that leaks environment variables.
It can lead to arbitrary component substitution, rendering unintended internal components or prototype pollution vectors.
It causes an infinite reconciliation loop because keys must be static strings.
It automatically bypasses React's built-in XSS protection for child text nodes.
questions.correctAnswer: It can lead to arbitrary component substitution, rendering unintended internal components or prototype pollution vectors.
questions.explanation: Using unvalidated user input to look up components from a lookup table or utilizing it insecurely can allow attackers to instantiate unintended components present in the scope, potentially accessing sensitive contexts or triggering unexpected side effects.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when object keys or component lookups come directly from external untrusted input.
questions.relatedConcept: Dynamic component resolution security risks
questions.codeSnippet:
const DynamicComponent = components[userInputKey];
return <DynamicComponent key={userProvidedKey} />;
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to test whether candidates understand application security beyond basic XSS when dealing with dynamic UI structures.

questions.question: Why is passing raw, unescaped user-supplied strings directly into style prop objects considered a risky pattern in React applications?
options: It immediately triggers a runtime SyntaxError in the browser's CSSOM parser.
It disables React's synthetic event system for all child components inside that div.
It can enable CSS injection attacks if the input breaks out of the property context or specifies malicious URLs (e.g., expression or url payloads).
It forces the browser to drop out of hardware acceleration for the entire document subtree.
questions.correctAnswer: It can enable CSS injection attacks if the input breaks out of the property context or specifies malicious URLs (e.g., expression or url payloads).
questions.explanation: React sanitizes string values passed to style properties against typical XSS, but malicious CSS values (such as crafted url() payloads or browser-specific expressions) can still introduce security vulnerabilities or UI redressing issues if user input is not strictly validated.
questions.hint: Consider how browsers interpret malicious property values inside inline styles.
questions.relatedConcept: CSS injection and style prop sanitization
questions.interviewTip: Good for gauging if a candidate considers styling vectors as part of their threat model.

questions.question: What is the primary architectural implication of lifting component state too high up the React tree into a global context without splitting or memoization?
options: React will throw a runtime cyclic dependency error due to circular context providers.
Context values can only be updated synchronously inside layout effects, causing missed frame drops.
Server-side rendering hydration will fail because global contexts bypass serialization boundaries.
Unrelated descendant components consuming the context will re-render whenever any part of the context value changes, even if they do not consume the updated properties.
questions.correctAnswer: Unrelated descendant components consuming the context will re-render whenever any part of the context value changes, even if they do not consume the updated properties.
questions.explanation: React context does not support selective subscriptions out of the box. Whenever the provided context value object changes reference, every consumer component re-renders regardless of whether the specific slice of data it cares about actually mutated.
questions.hint: Think about how consumers react when a context value reference changes entirely.
questions.relatedConcept: React Context re-render propagation and granularity trade-offs
questions.interviewTip: Interweaves state management decisions with performance optimization awareness.

questions.question: When designing a custom hook that returns a callback function, why is wrapping that returned callback in `useCallback` often considered premature optimization if the callback is passed to native DOM elements?
options: Native DOM elements do not participate in React's reconciliation diffing, so passing a new function reference has virtually zero cost compared to the overhead of the dependency array and hook allocation.
React automatically memoizes all inline functions passed to lowercase HTML intrinsic tags under the hood.
Using useCallback forces the function to be garbage collected on every render cycle, causing severe memory leaks.
Callback hooks cannot accept primitive values as dependencies if they are attached to native DOM events.
questions.correctAnswer: Native DOM elements do not participate in React's reconciliation diffing, so passing a new function reference has virtually zero cost compared to the overhead of the dependency array and hook allocation.
questions.explanation: Intrinsic HTML elements (like <div onClick={...}>) only care about the listener being attached or updated; they do not perform shallow prop equality checks like custom or memoized components do. Thus, useCallback adds memory and CPU overhead for no reconciliation benefit.
questions.hint: Consider whether native HTML elements perform prop shallow comparisons.
questions.relatedConcept: Premature optimization of useCallback with native DOM elements
questions.interviewTip: Distinguishes between rote application of hooks and actual performance profiling understanding.

questions.question: What is the primary architectural purpose of wrapping a component with `React.memo` when its props are primitive values compared to non-primitive objects?
options: It caches the entire DOM subtree generated by the component in a global memory registry to completely bypass reconciliation.
It skips re-rendering the component if shallow comparison of current and previous props indicates no changes.
It forces the component to render asynchronously off the main thread using React 18 concurrent features.
It automatically memoizes all internal hook values and local state computations within the component.
questions.correctAnswer: It skips re-rendering the component if shallow comparison of current and previous props indicates no changes.
questions.explanation: React.memo is a higher-order component that performs a shallow comparison of props. If the props have not changed by shallow equality, React skips re-rendering that component subtree. It does not cache the DOM, enforce async rendering on its own, or memoize internal hooks.
questions.hint: Think about what `React.memo` actually compares before deciding whether to execute the component function.
questions.relatedConcept: React.memo prop comparison and re-rendering optimization
questions.interviewTip: Intervers love asking about React.memo to see if candidates understand shallow equality pitfalls, such as passing inline objects or functions that break memoization.

questions.question: In React, what occurs if you mutate a state variable directly (e.g., `state.count = 5`) instead of using its setter function (e.g., `setCount(5)`), assuming `state` is a local component state object?
options: React will immediately detect the mutation via a Proxy and trigger a synchronous re-render.
JavaScript will throw a strict-mode mutation error because state objects are frozen by default inside React components.
The component will not re-render, and subsequent state updates may overwrite or lose the mutated changes due to stale state references.
React will queue an asynchronous microtask to reconcile the mutated property with the virtual DOM.
questions.correctAnswer: The component will not re-render, and subsequent state updates may overwrite or lose the mutated changes due to stale state references.
questions.explanation: React state must be treated as immutable. Mutating state directly bypasses React's scheduling and reconciliation mechanisms, meaning no re-render is triggered, and internal state tracking becomes out of sync.
questions.hint: Consider how React detects changes to trigger reconciliation and whether local state objects are automatically wrapped in proxies.
questions.relatedConcept: State immutability and direct mutation consequences
questions.interviewTip: This is a fundamental React trap. Interviewers ask this to test whether the candidate truly understands why immutability is strictly enforced in functional components.

questions.question: What happens when you return a cleanup function from a standard `useEffect` hook, but the component unmounts while an asynchronous operation triggered inside that effect is still pending?
options: The fetch network request is automatically aborted by the React runtime when the cleanup function runs.
React throws a runtime exception immediately upon unmounting because a promise resolution is pending.
The cleanup function prevents the asynchronous callback from executing entirely if the component unmounts before resolution.
The async operation continues running in the background, but state updates on the unmounted component are safely suppressed via the flag.
questions.correctAnswer: The async operation continues running in the background, but state updates on the unmounted component are safely suppressed via the flag.
questions.explanation: React effects do not automatically cancel ongoing asynchronous tasks like fetch requests or promises when a component unmounts. The cleanup function runs synchronously during unmount, allowing developers to set flags (like `isMounted`) to prevent state updates on unmounted components and avoid memory leak warnings.
questions.hint: Think about whether JavaScript promises or network requests know about React's component lifecycle automatically.
questions.relatedConcept: useEffect cleanup handling with pending asynchronous operations
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates understand that React cleanup functions do not magically cancel underlying network requests or async tasks without explicit abort controllers.

questions.question: Why might a custom React hook that manages a persistent global WebSocket connection trigger unexpected multiple connection attempts when used across multiple components, even when wrapped in `useEffect` with an empty dependency array `[]`?
options: React Strict Mode in development mounts, unmounts, and remounts components to verify effect resilience, causing an immediate connect-disconnect-connect cycle.
An empty dependency array forces the effect to re-run on every state change inside the hook.
Global WebSocket instances cannot be shared unless declared outside the React component tree entirely.
The useState hook inside a custom hook automatically resets the parent component's network context.
questions.correctAnswer: React Strict Mode in development mounts, unmounts, and remounts components to verify effect resilience, causing an immediate connect-disconnect-connect cycle.
questions.explanation: In React 18 Strict Mode for development, effects are intentionally run twice (mount -> unmount -> mount) to help developers find missing cleanup logic. For side effects like WebSockets, this manifests as double connection attempts unless handled correctly.
questions.hint: Consider development-only behaviors in React 18 that purposefully double-invoke lifecycle hooks.
questions.relatedConcept: React Strict Mode effect double-invocation with side effects
questions.interviewTip: This question screens for candidates who are familiar with React 18 development tooling quirks and know how to build robust, idempotent subscription hooks.

questions.question: What is the primary performance and execution implication of utilizing React's `lazy()` combined with `Suspense` for a component that is never rendered during the application lifecycle?
options: The component code chunk is downloaded immediately upon module evaluation but its React reconciliation and DOM insertion are deferred.
The component code chunk is neither downloaded nor parsed by the browser until the conditional branch evaluates to true and render is triggered.
The component code chunk is preloaded via a low-priority background fetch as soon as the parent component mounts, regardless of the conditional flag.
The component causes an immediate synchronous hydration error during initial page load due to an unresolved lazy boundary.
questions.correctAnswer: The component code chunk is neither downloaded nor parsed by the browser until the conditional branch evaluates to true and render is triggered.
questions.explanation: React.lazy() leverages dynamic import() under the hood, ensuring that the network request to fetch the corresponding bundle chunk is only initiated when the lazy component is rendered for the first time.
questions.hint: Think about how dynamic import() behaves alongside React lazy boundary rendering.
questions.relatedConcept: React.lazy code splitting and network chunk loading behavior
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test whether candidates understand bundle optimization and code-splitting boundaries in React.

questions.question: When utilizing React 18's `useId` hook to generate unique element IDs for form accessibility, what specific structural challenge does it solve in server-side rendering (SSR) environments compared to global counters?
options: It guarantees that IDs are globally unique across multiple independent React root instances running on the same webpage.
It generates cryptographically secure random tokens to prevent DOM element enumeration attacks.
It ensures stable, matching IDs between server-rendered HTML and client-side hydration even if component tree structures vary or components mount asynchronously out of order.
It allows React to automatically garbage-collect form elements when they are unmounted from the virtual DOM.
questions.correctAnswer: It ensures stable, matching IDs between server-rendered HTML and client-side hydration even if component tree structures vary or components mount asynchronously out of order.
questions.explanation: useId generates unique IDs based on the parent tree's tokenized path, ensuring hydration mismatches are avoided even if suspense boundaries or conditional rendering cause components to render asynchronously.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to global incrementing counters during asynchronous server-side rendering and client hydration.
questions.relatedConcept: React useId hook SSR hydration stability
questions.interviewTip: Great question to check if the candidate has practical experience dealing with SSR hydration bugs and accessibility requirements.

questions.question: What happens when you invoke `flushSync` from React-DOM to wrap a state update inside an event handler?
options: React throws an error because flushSync cannot be used inside synthetic event handlers.
React forces the DOM update synchronously right inside the callback, ensuring the subsequent console.log reads the updated DOM.
React defers the state update until the next macro-task, identical to standard batching behavior.
React batches the update together with all subsequent state updates in the current execution block.
questions.correctAnswer: React forces the DOM update synchronously right inside the callback, ensuring the subsequent console.log reads the updated DOM.
questions.explanation: flushSync forces React to flush any pending work and update the DOM synchronously inside the provided callback, meaning DOM mutations happen immediately before the next line of code executes.
questions.hint: Think about React's automatic batching and how escape hatches like flushSync override it.
questions.relatedConcept: flushSync and DOM batching escape hatches
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of React's concurrent batching mechanisms and when you might need to bypass them for imperative DOM interactions.

questions.question: In React 18, when multiple state updates are batched together inside a custom asynchronous function (e.g., using `async/await` with a `setTimeout` or a fetch response), how does React handle the re-rendering behavior?
options: State updates following an await keyword are never batched and will always trigger separate sequential re-renders.
Automatic batching applies to all asynchronous operations in React 18, so state updates are batched into a single re-render.
Automatic batching only applies inside native browser event handlers; async functions still cause individual renders unless wrapped in unstable_batchedUpdates.
React batches updates only if they are synchronous; asynchronous microtasks prevent any form of batching.
questions.correctAnswer: Automatic batching applies to all asynchronous operations in React 18, so state updates are batched into a single re-render.
questions.explanation: React 18 introduced automatic batching out-of-the-box for all state updates regardless of where they originate, including promises, setTimeout, native event handlers, and any other asynchronous events.
questions.hint: Think about what major rendering optimization feature was introduced globally in React 18.
questions.relatedConcept: React 18 Automatic Batching
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers often ask this to check if candidates are up-to-date with React 18 performance features compared to legacy versions.

questions.question: In React, when using the 'useMemo' hook with a dependency array that includes a value returned from another 'useMemo' hook, what determines the evaluation timing of the inner memoized value?
options: Both 'valA' and 'valB' are re-calculated on every render because they are defined inside the functional component body.
The inner 'useMemo' calculates its value only when 'valA' changes, regardless of the component render cycle.
The inner 'useMemo' is evaluated during the reconciliation phase, potentially before 'valA' is updated in the current render cycle.
React guarantees that 'computeB' will be executed before 'computeA' due to the dependency chain.
questions.correctAnswer: The inner 'useMemo' calculates its value only when 'valA' changes, regardless of the component render cycle.
questions.explanation: React's hook system ensures that 'valB' only triggers its compute function if the shallow comparison of the 'valA' dependency fails. This is a primary mechanism for performance optimization. Option 1 is incorrect because React does not guarantee order of evaluation for independent memo hooks, and Option 2 is false because memoization is precisely designed to avoid re-calculation on every render.
questions.hint: Consider the dependency resolution mechanism of React's hook reconciliation.
questions.relatedConcept: Hook dependency memoization lifecycle
questions.codeSnippet:
const valA = useMemo(() => computeA(), []);
const valB = useMemo(() => computeB(valA), [valA]);
questions.interviewTip: Understanding dependency arrays is critical for preventing unnecessary re-renders in large-scale applications.

questions.question: In React 18, when multiple state updates are batched inside a synthetic event handler, how does React handle the execution of batching across asynchronous boundaries such as 'setTimeout'?
options: The updates inside setTimeout are processed in two separate render cycles.
Automatic batching applies to the setTimeout callback, resulting in a single render for both count updates.
The first update is processed immediately, while subsequent updates are ignored.
React forces synchronous execution of the timeout callback to maintain transactional state consistency.
questions.correctAnswer: Automatic batching applies to the setTimeout callback, resulting in a single render for both count updates.
questions.explanation: React 18 introduced automatic batching for updates inside promises, setTimeout, native event handlers, and other asynchronous operations, ensuring that multiple state updates result in only a single re-render.
questions.hint: Think about the changes introduced in the React 18 concurrent rendering model regarding asynchronous callbacks.
questions.relatedConcept: Automatic Batching in React 18
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how React optimizes renders beyond simple component lifecycle events demonstrates deep knowledge of the React 18 architecture.

questions.question: Consider the following React component. What text is displayed inside the button after it is clicked once?
options: "Beta"
"Not a function"
"Alpha"
It throws a runtime TypeError during rendering
questions.correctAnswer: "Not a function"
questions.explanation: In React, when you pass a function to a state setter (like `setCallback`), React treats it as an functional updater: `(prevState) => nextState`. When `setCallback(() => "Beta")` is executed, React runs the passed function to compute the next state. The function returns the string "Beta", which becomes the new state. Therefore, on the next render, `callback` is the string "Beta" rather than a function, and the ternary operator evaluates to "Not a function". To correctly store a function in state, you must wrap it in another function, e.g., `setCallback(() => () => "Beta")`.
questions.hint: Analyze how React treats functional arguments passed to state dispatcher functions versus static values.
questions.relatedConcept: React useState functional updates and lazy initialization
questions.interviewTip: This question highlights a classic React gotcha when trying to store functions or components directly in state. An interviewer uses this to verify if a candidate understands the internal mechanics of state setters and the dual-purpose nature of passing functions in React APIs.

questions.question: What is the exact behavioral difference between calling `ReactDOM.render` and using `ReactDOM.createRoot` concurrent rendering APIs in React 18 when handling immediate state updates inside a high-frequency native DOM event listener?
options: ReactDOM.createRoot executes all state updates synchronously by default to preserve backward compatibility, while ReactDOM.render utilizes asynchronous fiber slicing.
ReactDOM.createRoot automatically batches updates inside native DOM event listeners, whereas legacy ReactDOM.render did not batch them outside of React event handlers.
ReactDOM.createRoot disables automatic batching for Promise callbacks, requiring explicit manual wrapping via unstable_batchedUpdates.
There is no functional difference in update scheduling; createRoot only adds support for server-side Suspense streaming.
questions.correctAnswer: ReactDOM.createRoot automatically batches updates inside native DOM event listeners, whereas legacy ReactDOM.render did not batch them outside of React event handlers.
questions.explanation: React 18 introduces out-of-the-box automatic batching for all updates, including those originating from native event listeners, timeouts, and promises, whereas legacy React only batched updates inside React event handlers.
questions.hint: Consider how React 18 changes automatic batching behavior outside of synthetic event handlers compared to older versions.
questions.relatedConcept: React 18 Automatic Batching and Concurrent Roots
questions.codeSnippet:
const root = ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById('root'));
root.render(<App />);
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates understand the architectural performance implications of upgrading to React 18 concurrent features.

questions.question: A component named 'Tracker' is rendered, the user clicks the button exactly 3 times, and then the parent component unmounts 'Tracker'. What will be printed to the console?
options: Ref: 0 Val: 0
Ref: 3 Val: 0
Ref: 3 Val: 3
Ref: 0 Val: 3
questions.correctAnswer: Ref: 3 Val: 0
questions.explanation: Because the dependency array of the useEffect hook is empty ([]), the effect runs only once on mount, and its cleanup function is registered capturing the lexical scope of the first render. In that initial render, 'val' is 0, so the stale closure will always reference 'val' as 0. However, 'valRef' is a persistent reference object whose '.current' property is mutated on every single render. After 3 clicks, the third render sets 'valRef.current' to 3. When the component unmounts, the cleanup function executes: it reads the mutated '.current' property (which is 3) and the closed-over 'val' variable (which is 0).
questions.hint: Think about how JavaScript closures capture local scope variables during a render versus how mutable ref objects bypass closure limitations.
questions.relatedConcept: React Hooks Closure capturing and useRef mutation semantics
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how React leverages JS closures is a common screening filter. Developers must know how to avoid stale closures inside async callbacks or cleanups using refs, without introducing unnecessary re-renders.

questions.question: In React, when using the 'useMemo' hook with a dependency array containing a primitive value and a reference type (e.g., an object), what happens if the object is recreated on every render while the primitive value remains unchanged?
options: The memoized value will be returned from cache because React performs a deep comparison of the 'config' object by default.
The memoized value will be recalculated every render because the 'config' object reference changes, regardless of its internal content.
The memoized value will persist as long as the component instance is mounted, as the hook ignores object references.
The hook will throw a runtime error because dependency arrays cannot contain reference types like objects.
questions.correctAnswer: The memoized value will be recalculated every render because the 'config' object reference changes, regardless of its internal content.
questions.explanation: React's dependency comparison for hooks like useMemo and useCallback uses 'Object.is', which checks for referential equality. If the object reference changes on every render, the memoization check fails, causing the function to re-execute.
questions.hint: Consider how React compares dependencies inside the array.
questions.relatedConcept: Referential equality in React dependency tracking
questions.interviewTip: Understanding referential stability is crucial for performance optimization in React; candidates should be able to explain when to use 'useMemo' versus 'useCallback'.

options: React compares the previous and next props of the `Item` component; if they are shallowly equal, it skips the function call and reuses the existing internal state.

React relies on the position in the tree and the element type. Since the `isOn` prop did not change, the type `Item` (at index 0) matches the previous render, so React updates the existing instance rather than creating a new one.
Because `Item` is stateless, React always discards the previous instance and creates a fresh component instance to ensure no stale closures are used.
React uses the `id` prop inside the rendered element to perform a diff; if `id={1}` remains constant, it preserves the DOM node and component state.
questions.correctAnswer: React relies on the position in the tree and the element type. Since the `isOn` prop did not change, the type `Item` (at index 0) matches the previous render, so React updates the existing instance rather than creating a new one.
questions.explanation: React's reconciliation algorithm matches elements in the virtual tree by comparing their position (index) and their Element type. Since the conditional `isOn ? <Item.../> : <Item.../>` resolves to the same type `Item` at the same position, React keeps the existing instance and updates its props.
