It does NOT perform a shallow equality check on props for standard components (that is `React.memo`'s job, but the question asks about React's default behavior). Option 1 is wrong because default reconciliation doesn't shallow-compare props to skip work; it compares types. Option 3 is wrong because stateless components still have identity in the tree; they aren't discarded and re-created unnecessarily. Option 4 is wrong because `id` is just a prop value, not a key; React uses the `key` prop for list reconciliation, not arbitrary props like `id` for general tree stability.
questions.hint: Think about how React matches nodes in the virtual tree during a re-render: does it look at prop values or the element's type and position?
questions.relatedConcept: React Reconciliation and Element Matching
questions.interviewTip: This tests if candidates understand that React diffs by type and position, not by prop equality (unless `React.memo` or `key` is explicitly used for lists). Many developers mistakenly think React always re-renders children or always compares props.

questions.question: In React, when using the 'useMemo' hook to optimize heavy computations, which of the following scenarios describes the correct implementation to ensure the memoized value is correctly updated when dependencies change?
options: The value will automatically track all variables used inside the factory function and recompute whenever 'a' or 'b' changes.
The value will only recompute if 'a' changes, potentially returning a stale 'computeExpensiveValue' result if 'b' updates.
The value will always recompute on every render regardless of dependencies because the hook is missing the dependency array argument.
The value will recompute whenever either 'a' or 'b' changes because React performs a shallow comparison of all variables used in the component scope.
questions.correctAnswer: The value will only recompute if 'a' changes, potentially returning a stale 'computeExpensiveValue' result if 'b' updates.
questions.explanation: useMemo relies strictly on the explicit dependency array provided. If 'b' is used inside the computation but omitted from the dependency array, React will continue to return the memoized result from the last time 'a' changed, leading to stale data.
questions.hint: React does not perform static analysis to detect variables used inside the hook's callback; it relies solely on the provided dependency array.
questions.relatedConcept: React Hook dependency integrity
questions.codeSnippet: const memoizedValue = useMemo(() => computeExpensiveValue(a, b), [a]);
questions.interviewTip: This tests the candidate's understanding of the 'rules of hooks' and the dangers of stale closures when managing memory and performance.

questions.question: In React, what is the specific runtime consequence of passing a new object literal (e.g., `{ value: 1 }`) as a prop to a child component that depends on `React.memo` for optimization, instead of using a stable object reference?
options: The component will not re-render because `React.memo` performs a deep comparison of object properties.
The component will re-render on every parent render because `React.memo` uses shallow comparison, and a new object literal always has a different identity.
The component will only re-render if the `value` property inside the object changes, ignoring the object reference.
React will throw a warning in the console but will not re-render the component.
questions.correctAnswer: The component will re-render on every parent render because `React.memo` uses shallow comparison, and a new object literal always has a different identity.
questions.explanation: `React.memo` performs a shallow comparison using `Object.is` on props. A new object literal `{ value: 1 }` creates a new reference on every render, causing `Object.is` to return `false`. Therefore, the shallow comparison fails, and the component re-renders despite the memoization. Option A is incorrect because `memo` does not perform deep comparison.
questions.hint: Consider how `Object.is` behaves with two distinct object instances that have identical contents.
questions.relatedConcept: React.memo shallow comparison and reference equality
questions.interviewTip: This tests if a candidate understands the performance implications of object creation in props and the limitations of `React.memo` without stable references (e.g., via `useMemo`).

title: Redis - Test 1: Core Fundamentals & Patterns
description: Comprehensive technical evaluation for Redis covering runtime mechanics, design principles, and problem solving.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q1] When configuring Redis with Redis Cluster enabled, what happens to slot migration and client routing when a master node fails, assuming cluster-require-full-coverage is set to its default value in modern Redis versions?
options: The cluster stops accepting writes across all slots until the failed master is fully restarted or replaced by a replica.
Only the hash slots served exclusively by the failed master become unavailable for writes, while slots on other masters remain fully operational.
All keys belonging to the failed master are automatically migrated to a randomly chosen healthy master node.
Client requests are automatically redirected to standalone fallback Redis instances configured via cluster-replica-fallback.
questions.correctAnswer: Only the hash slots served exclusively by the failed master become unavailable for writes, while slots on other masters remain fully operational.
questions.explanation: In Redis Cluster, hash slots are partitioned among master nodes. When a master fails, only the hash slots assigned to that specific master (and its replicas, if none are promoted yet) become unavailable. With cluster-require-full-coverage set to 'no' (which is the default in modern stable releases), the cluster continues serving read and write operations for all slots assigned to surviving master nodes.
questions.hint: Consider whether a master node failure impacts the entire keyspace or only its specific assigned hash slots.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Cluster slot availability and failure isolation
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check your deep understanding of Redis Cluster availability guarantees and partition behavior versus monolithic setups.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q2] How does Redis handle memory reclamation when the maxmemory limit is reached and maxmemory-policy is set to volatile-lru, but the keyspace contains zero keys with an associated expiration (TTL)?
options: It falls back to evicting random keys across the entire keyspace regardless of TTL.
It deletes keys that have a persistent memory layout overhead first, prioritizing internal dictionary buckets.
It immediately raises an OOM error on any write command, identical to the noeviction policy.
It disables snapshotting temporarily until memory drops below the configured watermark.
questions.correctAnswer: It immediately raises an OOM error on any write command, identical to the noeviction policy.
questions.explanation: Policies prefixed with 'volatile-' (such as volatile-lru, volatile-ttl, volatile-random) only consider keys that have an expire set. If no keys have an expiration set in the keyspace, Redis cannot find any candidate keys to evict under a volatile policy. Consequently, it behaves like the 'noeviction' policy and returns an OOM error for any command that allocates more memory.
questions.hint: Analyze what 'volatile' strictly means in the context of Redis key expiration policies.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis eviction policies and volatile key constraint handling
questions.interviewTip: This tests edge-case configuration knowledge regarding memory management and subtle policy differences under extreme load.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q3] When configuring Redis with `maxmemory-policy volatile-lru`, how does the eviction engine select keys to remove when the memory limit is reached?
options: It evaluates all keys in the keyspace and evicts the least recently used one that has an associated expiration flag.
It strictly iterates through all keys with an expiration flag in lexicographical order, evicting the oldest.
It scans the entire database using an exact LRU linked list across all volatile keys, guaranteeing absolute global accuracy.
It samples a random subset of keys with an expiration flag and evicts the least recently used among those sampled.
questions.correctAnswer: It samples a random subset of keys with an expiration flag and evicts the least recently used among those sampled.
questions.explanation: Redis approximates LRU to save memory overhead. Instead of maintaining a true, costly doubly-linked list for every key, it uses a probabilistic approximation by randomly sampling a small batch of keys (controlled by `maxmemory-samples`) and evicting the best candidate from that sample.
questions.hint: Think about why Redis avoids maintaining a precise, global doubly-linked list for LRU across millions of keys.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis memory eviction approximation algorithms
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to test whether candidates understand the trade-offs between exact algorithmic complexity and memory efficiency in systems like Redis.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q4] In Redis Cluster, what is the exact mechanism and consequence when a node receives a command for a slot it does not currently own, but the client did not send a `MOVED` or `ASK` redirection?
options: The node immediately returns a MOVED redirection error containing the IP and port of the slot's current owner node.
The node silently proxies the request to the correct master node in the background and returns the result to the client.
The cluster drops the connection due to protocol violation because clients are strictly required to track slot routing tables.
The node executes the command locally if it is part of the same shard, triggering an automatic cluster-wide resharding.
questions.correctAnswer: The node immediately returns a MOVED redirection error containing the IP and port of the slot's current owner node.
questions.explanation: Redis Cluster is decentralized; nodes do not proxy requests. If a node receives a key whose hash slot is not bound to its own hash slot table, it replies with a `MOVED` error, forcing the client to update its local slot map and reissue the command to the correct node.
questions.hint: Consider whether Redis Cluster nodes act as transparent proxies or if they expect the smart client to handle redirection.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Cluster slot routing and MOVED redirection
questions.interviewTip: This distinguishes candidates who merely use Redis from those who understand Redis Cluster topology and smart client interaction protocols.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q5] When configuring Redis persistence using AOF (Append Only File) with appendfsync set to 'everysec', what is the exact mechanism by which Redis handles fsync calls to prevent the main thread from blocking on I/O latency spikes?
options: Redis forks a child process using copy-on-write semantics, and the child asynchronously flushes the page cache to disk every second.
The main thread delegates fsync execution to a dedicated background thread pool, while queueing write commands into an in-memory buffer.
The main thread performs fsync asynchronously via non-blocking epoll notifications triggered by the operating system kernel.
Redis locks the AOF file descriptor and delegates the blocking write syscall to a synchronous background worker thread.
questions.correctAnswer: The main thread delegates fsync execution to a dedicated background thread pool, while queueing write commands into an in-memory buffer.
questions.explanation: With 'appendfsync everysec', Redis writes commands to the AOF buffer in the main thread (which is fast), but delegates the actual disk synchronization (fsync) to a background thread to prevent disk I/O stalls from blocking client request handling.
questions.hint: Think about how Redis separates fast in-memory network operations from slow disk flushes without sacrificing durability entirely.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis AOF appendfsync background thread architecture
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers probe this to test whether candidates understand the nuances of Redis's single-threaded event loop and how I/O bottlenecks are offloaded.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q6] How does Redis manage memory allocation overhead and prevent high internal fragmentation when storing millions of tiny keys and values, particularly regarding its default memory allocator?
options: It implements a custom fixed-block slab allocator entirely bypassing system allocators to eliminate fragmentation.
It mandates the use of 64-bit pointers with compressed pointer types similar to JVM to pack tiny objects tightly.
It relies on jemalloc's bin-based chunk allocation sizes and arena separation to group allocations of similar sizes together.
It utilizes a garbage-collected heap manager that periodically compacts memory blocks in-place during idle event-loop cycles.
questions.correctAnswer: It relies on jemalloc's bin-based chunk allocation sizes and arena separation to group allocations of similar sizes together.
questions.explanation: Redis is compiled by default with jemalloc (or libc if specified). jemalloc uses size classes (bins) and arenas to minimize internal fragmentation when allocating thousands of small objects, which is critical for Redis key-value footprints.
questions.hint: Consider the role of jemalloc vs standard glibc malloc in high-throughput database workloads.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis memory allocator jemalloc internal fragmentation handling
questions.interviewTip: Often asked when discussing capacity planning, out-of-memory (OOM) errors, and why `used_memory_rss` can differ significantly from `used_memory`.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q7] When configuring Redis Enterprise or open-source Redis with Lua scripting, what is the primary reason why scripts must be deterministic and avoid calling random commands like TIME or SRANDMEMBER without specific flags?
options: Lua engine garbage collection will crash if random values are allocated inside Redis internal memory arenas.
Redis locks the global event loop during script execution, causing non-deterministic code to trigger a deadlock timeout.
Non-deterministic functions automatically bypass Redis append-only file (AOF) persistence blocks, corrupting the write-ahead log checksum.
Master-replica replication and Redis Cluster durability rely on command propagation or AOF replay, where non-deterministic execution causes divergent dataset states across nodes.
questions.correctAnswer: Master-replica replication and Redis Cluster durability rely on command propagation or AOF replay, where non-deterministic execution causes divergent dataset states across nodes.
questions.explanation: Redis replicates Lua scripts by sending the script text itself to replicas and the AOF file (SCRIPT LOAD / EVAL). If a script is non-deterministic (e.g., using TIME or reading unstable runtime state), replicas and restored snapshots will execute divergent code paths, leading to split-brain or data corruption across the cluster.
questions.hint: Think about how Redis propagates state changes to replicas and persistence logs.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Lua Scripting Determinism and Replication
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test whether candidates understand distributed consistency models beyond basic key-value operations.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q8] In a high-throughput Redis deployment using Redis Cluster, what occurs internally when a client issues a multi-key command like MGET where the keys hash to different hash slots across distinct cluster nodes?
options: The client receives a -CROSSSLOT error because Redis Cluster mandates that all keys in a single command must hash to the exact same hash slot.
Redis Cluster automatically executes a distributed two-phase commit (2PC) across the involved shards to ensure atomic consistency.
The receiving node proxies the request to all other relevant nodes in parallel and merges the results transparently.
Redis transparently migrates the target keys in real-time to the node handling the first key in the command list.
questions.correctAnswer: The client receives a -CROSSSLOT error because Redis Cluster mandates that all keys in a single command must hash to the exact same hash slot.
questions.explanation: Redis Cluster does not support distributed transactions or multi-key operations across different hash slots natively to avoid network overhead and latency penalties. Commands involving keys in different slots are rejected with a -CROSSSLOT error, requiring clients or application logic to use hash tags (e.g., `{user1000}.profile`, `{user1000}.settings`) to force keys onto the same slot.
questions.hint: Consider Redis's design philosophy regarding multi-shard operations and hash slots.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Cluster Hash Slots and Cross-Slot Constraints
questions.interviewTip: Crucial for system design interviews involving sharded caching architectures and data modeling.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q9] How does Redis manage memory fragmentation when the operating system uses transparent huge pages (THP), and why does Redis recommend disabling THP?
options: THP prevents Redis from using jemalloc, forcing it to fall back to the system allocator which leaks memory during realloc operations.
THP causes copy-on-write during background saves to duplicate 2MB memory pages instead of 4KB pages, drastically increasing memory consumption and latency.
THP disables Redis's internal active defragmentation engine by locking physical page frames in kernel space.
THP causes Redis cluster node communication timeouts because huge pages cannot be serialized into RESP protocol buffers.
questions.correctAnswer: THP causes copy-on-write during background saves to duplicate 2MB memory pages instead of 4KB pages, drastically increasing memory consumption and latency.
questions.explanation: When Transparent Huge Pages are enabled, the Linux kernel allocates 2MB memory pages instead of standard 4KB pages. During background persistence operations (like fork() for RDB snapshots), Copy-on-Write (CoW) causes modified pages to be duplicated. With THP, even a small modification to a 2MB page forces the kernel to copy the entire 2MB block rather than a 4KB page, leading to massive memory bloat and latency spikes.
questions.hint: Think about how copy-on-write interacts with page sizes during background fork operations.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis memory management, Transparent Huge Pages, and Copy-on-Write overhead
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask about OS-level configurations like THP and vm.overcommit_memory to test if candidates understand Redis production deployment best practices.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q10] In Redis, what is the underlying mechanism and potential risk of using 'MEMORY PURGE' compared to relying on jemalloc's background purging?
options: MEMORY PURGE permanently frees all expired keys across all databases regardless of the maxmemory-policy setting, risking data loss.
MEMORY PURGE disables Redis's internal lazy-free thread pool, forcing synchronous deallocation of large hash tables.
MEMORY PURGE forces the underlying memory allocator (jemalloc) to immediately return dirty unused pages to the OS via madvise, which can cause a momentary CPU spike and latency stall.
MEMORY PURGE resets the jemalloc arenas, causing all active client connection buffers to be abruptly truncated and dropped.
questions.correctAnswer: MEMORY PURGE forces the underlying memory allocator (jemalloc) to immediately return dirty unused pages to the OS via madvise, which can cause a momentary CPU spike and latency stall.
questions.explanation: Redis uses jemalloc as its default memory allocator, which retains freed memory in arenas to satisfy future allocations quickly (dirty pages). 'MEMORY PURGE' explicitly commands jemalloc to release unused dirty pages back to the operating system using system calls like madvise(). This frees up RSS (Resident Set Size) for the OS, but the synchronous system calls can introduce noticeable latency spikes in high-throughput production environments.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to allocator-held memory when you force it back to the operating system.
questions.relatedConcept: jemalloc allocator behavior, memory purging, and latency management in Redis
questions.interviewTip: This tests deep operational knowledge of how Redis interacts with memory allocators under memory pressure constraints.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q11] When utilizing Redis Streams with consumer groups, what precise side-effect occurs to the Pending Entries List (PEL) when a consumer successfully executes the XACK command for a specific message ID?
options: The message entry is permanently removed from both the consumer group's PEL and the underlying stream history log.
The message entry's delivery counter in the PEL is reset to zero and its ownership is transferred back to the idle queue.
The message entry is marked as dead-lettered and moved to a separate tombstone list inside the stream data structure.
The message entry is removed from the consumer group's PEL, but remains intact within the underlying stream history log.
questions.correctAnswer: The message entry is removed from the consumer group's PEL, but remains intact within the underlying stream history log.
questions.explanation: XACK removes the message from the consumer group's Pending Entries List (PEL), indicating it has been successfully processed, but it does NOT delete the message from the main stream. Deletion from the stream requires an explicit XDEL or TRIM command.
questions.hint: Think about whether acknowledging a message destroys its record in the global log or just clears it from the consumer's pending tracking.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Streams PEL lifecycle and XACK side-effects
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of reliable message delivery semantics and state separation between stream logs and consumer group tracking in Redis.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q12] In a Redis deployment utilizing master-replica replication with asynchronous replication enabled, what specific consistency and ordering anomaly can occur immediately after a client issues a write command followed by a read command to a replica, assuming no explicit coordination mechanisms are used?
options: The replica may serve stale data or appear as if the write never happened, violating read-your-writes consistency.
The read command will always block until the asynchronous replication backlog catches up completely.
The replica will return a Redis execution error because asynchronous replication prevents concurrent read operations.
The write command will be automatically rolled back if the replica's replication offset lags behind by even one byte.
questions.correctAnswer: The replica may serve stale data or appear as if the write never happened, violating read-your-writes consistency.
questions.explanation: Because Redis replication is asynchronous by default, data flows from master to replica after the master responds to the client. Thus, an immediate read to the replica might hit an older state, violating read-your-writes consistency.
questions.hint: Consider the timing gap between when a master acknowledges a write and when the replica receives the replication stream.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Asynchronous Replication and Consistency Models
questions.interviewTip: Expect this question to evaluate your practical knowledge of distributed systems tradeoffs, replication lag, and CAP theorem nuances in caching/in-memory data stores.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q13] When configuring Redis Cluster with replica nodes, what occurs behind the scenes if a cluster node experiences a persistent network partition that isolates it from the majority quorum of master nodes, while its assigned replica remains fully connected to that quorum?
options: The isolated master continues writing locally until its replication buffer overflows, while the replica triggers a failover, resulting in a dual-master split-brain scenario if client routing is uncoordinated.

The isolated master eventually enters a state where it rejects write operations after cluster-node-timeout expires and majority quorum loss is detected, allowing its replica to safely win an election and promote itself.

The isolated master automatically demotes itself to a replica immediately upon detecting packet loss, instantly promoting the connected replica without requiring any failover delay or cluster state propagation.

The Redis Cluster bus protocol forces the isolated master to instantly crash via a segmentation fault to prevent stale reads, leaving the partition entirely without a master until manual intervention occurs.
questions.correctAnswer: The isolated master eventually enters a state where it rejects write operations after cluster-node-timeout expires and majority quorum loss is detected, allowing its replica to safely win an election and promote itself.
questions.explanation: Redis Cluster implements availability safeguards: an isolated master that loses communication with the majority of master nodes for longer than `cluster-node-timeout` plus the replication offset drift will stop accepting writes to prevent divergence. This allows the healthy replica to trigger a failover safely.
questions.hint: Think about how Redis prevents stale data accumulation and handles split-brain protection during network partitions.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Cluster network partitioning and failover safety mechanisms
questions.interviewTip: Interweaves distributed systems theory with Redis-specific configuration properties like cluster-node-timeout.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q14] Under what specific internal operational sequence does Redis execute a synchronous background save (BGSAVE) using Copy-On-Write (COW), and why might high-frequency write operations during this process paradoxically cause a massive, sudden spike in memory utilization?
options: BGSAVE forks a child process; operating system page tables are duplicated instantly, forcing every single memory page to be physically copied before the fork completes, instantly doubling memory consumption.

The parent process halts all writes and serializes the entire dataset into a temporary buffer, copying the entire database into swap space to prevent concurrency conflicts with active client connections.

The parent process forks a child via OS COW; as clients mutate existing keys, the Linux kernel duplicates individual memory pages on write, causing physical memory usage to scale linearly with the write rate during the snapshot.
Redis allocates a secondary duplicate database in memory prior to forking, executing a full deep-copy of all hash tables to ensure thread safety across multi-threaded background save worker pools.
questions.correctAnswer: The parent process forks a child via OS COW; as clients mutate existing keys, the Linux kernel duplicates individual memory pages on write, causing physical memory usage to scale linearly with the write rate during the snapshot.
questions.explanation: BGSAVE uses fork() which relies on Copy-On-Write (COW). The child shares the parent's page tables without copying physical memory initially. However, when the parent process modifies keys during the snapshot, the Linux kernel duplicates those specific 4KB memory pages, causing physical memory usage to increase in proportion to the write volume.
questions.hint: Focus on how the operating system handles virtual memory page duplication when a parent process modifies data shared with a forked child.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis persistence mechanics, fork(), and Copy-On-Write memory inflation
questions.interviewTip: Crucial for diagnosing production out-of-memory (OOM) incidents during heavy write loads and low free memory margins.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q15] How does Redis handle memory management when `maxmemory` is reached and `maxmemory-policy` is set to `noeviction`, but a client issues a write command that allocates new memory (e.g., `SET` or `LPUSH`)?
options: Redis automatically falls back to the `volatile-lru` policy for the duration of the write transaction.
Redis evicts the oldest key across the entire keyspace regardless of expiration status to accommodate the write.
The write command blocks until background compaction frees enough memory or a timeout occurs.
The write command fails and returns an error to the client, while read commands continue to function normally.
questions.correctAnswer: The write command fails and returns an error to the client, while read commands continue to function normally.
questions.explanation: When `maxmemory-policy` is set to `noeviction` (the default in older versions or specific configurations), Redis refuses memory-allocating write commands when the limit is breached, returning an error response (e.g., '(error) OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'conf.maxmemory''). Read-only commands and commands that free memory (like `DEL`) continue to work.
questions.hint: Think about what 'noeviction' explicitly states regarding dropping keys when memory is full.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis maxmemory-policy behavior under OOM conditions
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of Redis operational safety limits and failure modes under resource exhaustion.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q16] What is the behavior of a Redis transaction wrapped in `MULTI` and `EXEC` when a watched key (via `WATCH`) is modified by another client *after* the `MULTI` command is issued but *before* the `EXEC` command is executed?
options: The entire transaction is aborted, and `EXEC` returns a null reply or empty array indicating the transaction failed.
Only the specific command interacting with the modified key is rolled back, while the rest of the transaction executes successfully.
The transaction blocks until the concurrent modification completes and then retries automatically.
The transaction executes successfully, and the modified key's value is overwritten by the transaction's final state.
questions.correctAnswer: The entire transaction is aborted, and `EXEC` returns a null reply or empty array indicating the transaction failed.
questions.explanation: Redis `WATCH` provides optimistic locking. If a watched key is modified between the `WATCH` and `EXEC` commands, the entire transaction is aborted and `EXEC` returns a Null multi-bulk reply (or nil), signaling that no commands inside the block were executed.
questions.hint: Consider how optimistic locking differs from pessimistic locking in distributed data stores.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Optimistic Locking with WATCH/MULTI/EXEC
questions.interviewTip: Crucial for assessing concurrent data safety and race condition handling in Redis without locking up the single-threaded event loop.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q17] When utilizing Redis Streams with consumer groups, what is the precise state transition of a pending entry when a different consumer successfully executes XCLAIM on it?
options: The message is acknowledged and permanently removed from the Pending Entries List (PEL) of the original consumer.
The delivery counter is incremented, and the idle time is reset to zero while ownership transfers to the new consumer.
The message stream entry is duplicated, leaving the original entry under the first consumer's PEL and a new reference in the second.
The delivery counter resets to zero, but the idle time accumulates cumulatively from the original entry time.
questions.correctAnswer: The delivery counter is incremented, and the idle time is reset to zero while ownership transfers to the new consumer.
questions.explanation: When XCLAIM is invoked, it changes the ownership of a pending message to a specified consumer, explicitly resetting its idle time to 0 and incrementing its delivery attempt counter.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the internal metrics like idle time and delivery count when a message is forcefully reassigned.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Streams Consumer Groups XCLAIM mechanics
questions.interviewTip: Interweaves stream internals with reliability semantics in distributed consumer architectures.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q18] How does Redis handle memory deallocation and internal fragmentation when a large Redis hash containing thousands of fields is completely emptied via HDEL commands compared to executing a DEL on the entire key?
options: HDEL automatically shrinks the hash-pack or hashtable and immediately returns freed memory blocks to the OS kernel, while DEL marks memory lazily for background deallocation.
Both commands exhibit identical memory reclamation behaviors because Redis utilizes a global unified heap pool managed by a custom slab allocator.

HDEL shrinking individual internal encodings can leave underlying memory allocations fragmented or retained by jemalloc, whereas DEL drops the entire key structure instantly releasing whole memory pages back to the allocator.
HDEL triggers an immediate compacting defragmentation pass on the active memory page, whereas DEL relies exclusively on active defrag background threads.
questions.correctAnswer: HDEL shrinking individual internal encodings can leave underlying memory allocations fragmented or retained by jemalloc, whereas DEL drops the entire key structure instantly releasing whole memory pages back to the allocator.
questions.explanation: Incremental deletion via HDEL shrinks internal containers (like hash packs or dicts), but memory might remain allocated within the jemalloc arena and fragmented. DEL frees the container structure immediately, although asynchronous unlinking (UNLINK) handles lazy deallocation for large aggregates.
questions.hint: Consider how memory allocators like jemalloc handle partial chunks versus entire freed allocations.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis memory management, jemalloc interaction, and internal encodings
questions.interviewTip: Crucial for diagnosing production memory bloat where keys are incrementally shrunk instead of dropped.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q19] When configuring Redis Enterprise or open-source Redis with Lua scripting, what precise behavioral issue occurs when a Lua script executed via EVAL contains a non-deterministic call (such as calling redis.call('TIME')) in a Master-Replica architecture?
options: The non-deterministic function calls are automatically rewritten into deterministic commands during AOF generation.
The script runs successfully on the master, but replica nodes will execute the command lazily, leading to desynchronization.
The non-deterministic command causes the master to promote a replica automatically to preserve consistency.
The script execution is automatically aborted by Redis with an error to prevent replica divergence.
questions.correctAnswer: The script execution is automatically aborted by Redis with an error to prevent replica divergence.
questions.explanation: Redis requires all scripts to be deterministic so that replication streams and AOF logs can reproduce identical state on replicas. If a script calls non-deterministic commands like TIME, SRANDMEMBER (without count), or accesses system time, Redis flags an error or terminates execution if it violates safety constraints.
questions.hint: Consider how Redis replication relies on reproducing the exact same deterministic dataset state changes on replicas.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Lua scripting deterministic execution and replication consistency
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test deep knowledge of distributed consensus, replication guarantees, and constraints within Redis Lua script sandboxing.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q20] During a Redis cluster failover investigation, you notice that a replica node fails to win the election and promote itself to master despite the previous master being down. What is the most likely cause related to cluster configuration or network health?
options: The replica was previously manually configured with a replica-priority of 0, explicitly disabling automatic failover participation.
The replica's data offset is too far behind the failed master, exceeding the cluster-node-timeout multiplied by a specific factor.
The replica's cluster port is blocked, preventing it from broadcasting the CLUSTERDOWN state to other shards.
The replica has maxmemory-policy set to noeviction, which locks its cluster state machine during failover.
questions.correctAnswer: The replica was previously manually configured with a replica-priority of 0, explicitly disabling automatic failover participation.
questions.explanation: Setting replica-priority to 0 prevents a replica from ever being elected as master during a failover event, which is a common administrative setting for replicas intended solely for off-site backup or local read-scaling without eligibility for promotion.
questions.hint: Check settings specifically designed to control a replica's eligibility for automatic promotion.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Cluster replica-priority and automatic failover configuration
questions.interviewTip: Often asked when troubleshooting high availability setups where expected automated disaster recovery failed due to silent administrative flags.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q21] When configuring Redis to use the Lua scripting engine, what is the security implication of executing scripts that dynamically construct and pass Redis commands to 'redis.call()' using unsanitized user inputs?
options: Redis sandboxes all Lua scripts, blocking any nested calls to EVAL or SCRIPT, which automatically mitigates command injection.
It can lead to remote code execution or arbitrary command injection on the Redis server, as Lua scripts run with full privileges and can invoke EVAL recursively.
It only causes a syntax error because Redis commands inside Lua cannot contain variables.
It causes the Redis instance to enter read-only mode to protect against write-based injections.
questions.correctAnswer: It can lead to remote code execution or arbitrary command injection on the Redis server, as Lua scripts run with full privileges and can invoke EVAL recursively.
questions.explanation: Redis Lua scripts execute with high privileges, and allowing untrusted input to dynamically construct commands executed via redis.call (especially nested EVAL or administrative commands) bypasses intended application-layer boundaries, potentially leading to unauthorized data manipulation or server compromise.
questions.hint: Think about how Lua interacts with the Redis command execution engine and whether nested evaluations are restricted.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Lua Scripting Command Injection
questions.codeSnippet:
-- Example pattern inside a Lua script
redis.call('EVAL', user_supplied_string, 0)
questions.interviewTip: Interweaves security awareness with intermediate-to-advanced knowledge of Redis's internal Lua execution model.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q22] Which of the following describes the security vulnerability and operational risk associated with leaving the default Redis configuration exposed on the public internet without a password and with the 'CONFIG' command enabled?
options: An attacker can only read cached keys; Redis memory isolation prevents any interaction with the underlying host operating system.
The CONFIG command is strictly read-only by default, preventing any persistence file redirection attacks.

An attacker can use the CONFIG SET command to alter the directory ('dir') and filename ('dbfilename') of the RDB persistence file, and write a malicious SSH public key into authorized_keys to gain host access.
Exposing Redis publicly only allows Denial of Service via memory exhaustion, as configuration modification requires local Unix socket access.
questions.correctAnswer: An attacker can use the CONFIG SET command to alter the directory ('dir') and filename ('dbfilename') of the RDB persistence file, and write a malicious SSH public key into authorized_keys to gain host access.
questions.explanation: A classic Redis misconfiguration vulnerability involves using CONFIG SET to change the RDB dump path to the SSH directory (/root/.ssh/) and setting the dbfilename to 'authorized_keys', thereby achieving remote code execution on the host machine via SSH key injection.
questions.hint: Consider what happens when attackers combine persistence configuration commands with file write locations.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis CONFIG Exploitation and Host Takeover
questions.interviewTip: Tests operational security knowledge and understanding of how database configuration commands can be abused for host-level compromise.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q23] When configuring Redis persistence using a combination of RDB snapshots and AOF (Append-Only File) logs, what is the exact operational interaction that occurs when AOF rewrite (`BGREWRITEAOF`) is triggered while an RDB save operation is actively in progress via `BGSAVE`?
options: Redis executes both background forks concurrently, but the parent process redirects all incoming client write commands exclusively to a secondary temporary buffer to avoid corruption.
Redis immediately aborts the currently running `BGSAVE` operation because the AOF rewrite subsumes snapshot data and provides a more up-to-date point-in-time recovery mechanism.
The child process executing `BGREWRITEAOF` waits for the `BGSAVE` child process to exit, but parent-to-child pipe communication for incremental writes remains active.
Redis defers the execution of the AOF rewrite until the active background RDB snapshot process completely finishes, preventing concurrent I/O resource contention on disk.
questions.correctAnswer: Redis defers the execution of the AOF rewrite until the active background RDB snapshot process completely finishes, preventing concurrent I/O resource contention on disk.
questions.explanation: To prevent excessive disk I/O bottlenecks and potential saturation of storage bandwidth, Redis explicitly prevents simultaneous execution of `BGSAVE` and `BGREWRITEAOF`. If a `BGREWRITEAOF` is requested while a `BGSAVE` is in progress, the server queues or defers the AOF rewrite request until the RDB save finishes (returning an OK status to the client indicating the rewrite is scheduled).
questions.hint: Consider how Redis manages disk I/O contention between two heavyweight background processes that both write large files.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Persistence Concurrency Management (RDB vs AOF)
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your deep understanding of Redis's single-threaded event loop architecture combined with its background fork operations and resource throttling.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q24] How does Redis handle memory reclamation and client connection state behavior when the `maxmemory` limit is reached and the eviction policy is set to `noeviction` under heavy write concurrency?
options: Redis rejects any write commands that require additional memory allocation, returning an error to the client, while still allowing read-only commands and explicit memory-freeing operations like `DEL`.
Redis automatically disconnects all non-privileged connected clients and flushes the entire database keyspace to swap space or disk backup.
Redis temporarily halts all network I/O event processing across all threads until background garbage collection threads reclaim enough memory.
Redis silently drops incoming write packets at the TCP socket buffer level without parsing them or returning error responses.
questions.correctAnswer: Redis rejects any write commands that require additional memory allocation, returning an error to the client, while still allowing read-only commands and explicit memory-freeing operations like `DEL`.
questions.explanation: When `maxmemory` is reached and `noeviction` is configured, Redis refuses commands that allocate more memory (like `SET`, `HSET`, `LPUSH`, etc.) and returns a specific OOM (Out Of Memory) error. However, read operations (like `GET`) and operations that free memory (like `DEL` or `EXPIRE`) continue to execute normally.
questions.hint: Think about what 'noeviction' means: it refuses to remove keys, so what happens when a client tries to write new data?
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Memory Policies and Out-Of-Memory (OOM) Error Handling
questions.interviewTip: This question assesses whether you know the practical failure modes of Redis when memory bounds are hit without an active eviction strategy.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q25] In Redis, when evaluating Lua scripts using EVAL or EVALSHA, what is the strict execution and replication behavior regarding non-deterministic commands?
options: Redis automatically blocks Lua scripts from executing if they contain any built-in non-deterministic commands or call read-only commands out of order.
Redis modifies non-deterministic commands like TIME or SRANDMEMBER to return fixed pseudo-random or pre-evaluated results before master-replica propagation, ensuring deterministic replay.
Redis allows non-deterministic commands inside Lua scripts but relies entirely on the script's return value for downstream replica consistency, which can lead to drift.
Redis allows non-deterministic commands only if the script is explicitly marked as read-only using a special pragma comment within the script header.
questions.correctAnswer: Redis modifies non-deterministic commands like TIME or SRANDMEMBER to return fixed pseudo-random or pre-evaluated results before master-replica propagation, ensuring deterministic replay.
questions.explanation: Redis rewrites certain non-deterministic commands (like TIME) or forces deterministic behavior in Lua scripts so that replication streams sent to replicas and AOF files remain fully reproducible and consistent without divergence.
questions.hint: Consider how Redis maintains absolute replica consistency when scripts execute arbitrary internal commands.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Lua Scripting Determinism and Replication
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to test deep knowledge of distributed consensus, master-replica replication consistency, and advanced Redis scripting constraints.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q26] How does Redis handle memory management and key eviction when maxmemory-policy is set to volatile-lru, but all keys currently in the keyspace have a TTL set, and none are marked as expired?
options: Redis immediately returns an out-of-memory error for write commands because no keys are technically expired yet despite having a TTL.
Redis automatically converts the policy to allkeys-lru to find a candidate, ignoring whether the keys have an expiration or not.
Redis samples a subset of keys with an expiration set, applies the LRU approximation algorithm across that sample, and evicts the least recently used key among them.
Redis scans the entire keyspace linearly to find the absolute oldest key with a TTL, guaranteeing true LRU ordering at the cost of latency.
questions.correctAnswer: Redis samples a subset of keys with an expiration set, applies the LRU approximation algorithm across that sample, and evicts the least recently used key among them.
questions.explanation: volatile-lru restricts eviction candidates to keys that have an expire field set, and runs the internal approximate LRU sampling algorithm on that specific subset.
questions.hint: Remember that Redis does not use exact LRU; it uses a probabilistic approximation over a sampled subset.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Eviction Policies and Approximate LRU
questions.interviewTip: Useful for assessing whether a candidate understands the difference between volatile vs allkeys eviction policies and Redis's approximate LRU sampling mechanism.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q27] When executing a Lua script in Redis via EVAL or EVALSHA, which specific behavior prevents non-deterministic commands (like TIME or SINTERSTORE with non-deterministic iteration order) from breaking primary-replica replication consistency?
options: Redis automatically pauses replication streams until the script completes across all active cluster nodes simultaneously.
Lua scripts are executed inside an isolated sandbox where all time-related functions return 0 and set operations are strictly sorted by memory address.
Redis rejects any script containing command calls that are not explicitly whitelisted in the redis.replicate_commands() configuration block.
Redis rewrites non-deterministic commands into deterministic equivalents or flags the script as unsafe, blocking execution if it modifies state after calling them.
questions.correctAnswer: Redis rewrites non-deterministic commands into deterministic equivalents or flags the script as unsafe, blocking execution if it modifies state after calling them.
questions.explanation: To maintain replication safety, Redis restricts Lua scripts. If a script calls non-deterministic commands, Redis monitors state mutations. In modern Redis, scripts using `redis.replicate_commands()` allow fine-grained replication where individual write commands issued inside the script are replicated instead of the whole script, but calling non-deterministic commands after write commands causes a runtime error.
questions.hint: Think about how Redis ensures replicas end up with identical datasets despite potential script non-determinism.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Lua Scripting Replication Safety and Determinism
questions.codeSnippet: EVAL "redis.call('set', 'foo', 'bar'); return redis.call('get', 'foo')" 0
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to test deep knowledge of Redis cluster consistency models and limitations of Lua script execution.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q28] How does Redis handle memory management and eviction when `maxmemory` is reached while processing a write command against a volatile key (a key with an associated TTL) versus a non-volatile key, assuming `maxmemory-policy` is set to `volatile-lru`?
options: Keys without an expiration set are completely ignored by the eviction algorithm, preventing them from being removed even if they are the least recently used.
Non-volatile keys are prioritized for eviction because volatile keys are protected by their time-to-live metadata.
The eviction engine randomly samples keys from the entire keyspace regardless of whether they have a TTL or not.
Volatile keys are only evicted if no non-volatile keys can be found, falling back to an all-keys LRU strategy.
questions.correctAnswer: Keys without an expiration set are completely ignored by the eviction algorithm, preventing them from being removed even if they are the least recently used.
questions.explanation: Under policies prefixed with `volatile-` (such as `volatile-lru`, `volatile-lfu`, or `volatile-ttl`), Redis restricts its eviction candidate pool exclusively to keys that have an expire set. Non-volatile keys are completely ignored by these policies, which can lead to an Out Of Memory (OOM) error if all memory is consumed by keys without TTLs.
questions.hint: Pay close attention to the prefix in eviction policies like volatile-lru.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Memory Eviction Policies and Volatile Keys
questions.codeSnippet:
CONFIG SET maxmemory 100mb
CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy volatile-lru
questions.interviewTip: Senior engineers must understand memory management pitfalls, such as choosing a volatile eviction policy when keys lack TTLs.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q29] When configuring Redis with Redis Cluster, how does the cluster handle client redirection when a requested key maps to a hash slot currently undergoing migration between two master nodes?
options: The proxy automatically pauses writes globally across the cluster until the slot migration state machine completes entirely.
The receiving node replies with an -ASK redirection error pointing the client to query the migration destination node directly after sending an ASKING command.
The cluster drops the connection and returns a cluster-down state exception to enforce strict linearizability.
The node holding the slot internally buffers the read or write operation in a memory-mapped staging file until migration finalizes.
questions.correctAnswer: The receiving node replies with an -ASK redirection error pointing the client to query the migration destination node directly after sending an ASKING command.
questions.explanation: During slot migration in Redis Cluster, a -ASK redirection is returned if the hash slot is in-flight. The client must send the ASKING command to the target node before retrying the query to ensure the command is accepted on a node that does not yet formally own the slot.
questions.hint: Think about the ephemeral redirection code used specifically during live slot rebalancing.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Cluster slot migration and -ASK redirection protocol
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test deep knowledge of distributed consensus, state transitions, and client-side routing behavior in Redis Cluster.

questions.question: [Redis • Test 1 • Q30] In Redis memory management, what is the primary structural mechanism that allows Hash types with a small number of elements to bypass standard dict and robj overheads?
options: They are flattened into string keys using colon separators with an internal bitmask index.
They utilize a sparse array backed by 64-bit SIMD register allocations.
They are encoded as a ziplist (or listpack in newer versions), storing fields and values sequentially as contiguous memory blocks.
They are converted directly into immutable bitmap bitmaps to eliminate pointer chasing.
questions.correctAnswer: They are encoded as a ziplist (or listpack in newer versions), storing fields and values sequentially as contiguous memory blocks.
questions.explanation: Redis optimizes small hashes, lists, and sorted sets by encoding them using memory-efficient contiguous structures like ziplists or listpacks instead of hash tables or skip lists, trading CPU overhead for high cache locality.
questions.hint: Look for the memory-efficient sequential encoding structure used for small collections.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis memory optimization and internal encodings (ziplist/listpack)
questions.interviewTip: Good interviewers test your understanding of Redis internal object representations and space-time trade-offs under low memory limits.

questions.question: When utilizing Redis Cluster with hash slots, what happens during a resharding operation (e.g., via redis-cli cluster reshard) when a key is actively being migrated from a source node to a target node, and a client issues a normal GET command for that key to the source node?
options: The source node transparently proxies the request to the target node and returns the result without informing the client.
The source node returns an -ASK redirection error containing the target node's IP and port, and the client must execute ASKING on the target node before retrying.
The source node immediately returns a -MOVED redirection error, permanently updating the client's internal slot-to-node mapping.
The source node blocks the client connection until the migration of that specific key and its slot is entirely completed.
questions.correctAnswer: The source node returns an -ASK redirection error containing the target node's IP and port, and the client must execute ASKING on the target node before retrying.
questions.explanation: During live cluster resharding, keys migrating from source to target are in a transition state. If the source node does not find the key in its local dataset, but knows it is currently being migrated for that slot, it replies with an -ASK redirection error. Unlike -MOVED, -ASK is temporary and requires the client to send the ASKING command to the target node before executing the query once.
questions.hint: Think about the distinction between temporary slot migration redirects and permanent slot ownership changes in Redis Cluster.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Cluster Resharding and ASK Redirection Semantics
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify deep practical understanding of Redis Cluster availability and how clients handle distributed state transitions during rebalancing.

questions.question: In a Redis cluster using asynchronous replication, what is the precise behavior of the 'WAIT' command when the 'numslaves' parameter exceeds the number of currently synchronized replicas, and the timeout is reached?
options: It returns an error indicating that the cluster is in a read-only state due to replica unavailability.
It returns the total number of replicas that successfully acknowledged the write before the timeout occurred.
It blocks indefinitely until the required number of replicas becomes available, ignoring the timeout.
It rolls back the write operation on the master and returns a failure status to the client.
questions.correctAnswer: It returns the total number of replicas that successfully acknowledged the write before the timeout occurred.
questions.explanation: The WAIT command returns the number of replicas that have acknowledged the write up to the point of the timeout. If the requested number is not reached, it does not roll back the data nor error out; it simply provides the count of acknowledgments received within that window.
questions.hint: Consider if WAIT is an atomic transaction rollback mechanism or a synchronization confirmation utility.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis WAIT command semantics
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands that Redis replication is asynchronous by default and that WAIT is an observability tool for consistency, not a transactional guarantee.

questions.question: In Redis, when using the 'WATCH' command on a key in a multi-exec transaction, what is the specific consequence if that key is modified by another client before the 'EXEC' command is issued?
options: The transaction continues but the modified key is excluded from the final state.
The transaction is aborted and EXEC returns a Null reply to signify the failure.
The transaction is queued and executes only if the modification occurs after the first command.
The transaction blocks until the key is released by the competing client.
questions.correctAnswer: The transaction is aborted and EXEC returns a Null reply to signify the failure.
questions.explanation: When a key is watched, the client monitors for changes. If any watched key is modified by another client before the EXEC command, the entire transaction is aborted and EXEC returns a Null reply. This ensures optimistic locking consistency.
questions.hint: Consider the protocol's behavior when a transaction fails to meet its optimistic locking requirements.
questions.relatedConcept: Optimistic Locking and Transactional Integrity
questions.interviewTip: Understanding optimistic locking is critical for high-concurrency systems using Redis; ensure you discuss why this approach is preferred over pessimistic locking in specific scenarios.

questions.question: In a Redis cluster environment using asynchronous replication, what happens if a master node crashes after executing a command but before the acknowledgment of the replication to its replicas has completed?
options: The command is automatically rolled back on the master node upon recovery.
The command is considered lost unless WAIT was explicitly used with a sufficient threshold.
The command is automatically committed to the new master during the failover process via the replication log.
The command remains in the replication buffer and is automatically synchronized once a slave is promoted to master.
questions.correctAnswer: The command is considered lost unless WAIT was explicitly used with a sufficient threshold.
questions.explanation: Redis replication is asynchronous by default. If the master crashes before the write is replicated, the data is lost because the master does not guarantee durability across network partitions or crashes without explicit synchronous replication commands like WAIT.
questions.hint: Consider the durability guarantees of asynchronous master-slave replication in Redis.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis asynchronous replication and data loss scenarios
questions.interviewTip: Distinguishing between Redis performance-oriented defaults and strong consistency requirements is a hallmark of a senior engineer.

questions.question: In Redis, when evaluating Lua scripts using EVAL or EVALSHA, how are keys and non-key arguments explicitly separated to support cluster routing and read-only replicas?
options: Keys must be prefixed with a dollar sign ($) while arguments are prefixed with an at-sign (@) within the Lua script invocation.
The first numeric argument (e.g., '1') specifies how many subsequent arguments represent keys, separating them from general arguments.
Redis automatically parses the script's abstract syntax tree to infer keys, rendering explicit separation optional.
All arguments passed after the script body are treated strictly as keys unless prefixed with an exclamation mark.
questions.correctAnswer: The first numeric argument (e.g., '1') specifies how many subsequent arguments represent keys, separating them from general arguments.
questions.explanation: Redis requires the caller to explicitly pass the count of keys as the second argument to EVAL/EVALSHA (after the script itself). This number tells Redis how many of the following arguments belong to the KEYS array, with any remaining parameters falling into ARGV. This is strictly necessary for Redis Cluster to route commands to the correct shard.
questions.hint: Look at the numeric parameter immediately following the script string in the EVAL command signature.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Lua Scripting KEYS and ARGV separation
questions.codeSnippet: EVAL "return redis.call('get', KEYS[1])" 1 mykey myargument
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers probe Lua scripting mechanics to see if candidates understand Redis Cluster constraints and how distributed hash slots are resolved.

questions.question: In Redis, how does the replication backlog buffer size affect full resynchronizations when a replica reconnects after a temporary disconnection?
options: Redis automatically increases the backlog buffer dynamically in memory until the replica finishes catching up, completely preventing full resynchronizations.
If the disconnected time exceeds the backlog capacity causing missing offsets to be overwritten, Redis falls back to a full synchronization via RDB transfer.
The replication backlog is only used during primary initialization and is never referenced after a replica establishes its initial connection.
If the backlog overflows, Redis drops the replica permanently from the cluster configuration until it is manually re-added and restarted.
questions.correctAnswer: If the disconnected time exceeds the backlog capacity causing missing offsets to be overwritten, Redis falls back to a full synchronization via RDB transfer.
questions.explanation: The replication backlog is a fixed-size ring buffer that stores write commands sent to replicas. If a replica is disconnected for too long and the backlog wraps around, overwriting the commands the replica missed, a partial resynchronization (PSYNC) becomes impossible, forcing a full RDB-based resynchronization.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when a ring buffer fills up and wraps around before a reader consumes the older data.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Replication Backlog and PSYNC Mechanism
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask about replication internals to test your understanding of High Availability trade-offs, network partitions, and memory management under failure scenarios.

questions.question: In Redis, when using the 'WATCH' command on a key in an optimistic locking scenario, what specific condition leads to the transaction (MULTI/EXEC block) failing, even if the watched key's value remains logically identical to its initial state?
options: The WATCH command only triggers a failure if the key is deleted; updates to the same value are ignored by the internal modification flag.
If the key is updated to the exact same value it previously held, the WATCH command will detect the version increment and cause EXEC to return a null multi-bulk response.
Redis WATCH only tracks the existence of the key, not its value; therefore, updating the key to the same value will never trigger a transaction failure.
The transaction fails only if the connection is interrupted; key modification tracking is ignored if the underlying data structure type remains unchanged.
questions.correctAnswer: If the key is updated to the exact same value it previously held, the WATCH command will detect the version increment and cause EXEC to return a null multi-bulk response.
questions.explanation: Redis implements optimistic locking using a per-key dirty flag. When a client performs a write operation on a watched key, the key is marked as dirty regardless of whether the final value is different from the original. Since the dirty flag is set upon any write (even an 'identical' update), the EXEC command identifies the key as modified and refuses to execute the transaction to prevent race conditions.
questions.hint: Think about how Redis tracks changes to keys during a WATCH session: does it compare values or just check for write activity?
questions.relatedConcept: Optimistic Locking and WATCH semantics
questions.interviewTip: This question reveals if the candidate understands the difference between 'logical' value change and 'physical' state change in Redis internals.

questions.question:
Consider the following Lua script executed with EVAL in Redis:
```
local cur = redis.call('GET', 'counter')
if not cur then
    redis.call('SET', 'counter', 0)
end
redis.call('INCR', 'counter')
redis.call('INCR', 'counter')
error('forced')
redis.call('INCR', 'counter')
return redis.call('GET', 'counter')
```
After the script finishes (whether it succeeds or aborts), what will be the state of the key `counter`?
options: The key will be created with value 2
No changes are applied; the key remains as it was before the script
The key will be created with value 3
The key will be created with value 4
questions.correctAnswer: No changes are applied; the key remains as it was before the script
questions.explanation: Redis executes a Lua script atomically. If the script raises an error (as done with `error('forced')`), the entire script is rolled back and none of the write commands (`SET` or `INCR`) take effect. Therefore the key `counter` is left untouched (or stays at its previous value if it already existed).
questions.hint: Remember that a Redis Lua script either runs completely or makes no changes at all.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Lua scripting atomicity and error handling
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify that candidates know a script's all‑or‑nothing nature and that partial writes are not persisted on script errors.

questions.question: In Redis, when using the Lua scripting environment, what is the impact of performing a write operation after a read operation on a key that has been modified by a non-deterministic command within the same script?
options: The script will proceed, but the write operation will be ignored by replicas.
The script will be aborted and raise an error to maintain replication integrity.
The script will execute successfully, but the non-deterministic result will be broadcast to replicas as a fixed value.
The script will be terminated and the Redis server will transition into a read-only state.
questions.correctAnswer: The script will be aborted and raise an error to maintain replication integrity.
questions.explanation: Redis enforces that scripts must be deterministic. If a script performs a write operation after a read operation, and that read could have been affected by a non-deterministic command (like TIME or a random command) executed earlier in the script, Redis will block the write to prevent replication divergence.
questions.hint: Consider how Redis ensures scripts produce identical state changes on both the primary and all replicas.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Lua Scripting Determinism
questions.interviewTip: This tests depth regarding Redis replication guarantees and the strict constraints required for script atomicity.

questions.question: Considering Redis Lua script semantics, what Redis RESP protocol reply type does the client receive when a script executed via `EVAL` contains the statement `return 0`?
options: Bulk string "0"
Integer reply
Nil reply
Status reply OK
questions.correctAnswer: Integer reply
questions.explanation: In Redis Lua, `return 0` yields an integer reply per the RESP protocol, distinguishing it from `return "0"` (bulk string) and `return nil` (nil). This tests the subtle distinction between Lua return types and Redis reply formatting.
questions.hint: Remember that Redis Lua scripts map return types directly to RESP types; `0` is not a string unless explicitly quoted as `"0"`.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis Lua scripting return type semantics
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to gauge depth of understanding beyond basic EVAL usage, focusing on protocol-level behavior and edge cases.

title: Redis - Test 2: Technical Assessment
description: Test 2 for Redis. Every question is unique against the whole question database — no repeats, no renumbered or reworded variants of an existing question.

questions.question:
You execute the following sequence of Redis commands from a client:
```
WATCH mykey otherkey
GET mykey
MULTI
SET mykey "newvalue"
EXEC
```
While this client is paused between the `WATCH` and `EXEC`, another client runs `INCR mykey`. What will be the result of the `EXEC` command?
options: The transaction succeeds and `mykey` is set to "newvalue".
The transaction fails and `EXEC` returns a null multi-bulk reply, leaving `mykey` unchanged.
Only the modifications to `otherkey` are applied, while the change to `mykey` is discarded.
`EXEC` raises an error indicating that the watched key was modified.
questions.correctAnswer: The transaction fails and `EXEC` returns a null multi-bulk reply, leaving `mykey` unchanged.
questions.explanation: When any key watched by `WATCH` is modified by another client before `EXEC`, Redis aborts the transaction. `EXEC` returns a null multi‑bulk reply (nil) and none of the queued commands are applied. The other options describe behaviours that do not occur: the transaction does not succeed, no partial execution happens, and Redis does not raise an error—it simply returns nil.
questions.hint: Remember how optimistic locking works with `WATCH` in Redis.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis optimistic concurrency control using WATCH/MULTI/EXEC
questions.interviewTip: This question reveals whether the candidate understands Redis's transaction semantics and how to handle race conditions.

questions.question: A Redis HyperLogLog structure is used to estimate the cardinality of a large set. After adding 100,000 distinct elements with `PFADD`, you call `PFCOUNT`. Which statement about the returned value is correct?
options: The value returned by `PFCOUNT` will be exactly 100,000.
`PFCOUNT` returns the number of registers that are currently non‑zero.
The value is an approximation with a typical standard error of about 0.81 %.
The returned count is always a power of two.
questions.correctAnswer: The value is an approximation with a typical standard error of about 0.81 %.
questions.explanation: HyperLogLog provides an approximate cardinality with a known standard error of 0.81 % (≈ ± 810 for 100,000 elements). It does not give an exact count, nor does it expose internal register details or enforce a power‑of‑two result. Hence option 2 is correct.
questions.hint: Think about the probabilistic nature of HyperLogLog.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis HyperLogLog data structure and its error characteristics
questions.interviewTip: The question checks if the candidate knows the trade‑off between memory efficiency and accuracy in Redis's probabilistic data structures.

questions.question: Suppose you execute the following sequence of commands in an active Redis connection. What will be the final state of the keys 'mykey' and 'otherkey' in the database?
options: The transaction is completely aborted and rolled back because of the INCR type error; neither 'mykey' nor 'otherkey' is modified.
'mykey' is set to "hello", but the execution halts immediately on the INCR error, leaving 'otherkey' unset.
The EXEC call fails at the syntax-queuing stage, so no commands are executed and both keys remain unchanged.
Both 'mykey' is set to "hello" and 'otherkey' is set to "world", while the response to the INCR command returns a runtime error.
questions.correctAnswer: Both 'mykey' is set to "hello" and 'otherkey' is set to "world", while the response to the INCR command returns a runtime error.
questions.explanation: In Redis, commands in a transaction (MULTI/EXEC block) that fail at runtime (such as calling INCR on a string value) do not cause a rollback of the entire transaction, nor do they halt execution of subsequent commands. Redis will execute every command in the queue and return the respective success or error result for each. This design choice is made to keep Redis highly performant and simple, relying on the client application to avoid type mismatches.
questions.hint: Redis transactions do not support rollbacks when a command successfully queues but fails during execution due to runtime types.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis transactions error handling and lack of rollback
questions.codeSnippet:
MULTI
SET mykey "hello"
INCR mykey
SET otherkey "world"
EXEC
questions.interviewTip: This question tests a developer's understanding of the fundamental differences between SQL database transactions and Redis transactions. It is a critical distinction for preventing silent data consistency issues in production.

questions.question: When invoking the 'SCAN' command with a 'MATCH' filter and a 'COUNT' hint, what is the underlying reason that a call may return an empty list of keys alongside a non-zero cursor, even when there are thousands of matching keys in the database?
options: Redis retrieves up to 'COUNT' elements from its internal hash table first, and then applies the 'MATCH' filter to only those elements, resulting in empty returns if no matches occur in that chunk.
The 'MATCH' filter is evaluated asynchronously via a background thread, which often fails to populate the active thread's scan buffer in time.
The 'COUNT' option represents the maximum number of matches to search for; if the cursor is non-zero, it means the search was deferred to avoid blockages.
Redis hash buckets containing matching patterns are skipped on the initial pass to prevent hash collisions, requiring subsequent cursor increments.
questions.correctAnswer: Redis retrieves up to 'COUNT' elements from its internal hash table first, and then applies the 'MATCH' filter to only those elements, resulting in empty returns if no matches occur in that chunk.
questions.explanation: The 'SCAN' command iterates over the dictionary of keys in the Redis database. The 'COUNT' argument is merely a hint that tells Redis how many elements to grab from the hash table structure in a single iteration step. The 'MATCH' filter is applied *after* these elements are fetched. If none of the keys fetched in that specific slice of the hash table match the pattern, the list of returned keys will be empty, but the non-zero cursor must still be used to continue iterating through the rest of the table.
questions.hint: Think about whether the filtering happens before or after the keys are pulled from the underlying hash table buckets.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis SCAN command mechanics and MATCH filtering
questions.codeSnippet: SCAN 0 MATCH "user:*" COUNT 10
questions.interviewTip: Developers often write infinite loops or incorrect termination conditions in their code when using SCAN because they assume a non-empty result is guaranteed if matching keys exist. Knowing this detail prevents critical application-level performance bugs.

questions.question: In a high-throughput Redis Pub/Sub architecture, if a subscribing client's message consumption rate falls significantly behind the publisher's message rate, how does Redis prevent this slow consumer from exhausting the server's memory?
options: It applies backpressure by throttling the publisher's thread to match the consumption rate of the slowest subscriber.
It terminates the connection of the slow subscriber once its dedicated client output buffer exceeds the configured limits.
It drops older messages from the slow subscriber's output buffer on a FIFO basis while keeping the connection alive.
It serializes the overflow messages for the slow client to a temporary disk-backed buffer.
questions.correctAnswer: It terminates the connection of the slow subscriber once its dedicated client output buffer exceeds the configured limits.
questions.explanation: Redis uses client output buffer limits to protect itself from memory exhaustion. For Pub/Sub clients, the default configuration (`client-output-buffer-limit pubsub 32mb 8mb 60`) means that if a client's output buffer exceeds a hard limit of 32MB, or remains above a soft limit of 8MB for 60 continuous seconds, Redis will forcibly close the connection to immediately free up the memory.
questions.hint: Think about how Redis prioritizes its single-threaded execution speed and absolute memory bounds over slow-client tolerance.
questions.relatedConcept: Redis client output buffer management and Pub/Sub scaling limits
questions.interviewTip: An interviewer wants to see if you understand the risks of using Redis Pub/Sub for high-throughput messaging. Highlighting how slow consumers can cause unexpected disconnects shows real-world production experience.

questions.question: When using Redis HyperLogLog commands (such as PFADD), Redis transitions the underlying key between 'sparse' and 'dense' encodings based on the 'hll-sparse-max-bytes' configuration. What is the primary operational trade-off of increasing this configuration value?
options: It increases the maximum memory required for high-cardinality keys beyond the standard 12KB ceiling.
It reduces the statistical error rate of PFCOUNT for large datasets by allocating more register bits.
It saves memory for low-cardinality keys but increases CPU usage for updates because the sparse representation is more computationally expensive to modify.
It improves the performance of PFMERGE operations at the expense of higher memory allocation latency during write peaks.
questions.correctAnswer: It saves memory for low-cardinality keys but increases CPU usage for updates because the sparse representation is more computationally expensive to modify.
questions.explanation: The sparse representation of HyperLogLog is highly space-optimized but much more CPU-intensive to update because it requires scanning and updating a packed representation.
