questions.explanation: An empty object literal {} is completely compatible with an interface where all properties are optional because structural subtyping allows missing optional properties without triggering excess property checks (excess property checks only apply to fresh object literals containing properties not found in the target type).
questions.hint: Consider whether excess property checks trigger when no properties are provided at all.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript Structural Typing with Optional Properties
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates understand the nuance between excess property checks and standard structural subtyping.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q25] What happens when you apply the `keyof` operator to a type that has a numeric index signature in TypeScript?
options: Keys evaluates to type `string`.
Keys evaluates to `number | string`.
TypeScript throws a compilation error because index signatures cannot be used with keyof.
Keys evaluates to type `number`.
questions.correctAnswer: Keys evaluates to type `number`.
questions.explanation: In TypeScript, when an interface or type has a numeric index signature, the `keyof` operator evaluates to `number` (and similarly, a string index signature evaluates to `string | number` because JavaScript object keys are coerced to strings, but specifically numeric index signatures yield `number`).
questions.hint: Think about what type JavaScript uses to index arrays or objects with numeric keys.
questions.relatedConcept: Numeric index signatures and keyof operator behavior
questions.interviewTip: Intervers use this to test your understanding of type-level operators and how JavaScript's runtime behavior maps to TypeScript's type system.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q26] Consider the following TypeScript code utilizing conditional types and deferred type checking. What is the precise reason TypeScript throws a compilation error on this snippet?
options: The return type `Unwrap<T>` is a conditional type that depends on the generic type parameter `T`, making it non-distributive or unconstrained, so the compiler cannot guarantee that `val` (of type `T`) is assignable to `Unwrap<T>` prior to instantiation.
The `infer` keyword cannot be used inside functions, only within type alias declarations.
Conditional types are evaluated only at runtime and cannot be used as function return annotations.
The variable `val` must be explicitly cast to `any` before it can be returned from a function with a conditional return type.
questions.correctAnswer: The return type `Unwrap<T>` is a conditional type that depends on the generic type parameter `T`, making it non-distributive or unconstrained, so the compiler cannot guarantee that `val` (of type `T`) is assignable to `Unwrap<T>` prior to instantiation.
questions.explanation: TypeScript considers conditional types whose checked type is a generic parameter (like `T extends ...`) to be dependent on that generic type. Because the compiler cannot verify that the generic type `T` is unconditionally assignable to the conditional return type `Unwrap<T>` for all possible instantiations of `T`, it flags a type safety error until a type assertion or constraint is applied.
questions.hint: Focus on why the compiler cannot prove assignability of an unconstrained generic type to a conditional type.
questions.relatedConcept: Generic conditional type assignability checks
questions.interviewTip: This tests deep familiarity with TypeScript's type checker limitations regarding generic conditional types and function return type verification.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q27] What is the primary runtime memory and performance trade-off of utilizing TypeScript 'enum' constructs compared to 'const enum' when compiled to standard JavaScript (ES5/ES6)?
options: Standard enums are optimized away by the TypeScript compiler into primitive numbers, while const enums require an external polyfill library to execute safely.

Standard enums generate bidirectional object maps at runtime, increasing bundle size and adding property lookup overhead, whereas const enums are completely inlined at usage sites leaving zero runtime artifacts.
Standard enums execute entirely on the type-checker level with no output, while const enums create heavy prototype inheritance chains at runtime.
Both standard and const enums generate identical IIFE objects at runtime, making their performance impact indistinguishable in modern V8 engines.
questions.correctAnswer: Standard enums generate bidirectional object maps at runtime, increasing bundle size and adding property lookup overhead, whereas const enums are completely inlined at usage sites leaving zero runtime artifacts.
questions.explanation: Standard TypeScript enums produce a physical JavaScript object mapping names to values and values to names (for reverse mapping), consuming memory and adding property lookups. Const enums are stripped entirely during compilation, replacing references directly with their literal values.
questions.hint: Consider how the compiler translates enum objects versus how it handles const declarations during lowering.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript Enum Compilation Overhead & Inlining Optimization
questions.codeSnippet: enum Direction { Up, Down }\nconst enum Status { Active, Inactive }
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test whether developers understand the distinction between TypeScript's type-level abstractions and their actual generated JavaScript runtime footprints.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q28] When leveraging TypeScript conditional types with distributive behavior over union types, what is the primary performance and complexity trap to avoid in large-scale type definitions?
options: Distributive conditional types disable all structural subtyping checks, leading to silent memory leaks in the V8 garbage collector during runtime execution.
Distributive conditional types force the TypeScript compiler to convert all union types into intersections, causing infinite recursion errors at runtime.

Distributive conditional types automatically trigger exponential type-checking instantiation and combinatorial explosion when evaluated over large union types, drastically slowing down IDE language server responsiveness.
Distributive conditional types prevent tree-shaking of unused modules during the Webpack or Vite bundling phase.
questions.correctAnswer: Distributive conditional types automatically trigger exponential type-checking instantiation and combinatorial explosion when evaluated over large union types, drastically slowing down IDE language server responsiveness.
questions.explanation: When a conditional type is distributive, TypeScript evaluates each member of the union separately. If fed a large union (e.g., unions of keys or nested structures), this creates a combinatorial explosion in instantiation paths, heavily impacting TypeScript compiler (tsc) performance.
questions.hint: Think about how TypeScript evaluates type aliases over massive union sets and the impact on the compiler's type instantiation pool.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript Type-Checking Complexity & Combinatorial Union Explosion
questions.codeSnippet: type Distributive<T> = T extends any ? Wrapper<T> : never;
questions.interviewTip: Senior engineers are often asked this to demonstrate awareness of compile-time performance bottlenecks in enterprise monorepos with heavy type-level programming.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q29] When a reviewer flags the use of TypeScript's 'any' type in a strict codebase, which idiomatic feature should they typically recommend as a type-safe alternative for values whose type is unknown at write-time?
options: never
void
Record<string, object>
unknown
questions.correctAnswer: unknown
questions.explanation: The 'unknown' type is the type-safe counterpart to 'any'. While anything is assignable to 'unknown', 'unknown' is not assignable to anything except itself and 'any' without performing a type narrowing check, preventing unsafe operations.
questions.hint: Think of the type that forces you to prove or narrow the type before you can call methods on it.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript type safety vs 'any' escape hatches
questions.interviewTip: Interweaves idiomatic code review standards with type-level mechanics.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q30] What code review concern does an idiomatic TypeScript linter flag when it encounters a non-null assertion operator ('!') placed at the end of a method chain?
options: It suppresses TypeScript's null-safety checks and can easily cause runtime TypeError crashes if any intermediate link is undefined.
It triggers an automatic boxing performance penalty because primitives are converted to wrapper objects.
It creates a circular module dependency warning during the compilation phase.
It forces the TypeScript compiler to downgrade the target ES version to ES5.
questions.correctAnswer: It suppresses TypeScript's null-safety checks and can easily cause runtime TypeError crashes if any intermediate link is undefined.
questions.explanation: The non-null assertion operator (!) blindly tells the compiler to trust that a value is neither null nor undefined. If an intermediate property turns out to be undefined at runtime, the application will throw a TypeError, undermining TypeScript's safety guarantees.
questions.hint: Consider what the '!' operator instructs the compiler to ignore.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript Non-null Assertion Operator anti-patterns
questions.codeSnippet: const length = user.getProfile()!.settings!.theme!.length;
questions.interviewTip: Evaluates a candidate's practical intuition regarding defensive coding and type assertions.

questions.question: What is the primary compilation and runtime behavior of TypeScript 'const enum' compared to a standard 'enum'?
options: Const enums generate a bidirectional JavaScript lookup object at runtime, identical to standard enums.
Const enums are completely removed during compilation, and member accesses are inlined with their literal values where possible.
Const enums throw a TypeScript compilation error if used outside of ambient declaration files (.d.ts).
Const enums defer their evaluation to runtime using a self-invoking function to populate the namespace.
questions.correctAnswer: Const enums are completely removed during compilation, and member accesses are inlined with their literal values where possible.
questions.explanation: TypeScript 'const enum' declarations do not emit any JavaScript object code at runtime. Instead, references to the enum members are inlined with their evaluated literal values during compilation, which reduces runtime footprint unless 'isolatedModules' or special flags dictate otherwise.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the generated JavaScript output for enum values vs constant enum values.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript Const Enums Inlining
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask about const enums to test your understanding of TypeScript's zero-cost abstractions versus runtime overhead and how bundling changes.

questions.question: What is the primary difference in behavior when using a 'const assertion' (as const) on an object literal versus a standard object declaration in TypeScript?
options: The object becomes immutable at runtime, preventing any changes to its properties via Object.defineProperty.
All properties of 'point' become readonly and the types are narrowed to literal types instead of generic primitives.
The object type is inferred with widened types, allowing future reassignment of individual property values.
It triggers a compile-time error if the object literal contains any function properties or nested objects.
questions.correctAnswer: All properties of 'point' become readonly and the types are narrowed to literal types instead of generic primitives.
questions.explanation: A 'const assertion' tells the compiler to treat the object as a readonly literal type. Properties become readonly and are assigned their specific literal values (e.g., 10 instead of number). It does not affect runtime immutability, as the object remains a standard JavaScript object subject to mutation if cast back.
questions.hint: Consider how TypeScript treats primitive types versus their literal equivalents.
questions.relatedConcept: const assertions and literal type widening
questions.codeSnippet:
const point = { x: 10, y: 20 } as const;

// Which of the following is true about 'point'?
questions.interviewTip: Understanding type narrowing and immutability markers is critical for building strictly typed configuration objects.

questions.question: In TypeScript, when using Discriminated Unions with a type guard, what is the behavior of the 'never' type in the 'default' case of a switch statement?
options: The code will fail at runtime because 'shape' is not assignable to 'never'.
The compiler will throw an error if a new member is added to the Shape union that is not handled in the switch.
The default branch is unreachable, so the variable '_exhaustiveCheck' is ignored by the compiler.
The switch statement will return 'undefined' if an unhandled member is passed.
questions.correctAnswer: The compiler will throw an error if a new member is added to the Shape union that is not handled in the switch.
questions.explanation: This pattern is known as exhaustive checking. By assigning the remaining 'shape' (which is inferred as 'never' in the default case) to a variable of type 'never', the TypeScript compiler forces the developer to handle all possible members of the union. If a new member is added to the union type, 'shape' will no longer be 'never' in the default branch, causing a compilation error.
questions.hint: Think about how TypeScript narrows types when using a default branch in a exhaustive union check.
questions.relatedConcept: Discriminated Unions and Exhaustive Checking
questions.interviewTip: Understanding this pattern demonstrates a high level of proficiency in writing type-safe code that prevents runtime errors when union types evolve.

questions.question: What is the outcome of the following TypeScript snippet involving mapped types and template literal types?
options: type Result = "a" | "b"
type Result = "getA" | "getB"
type Result = "geta" | "getb"
type Result = never
questions.correctAnswer: type Result = "getA" | "getB"
questions.explanation: The mapped type uses key remapping ('as') to transform the keys using template literal types and the Capitalize intrinsic. The resulting keys are 'getA' and 'getB'. Therefore, 'keyof Mapped' evaluates to the union of these transformed strings.
questions.hint: Focus on the key remapping syntax and how Capitalize interacts with string literals in types.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript Mapped Types and Key Remapping
questions.interviewTip: Understanding advanced type manipulation is crucial for building robust utility libraries or complex generic wrappers.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between TypeScript's `unknown` type and `any` type when performing property access or operations?
options: `unknown` allows property access if the value is inferred to be an object, whereas `any` throws a compile-time error for primitive types.
`any` bypasses all type checking, allowing arbitrary operations, whereas `unknown` requires type narrowing or assertion before operations can be performed.
`unknown` is an alias for `never`, meaning no values can be assigned to it, whereas `any` accepts any assignment.
`any` requires explicit casting for arithmetic operations, whereas `unknown` automatically coerces to numbers.
questions.correctAnswer: `any` bypasses all type checking, allowing arbitrary operations, whereas `unknown` requires type narrowing or assertion before operations can be performed.
questions.explanation: The `any` type opts out of type checking entirely, allowing any method or property access. The `unknown` type is its type-safe counterpart; TypeScript forces developers to perform a type check, type guard, or type assertion before interacting with a value of type `unknown`.
questions.hint: Think about type safety and compiler guarantees regarding operations on unrefined types.
questions.relatedConcept: unknown vs any type safety semantics
questions.codeSnippet:
let val: unknown = 'hello';
// val.length; // Error or allowed?
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers often ask this to verify whether you understand modern TypeScript's approach to type safety versus opting out of it.

questions.question: What is the primary difference in behavior between TypeScript's `interface` merging and `type` alias declarations when multiple declarations of the same name exist in the same scope?
options: Type aliases support declaration merging through intersection types, whereas interfaces only allow property overriding.
Interfaces automatically merge their property definitions into a single type, whereas type aliases throw a duplicate identifier error.
Interfaces support declaration merging only when declared across different modules, whereas type aliases merge globally.
Type aliases allow runtime extension of properties, whereas interfaces are strictly compile-time constructs that cannot merge.
questions.correctAnswer: Interfaces automatically merge their property definitions into a single type, whereas type aliases throw a duplicate identifier error.
questions.explanation: TypeScript interfaces are open and support declaration merging, meaning multiple declarations with the same name automatically combine their members. Type aliases, on the other hand, are distinct identifiers and will trigger a duplicate identifier error if redeclared in the same scope.
questions.hint: Think about which construct allows you to 'add' fields to an existing definition by simply declaring it a second time with the same name.
questions.relatedConcept: Declaration Merging vs Type Aliases
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test a candidate's understanding of structural typing limits and how TypeScript handles extension mechanisms between interfaces and types.

questions.question: In TypeScript, when utilizing a 'const assertion' (as const) on an array literal, which of the following best describes the resulting type inference compared to a standard array literal?
options: DataType becomes 'number[]'
DataType becomes 'readonly [1, 2, 3]'
DataType becomes 'readonly number[]'
DataType becomes '[1, 2, 3]'
questions.correctAnswer: DataType becomes 'readonly [1, 2, 3]'
questions.explanation: A const assertion ensures that the array is treated as a readonly tuple containing literal types, rather than a mutable array or a widened readonly array. 'number[]' is the default inference without 'as const', and 'readonly number[]' occurs with 'as const' only if the array contains expressions that cannot be strictly narrowed to literals.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between literal types and widened primitive types.
questions.relatedConcept: Const Assertions and Type Narrowing
questions.codeSnippet:
const data = [1, 2, 3] as const;
type DataType = typeof data;
questions.interviewTip: Const assertions are frequently used in modern TS to create immutable state or action types for Redux-like patterns; understanding this demonstrates a grasp of deep type inference.

questions.question: What is the result of accessing a property on a variable typed as 'unknown' in TypeScript without narrowing?
options: It returns 'undefined' at runtime and compiles successfully without errors.
A compile-time error occurs because 'unknown' requires narrowing before property access.
It compiles, but throws a 'TypeError: Cannot read property of undefined' at runtime.
It treats the variable as 'any', allowing the access but losing type safety.
questions.correctAnswer: A compile-time error occurs because 'unknown' requires narrowing before property access.
questions.explanation: In TypeScript, 'unknown' is the type-safe counterpart to 'any'. You cannot perform operations (like property access or function calls) on an 'unknown' type until you narrow it using a type guard or an assertion. 'any' would allow the access, but 'unknown' forces the developer to check the type first.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between the 'unknown' and 'any' types regarding safety and static analysis.
questions.relatedConcept: Type Safety and Type Narrowing
questions.interviewTip: Ask this to verify if the candidate understands why 'unknown' was introduced in TS 3.0 as a safer alternative to 'any'.

questions.question: What is the result of evaluating the following TypeScript expression involving literal types and template string types?
options: The expression results in true.
The expression results in false.
A compilation error occurs because 'getData' is not a valid Action.
The expression results in undefined.
questions.correctAnswer: The expression results in false.
questions.explanation: The template literal type `Action` resolves to the union type `'getData' | 'setData'`. When the code compares `val` (which is 'getData') to 'getData', it is true, but `val === 'setData'` is false. The logical AND operation results in false.
questions.hint: Template literal types generate a union of all possible string combinations.
questions.relatedConcept: Template Literal Types and Union Types
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate how template literal types improve type safety when working with dynamic string naming patterns like property accessors or event emitters.

questions.question: In TypeScript, consider the following code: `let x: any = 'foo'; let y = x.split('.');`. What is the value of `typeof y` if the string is 'a.b.c'?
options: string
object
array
undefined
questions.correctAnswer: object
questions.explanation: The `split` method of a string returns an array of substrings. Arrays are objects in JavaScript and TypeScript, so `typeof y` will be 'object'. The distractor 'array' is a common mistake because people often think arrays have a distinct type in `typeof`, but they do not. The distractor 'string' is incorrect because `split` does not return a single string. The distractor 'undefined' is incorrect because the method exists and returns a valid value.
questions.hint: Arrays are objects in JavaScript/TypeScript.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript any type and typeof behavior
questions.codeSnippet:
let x: any = 'a.b.c';
let y = x.split('.');
questions.interviewTip: This question tests the candidate's understanding of the `any` type in TypeScript, how it interacts with JavaScript runtime behavior, and the behavior of the `typeof` operator on arrays.

title: TypeScript - Test 2: Technical Assessment
description: Test 2 for TypeScript. Every question is unique against the whole question database — no repeats, no renumbered or reworded variants of an existing question.

questions.question: What is the result of evaluating the following TypeScript expression: `typeof (null as any).someProperty`?
options: undefined
null
any
Throws a TypeError at runtime
questions.correctAnswer: Throws a TypeError at runtime
questions.explanation: Even though TypeScript allows accessing properties on 'any' at compile time, the runtime evaluates the expression as an attempt to read a property of 'null', which causes a TypeError in standard JavaScript/TypeScript environments.
questions.hint: Think about how TypeScript's type system interacts with JavaScript's runtime behavior regarding null pointers.
questions.relatedConcept: Runtime type safety vs Compile-time type erasure
questions.interviewTip: Interviews use this to see if the candidate understands that TypeScript types vanish at runtime and that 'any' is not a magic shield against runtime exceptions.

questions.question: Given the following conditional type, what is the evaluated type of 'Result'?
options: string | number
string | number | never
string
any
questions.correctAnswer: string | number
questions.explanation: TypeScript uses 'distributive conditional types' when the type being checked (T) is a union. It maps over the union, applying the conditional to each member. 'boolean' is effectively 'true | false', neither of which have an 'id' property, resulting in 'never', which is filtered out of the resulting union.
questions.hint: Consider how conditional types treat union types during evaluation.
questions.relatedConcept: Distributive conditional types
questions.codeSnippet:
type ExtractId<T> = T extends { id: infer U } ? U : never;
type Result = ExtractId<{ id: string } | { id: number } | boolean>;
questions.interviewTip: This tests deep knowledge of advanced type inference and the mechanics of conditional type mapping.

questions.question: What is the result of using the 'in' operator to check for a key in a TypeScript object defined by an index signature versus one defined by explicit properties?
options: r1 is true, r2 is true
r1 is true, r2 is false
r1 is false, r2 is false
r1 is false, r2 is true
questions.correctAnswer: r1 is true, r2 is false
questions.explanation: In TypeScript, the 'in' operator checks for the existence of a key at runtime. For type 'A', the index signature implies the object might have any string key, but the object 'a' actually contains 'x'. For 'B', checking 'y' returns false because 'y' is not a property of 'b', and TypeScript's type system does not prevent 'in' from being used on specific property types.
questions.hint: Consider how the 'in' operator behaves at runtime versus how TypeScript validates object shapes.
questions.relatedConcept: Runtime type checking vs Compile-time structural typing
questions.interviewTip: Understanding the difference between TypeScript's compile-time safety and JavaScript's runtime behavior is crucial for debugging.

questions.question: When using 'keyof' on a type that includes a numeric index signature, what is the resulting type union?
options: type Keys = string | number
type Keys = 'name'
type Keys = number | 'name'
type Keys = string
questions.correctAnswer: type Keys = number | 'name'
questions.explanation: In TypeScript, when a type has a numeric index signature, 'keyof' returns the union of the number type and any explicitly defined string keys. Since 'name' is a string literal key, the result is 'number | 'name''.
questions.hint: Recall the special behavior of index signatures in keyof operations.
questions.relatedConcept: Mapped Types and keyof operator
questions.codeSnippet:
type Dictionary = { [key: number]: string; name: string };
type Keys = keyof Dictionary;
questions.interviewTip: This tests depth of knowledge regarding how TypeScript handles dynamic keys vs static keys.

questions.question: In TypeScript, when using mapped types to transform a read-only interface into a mutable one, what is the effect of the '-readonly' modifier within the mapped type declaration?
options: It generates a compile-time error if T contains any mutable properties.
It removes the 'readonly' modifier from each property of T.
It forces all properties of the resulting type to be optional.
It acts as a runtime instruction to delete the 'readonly' property descriptor.
questions.correctAnswer: It removes the 'readonly' modifier from each property of T.
questions.explanation: The '-' modifier (or plus '+') is used in mapped types to act as a prefix for modifiers like 'readonly' or '?' to strip them or add them, respectively, during type transformation.
questions.hint: Think of '-' as an operator that subtracts a type modifier.
questions.relatedConcept: Mapped Type Modifiers
questions.interviewTip: Understanding advanced mapped types is key to building reusable type utilities similar to those in the standard library.

questions.question: How does the 'satisfies' operator differ from explicit type annotation when assigning an object to a variable that has a union-based type definition?
options: It performs a structural subtyping check at runtime instead of compile-time.
It marks the variable as constant, preventing any future property reassignments.
It validates the object against the type without widening the variable's inferred type.
It forces the compiler to ignore excess properties during the object literal initialization.
questions.correctAnswer: It validates the object against the type without widening the variable's inferred type.
questions.explanation: The 'satisfies' operator ensures an expression matches a type, but preserves the most specific inferred type of the object (including extra properties), whereas explicit annotation widens the type to match exactly what is defined.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to the inferred type of 'c2' compared to 'c1'.
questions.relatedConcept: Type Satisfaction
questions.interviewTip: This feature is crucial for maintaining type safety while avoiding unnecessary type narrowing or loss of precision in configuration objects.

questions.question: When utilizing TypeScript's 'as const' assertion on an object literal, what is the resulting type behavior for its nested properties?
options: Only the top-level properties become readonly, while nested properties remain mutable.
The object is treated as a standard 'Readonly<T>' interface with primitive types inferred.
The object properties are inferred as their widened base types (e.g., 'string' instead of 'dark').
All properties become deeply readonly and literals are narrowed to their specific values.
questions.correctAnswer: All properties become deeply readonly and literals are narrowed to their specific values.
questions.explanation: The 'as const' assertion (const assertion) performs a deep readonly transformation and narrows literals to their exact values, rather than widening them to general types like 'string'.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between a shallow Readonly utility and a recursive constant assertion.
questions.relatedConcept: Const assertions and recursive type narrowing
questions.codeSnippet: const config = { settings: { theme: 'dark' } } as const;
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to see if the candidate understands how 'as const' differs from generic readonly constraints.

questions.question: In the context of TypeScript's Discriminated Unions, what must be true for the compiler to successfully perform control flow analysis when narrowing an object type?
options: The discriminant property must be a literal type or a union of literal types present in every member of the union.
The discriminant property must be named 'type' or 'kind' globally for the compiler to recognize it.
Every member of the union must have the exact same number of properties.
The discriminant property must be defined as an optional field in the interface definition.
questions.correctAnswer: The discriminant property must be a literal type or a union of literal types present in every member of the union.
questions.explanation: TypeScript's type narrowing relies on the discriminant property being a literal type (e.g., 'circle' or 'square') so that the compiler can exclude other union members after a check (e.g., 'if (s.kind === 'circle')').
questions.hint: What allows the compiler to discard members of a union during an 'if' or 'switch' statement?
questions.relatedConcept: Discriminated unions and exhaustive narrowing
questions.codeSnippet: type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; radius: number } | { kind: 'square'; side: number };
questions.interviewTip: This tests the candidate's ability to architect type-safe state machines using union patterns rather than loose interfaces.

questions.question: In TypeScript, when using a Discriminated Union, what happens if the discriminator property is missing in an object literal assigned to the union type?
options: The object is inferred as an empty object type, and no error is thrown.
A compile-time error occurs because the discriminator 'kind' is required.
The object is implicitly assigned the 'circle' type because it contains 'radius'.
The compiler issues a warning but allows the assignment if strict null checks are disabled.
questions.correctAnswer: A compile-time error occurs because the discriminator 'kind' is required.
questions.explanation: TypeScript's discriminated unions require the discriminator property ('kind') to be present to determine which variant of the union the object belongs to. Without it, the object does not satisfy either branch of the union.
questions.hint: Think about how TypeScript narrows types based on a shared literal property.
questions.relatedConcept: Discriminated Union Exhaustiveness
questions.codeSnippet:
type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; radius: number } | { kind: 'square'; side: number };
const s: Shape = { radius: 10 };
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands how the compiler uses literal types to enforce shape constraints.

questions.question: What is the result of using a conditional type to filter keys based on their value types, specifically when the condition involves 'any'?
options: Result is 'b'
Result is 'a' | 'c'
Result is 'a' | 'b' | 'c'
Result is never
questions.correctAnswer: Result is 'a' | 'b' | 'c'
questions.explanation: In TypeScript, the 'any' type is special; when used in a conditional type, it distributes over the union of 'true' and 'false' branches. Since everything extends 'any', the condition 'T[K] extends any' is always true for every property, resulting in all keys being preserved.
questions.hint: Remember that 'any' effectively short-circuits conditional type checks because it is compatible with everything.
questions.relatedConcept: Conditional Type Distribution
questions.codeSnippet:
type FilterAny<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends any ? K : never }[keyof T];
type Result = FilterAny<{ a: string; b: any; c: number }>;
questions.interviewTip: Distinguishing between 'any' and 'unknown' is a hallmark of an advanced TypeScript developer.

questions.question: In TypeScript, when using the 'infer' keyword within a conditional type to extract the return type of a function, what happens if the type parameter being inspected is a union of function types?
options: Result resolves to 'string'
Result resolves to 'never'
TypeScript throws a compilation error regarding ambiguous inference
Result resolves to 'string | number'
questions.correctAnswer: Result resolves to 'string | number'
questions.explanation: When a conditional type is distributed over a union type (T extends U ? V : W), the distribution occurs before the inference. Thus, the compiler evaluates the return type for each member of the union independently and returns the union of those results.
questions.hint: Recall the distributive property of conditional types over unions.
questions.relatedConcept: Distributive Conditional Types and Type Inference
questions.codeSnippet:
type ReturnTypeUnion<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;
type Result = ReturnTypeUnion<(() => string) | (() => number)>;
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands that generics behave differently when passed unions versus concrete types.

questions.question: What is the primary difference in behavior between using a 'keyof' type operator on an interface versus a 'keyof typeof' on a standard object instance?
options: T1 and T2 are equivalent as they both resolve to '"a" | "b"'
T1 includes only explicit keys, while T2 includes prototype chain properties
T1 is a type alias whereas T2 is a runtime value
T1 resolves to string literal types, while T2 resolves to index signature types
questions.correctAnswer: T1 and T2 are equivalent as they both resolve to '"a" | "b"'
questions.explanation: Both keyof Config and keyof typeof config resolve to the union of string literal types 'a' | 'b'. The 'typeof' operator is used here to transform the runtime object into a TypeScript type that represents the object's structure.
questions.hint: Does the type system distinguish the key set of an interface vs an inferred object structure?
questions.relatedConcept: Type Query and Index Types
questions.interviewTip: This validates knowledge of how TypeScript bridges the gap between runtime values and compile-time type definitions.

questions.question: When using TypeScript's conditional types to infer a return type, why does the following construct result in the 'never' type when T is a union type?
options: The conditional type is applied to each member of the union independently, resulting in 'string | never', which simplifies to 'string'.
The conditional type treats the union as a distribution; since the second member fails the check, it resolves to 'never', resulting in 'string | never'.
The conditional type evaluates the entire union type as a single entity, failing the 'success: true' check for the combined structure.
TypeScript requires the 'infer' keyword to correctly distribute conditional types over union members.
questions.correctAnswer: The conditional type treats the union as a distribution; since the second member fails the check, it resolves to 'never', resulting in 'string | never'.
questions.explanation: Distributive conditional types apply the conditional to each member of the union. 'ExtractResult' maps {success: true...} to 'string' and {success: false...} to 'never'. The union of these results is 'string | never', which simplifies to 'string'. Option 0 is a distractor describing the result correctly but misrepresenting the mechanism, while Option 2 accurately describes the distribution process.
questions.hint: Consider how TypeScript distributes types over union members in conditional types.
questions.relatedConcept: Distributive Conditional Types
questions.codeSnippet:
type ExtractResult<T> = T extends { success: true } ? T['data'] : never;
type Result = ExtractResult<{ success: true; data: string } | { success: false; error: Error }>;
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how generics behave with unions is critical for building library-level utility types.

questions.question: What is the primary reason that a TypeScript 'readonly' property on an interface does not guarantee complete immutability of the referenced object?
options: TypeScript's structural type system ignores 'readonly' modifiers during assignment unless 'exactOptionalPropertyTypes' is enabled.
The 'readonly' modifier is stripped during the transpilation process to JavaScript, meaning it only provides compile-time checks for shallow reassignment.
The 'readonly' modifier in interfaces only applies to the assignment of the property itself, not to the properties of the object assigned to it.
Because the 'settings' object was defined as an object literal, it is treated as mutable regardless of the interface definition.
questions.correctAnswer: The 'readonly' modifier in interfaces only applies to the assignment of the property itself, not to the properties of the object assigned to it.
questions.explanation: The 'readonly' modifier prevents reassignment of the property (e.g., c.settings = {...} would error), but it does not make the object referred to by that property deeply immutable. You can still mutate the nested properties of the object itself. Option 2 is a distractor because structural typing does not affect the 'readonly' behavior in this manner.
questions.hint: Think about the difference between shallow and deep immutability in TypeScript interfaces.
questions.relatedConcept: Shallow Immutability
questions.interviewTip: Mentioning 'Readonly<T>' utility type as a potential solution shows deeper knowledge of the standard library.

questions.question: What is the final type of the variable 'result' after the following TypeScript operation? Assume strict mode is enabled.
options: string
keyof Data
questions.explanation: The 'keyof' operator on a union type produces a union of the keys that are present in every member of that union. Since both '{ a: number }' and '{ b: string }' are distinct types, the result is the union of their shared keys ('never' if none) or specifically here, the literal types 'a' | 'b'.
questions.hint: Think about how keyof interacts with union types versus intersection types.
questions.relatedConcept: keyof operator behavior on unions
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate to explain why keyof behaves differently on objects compared to unions to gauge depth of type system understanding.

questions.question: In TypeScript, what is the behavior of the following code regarding type narrowing within the 'if' block?
options: In block B, 'val' is narrowed to 'undefined'.
In block B, 'val' remains 'string | number | undefined'.
In block B, 'val' is narrowed to 'never'.
In block B, 'val' is narrowed to 'null'.
questions.correctAnswer: In block B, 'val' is narrowed to 'undefined'.
questions.explanation: TypeScript's control flow analysis performs exhaustiveness checking. Since the function signature defines 'val' as 'string | number | undefined', removing 'string' and 'number' via the 'if' condition leaves only 'undefined' in the 'else' branch.
questions.hint: Consider the excluded types by the conditional check.
questions.relatedConcept: Control flow analysis and type narrowing
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands how the compiler automatically calculates the remaining possible type space in branches.

questions.question: In TypeScript, when using the 'private' modifier on a class property, what happens when the code is compiled to JavaScript using the standard 'tsc' compiler?
options: The compiler throws an error, and the code fails to build because 'secret' is inaccessible.
The code compiles successfully, and the console outputs 'hidden' at runtime.
The code compiles, but the JavaScript engine throws a ReferenceError at runtime due to private scope enforcement.
The compiler renames the property to '__secret' to prevent access in the generated JavaScript code.
questions.correctAnswer: The code compiles successfully, and the console outputs 'hidden' at runtime.
questions.explanation: TypeScript's 'private' modifier is a compile-time construct only. It is stripped away during transpilation to standard JavaScript. Therefore, at runtime, the property exists and can be accessed via bracket notation or by casting to 'any'.
questions.hint: Consider the relationship between TypeScript's type system and the generated JavaScript output.
questions.relatedConcept: Compile-time vs Runtime type erasure
questions.interviewTip: Ask candidates to explain how to achieve actual runtime privacy.

questions.question: Which of the following scenarios best describes the behavior of TypeScript's 'discriminated union' narrowing using a 'switch' statement?
options: The code fails to compile because the compiler cannot determine the type of 's' inside the switch blocks.
The 'switch' statement does not support type narrowing; an 'if-else' chain must be used instead.
The compiler correctly narrows the type 's' based on the 'kind' property in each case branch.
The compiler will infer that 's' is 'never' in the default case, even if an exhaustive switch is not used.
questions.correctAnswer: The compiler correctly narrows the type 's' based on the 'kind' property in each case branch.
questions.explanation: TypeScript uses the literal types of the 'kind' property to perform control flow-based type narrowing. Within the 'circle' case, 's' is automatically narrowed to '{ kind: 'circle'; radius: number }', allowing access to the 'radius' property.
questions.hint: Think about how TypeScript tracks control flow and state changes within blocks.
questions.relatedConcept: Discriminated Unions and Type Narrowing
questions.interviewTip: This question reveals if a developer understands idiomatic TypeScript patterns for handling polymorphic data without relying on 'instanceof' or 'any' types.

questions.question: What is the primary result of using the 'satisfies' operator versus an explicit type annotation when initializing a configuration object in TypeScript?
options: config1 preserves the specific literal type of its properties; config2 narrows them to the base types defined in Config.
config1 requires an explicit cast to access 'extra'; config2 allows 'extra' access without any type assertion.
Both variables result in identical type inference where 'extra' is discarded at runtime.
config1 throws a compile-time error due to excess properties; config2 does not, but preserves the inferred type of its properties.
questions.correctAnswer: config1 throws a compile-time error due to excess properties; config2 does not, but preserves the inferred type of its properties.
questions.explanation: Explicit type annotations (config1) strictly enforce that the object matches the shape, causing an error on excess properties. 'satisfies' checks for structural compatibility without discarding the specific inferred types (e.g., if 'port' was 8080, config2 knows it is 8080, whereas config1 only knows it is a number).
questions.hint: Think about how 'satisfies' handles property widening versus strict assignment.
questions.relatedConcept: satisfies operator type inference
questions.interviewTip: This tests knowledge of modern TypeScript features that solve the trade-off between strict type checking and type inference preservation.

questions.question: In TypeScript, when using a Template Literal Type as a key for a mapped type, what is the behavior if the template includes a conditional type check for specific string segments?
options: TypeScript successfully validates that all keys defined in Endpoint are present in the object.
The compiler throws an error because template literal types cannot be used as mapped type keys.
The object will fail because 'getAPI' and 'getUI' are not considered valid identifiers for mapped types.
TypeScript requires an explicit index signature, otherwise the mapped type defaults to 'any'.
questions.correctAnswer: TypeScript successfully validates that all keys defined in Endpoint are present in the object.
questions.explanation: TypeScript fully supports template literal types as keys in mapped types. The compiler correctly maps the union of literal types to the expected object shape.
questions.hint: Mapped types can iterate over any union of string-like types, including those generated by template literals.
questions.relatedConcept: Template literal types in mapped types
questions.interviewTip: This demonstrates proficiency with advanced type transformations and DSL-like type construction.

questions.question: What is the primary security concern when using TypeScript's 'as unknown as T' assertion to bypass type safety when processing data from an external API?
options: It causes the TypeScript compiler to emit unsafe JavaScript that skips all property checks at runtime.
It silences the compiler but does not provide runtime validation, potentially allowing malicious payloads to reach application logic.
It automatically upgrades the prototype of the object to match the 'User' interface definition.
It prevents the object from being serialized back to JSON if it contains extra properties.
questions.correctAnswer: It silences the compiler but does not provide runtime validation, potentially allowing malicious payloads to reach application logic.
questions.explanation: Type assertions in TypeScript are compile-time constructs only and are removed during transpilation. Asserting a type ('as T') does not perform any runtime check, meaning if the API returns unexpected data, the application will treat it as a valid User, leading to potential security vulnerabilities or runtime errors.
questions.hint: Consider that TypeScript types do not exist in the final JavaScript bundle.
questions.relatedConcept: Runtime type safety vs. compile-time type erasure
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate how they would safely validate API responses instead of using 'as' assertions.

questions.question: Which scenario best illustrates the 'Declaration Merging' vulnerability when extending global interfaces in TypeScript?
options: It forces the JavaScript engine to reallocate memory for all existing string objects, causing performance degradation.
It prevents the use of strict mode in the resulting JavaScript output.
Polluting global built-in prototypes with custom methods can lead to name collisions and unexpected behavior if multiple libraries perform similar merges.
It restricts the global namespace, causing subsequent modules to throw compile-time errors.
questions.correctAnswer: Polluting global built-in prototypes with custom methods can lead to name collisions and unexpected behavior if multiple libraries perform similar merges.
questions.explanation: Declaration merging allows developers to extend existing types, but when applied to built-in objects like String or Array, it modifies the global prototype. This can cause severe issues if different libraries try to define the same method name or if a third-party script overrides the implementation, leading to unpredictable or insecure application behavior.
questions.hint: Think about the scope of modifying global objects in a modularized environment.
questions.relatedConcept: Global namespace pollution via declaration merging
questions.codeSnippet:
interface String { encrypt(): string; }
String.prototype.encrypt = function() { return btoa(this.toString()); };
questions.interviewTip: Candidates should understand that while merging is a powerful TypeScript feature, it should be avoided for global primitives.

questions.question: In TypeScript, when utilizing declaration merging between an 'interface' and a 'namespace' of the same name, what is the mandatory requirement for the interface to correctly extend or interact with the exported members of the namespace?
options: The interface must be declared before the namespace, and the namespace must be marked with the 'declare' keyword.
Declaration merging between an interface and a namespace is only possible if the interface is defined within a module that uses 'export ='.
The interface members must be prefixed with the namespace name to be considered part of the merged declaration.
The interface must be declared after the namespace, and members must be explicitly exported using the 'export' keyword.
questions.correctAnswer: The interface must be declared after the namespace, and members must be explicitly exported using the 'export' keyword.
questions.explanation: TypeScript allows declaration merging between interfaces and namespaces. For the interface to see and interact with the namespace's exported members, the namespace must explicitly export them, and the interface must be defined in the same block or merged scope.
questions.hint: Think about how module scopes and exports interact during the declaration merging process.
questions.relatedConcept: Declaration Merging
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands how TypeScript extends JavaScript's prototype-based behavior with static type-system constructs.

questions.question: When using TypeScript's 'Template Literal Types', why does the compiler fail to infer a specific literal type when a template string contains a union of numeric literals but is assigned to a generic type constrained by 'string'?
options: The compiler defaults to the 'string' primitive type unless the function signature explicitly maps input types to return types using mapped types.
Template literal types cannot contain numeric unions and will always resolve to 'string' immediately upon instantiation.
TypeScript intentionally avoids narrowing generic constraints based on template literals to prevent exponential compile-time complexity.
The 'Template' type must be explicitly cast to 'any' to bypass the string constraint defined in the generic.
questions.correctAnswer: The compiler defaults to the 'string' primitive type unless the function signature explicitly maps input types to return types using mapped types.
questions.explanation: When a template literal is passed into a generic constrained by 'string', TypeScript defaults to the base primitive 'string' rather than the specific template literal, unless the generic is mapped or constrained more strictly to ensure preservation of the literal type.
questions.hint: Consider how generic type inference interacts with wider vs. narrower type constraints.
questions.relatedConcept: Template Literal Types and Generic Inference
questions.interviewTip: Answering this demonstrates an advanced understanding of how the TypeScript compiler handles type widening within generic functions.

questions.question: What is the behavior of the TypeScript compiler when resolving a discriminated union type if the discriminant property is missing from an object literal?
options: The object literal is inferred as the first member of the union by default.
A compile-time error occurs because the object literal does not match any member of the union.
The code compiles successfully because TypeScript performs structural type checking without regard for discriminants.
The code compiles but throws a runtime TypeError when accessed.
questions.correctAnswer: A compile-time error occurs because the object literal does not match any member of the union.
questions.explanation: TypeScript's control flow analysis requires the discriminant property to be present to correctly narrow the type. Since neither member of the union is satisfied, it reports an error.
questions.hint: Consider how TS determines which member of a union an object literal belongs to.
questions.relatedConcept: Discriminated Union Type Safety
questions.codeSnippet:
type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; radius: number } | { kind: 'square'; side: number };
const myShape: Shape = { radius: 10 };
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate how they would make the property optional if they still wanted the union logic to hold.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the behavior of a 'readonly' modifier on a property in an interface compared to 'readonly' on a mapped type?
options: The '-readonly' syntax has no effect on properties defined as 'readonly' in an interface.
The mapped type will still be readonly because interface-level modifiers cannot be overridden.
The '-readonly' syntax in a mapped type explicitly removes the readonly constraint from the original interface properties.
The code will fail to compile because mapped types cannot iterate over interface properties.
questions.correctAnswer: The '-readonly' syntax in a mapped type explicitly removes the readonly constraint from the original interface properties.
questions.explanation: The '-' prefix in a mapped type is a modifier that specifically removes the readonly (or optional) property from the target type.
questions.hint: The '-' operator in TypeScript mapped types is a feature for modifying existing type constraints.
questions.relatedConcept: Mapped Type Modifiers
questions.codeSnippet:
interface Config { readonly id: string; }
type MutableConfig = { -readonly [P in keyof Config]: Config[P] };
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands advanced type manipulation beyond basic interfaces.

questions.question: What is the consequence of utilizing the 'override' modifier on a class method in TypeScript 4.3+ when no corresponding method exists in the base class?
options: The method is treated as a new method with a warning.
The runtime prototype chain for the method is discarded.
The 'override' keyword is ignored and the method is treated as a regular member.
A compile-time error is generated.
questions.correctAnswer: A compile-time error is generated.
questions.explanation: TypeScript's 'override' modifier requires the base class to have a member with the same name. If no such member exists in the base class, the compiler raises an error ('This member cannot have an 'override' modifier because it is not declared in the base class'), preventing silent bugs where the developer expects to be overriding a method that was removed or renamed.
questions.hint: Think about what the 'override' keyword is meant to enforce regarding the class hierarchy.
questions.relatedConcept: Class member modifiers and inheritance safety
questions.interviewTip: This tests knowledge of modern TypeScript features designed to improve refactoring safety in object-oriented code.

questions.question: When using 'noUncheckedIndexedAccess', what is the inferred type of a property accessed via a dynamic string index on an interface?
options: number | undefined
number
any
unknown
questions.correctAnswer: number | undefined
questions.explanation: With 'noUncheckedIndexedAccess' enabled, TypeScript treats any indexed access as potentially undefined because the index might not exist in the object at runtime, even if the index signature return type suggests otherwise. Therefore, accessing c['b'] results in 'number | undefined'.
questions.hint: Consider how the compiler mitigates runtime errors for non-existent object keys.
questions.relatedConcept: Compiler configuration and type safety of index signatures
questions.interviewTip: This tests familiarity with strict compiler options that go beyond basic type definitions to prevent common runtime crashes.

questions.question: In TypeScript, what is the fundamental behavioral difference between a 'type' alias and an 'interface' when defining recursive structures?
options: There is no functional difference; both handle recursive references with identical compile-time performance.
Interfaces can be directly referenced in their own declaration, while type aliases require an explicit wrapper or explicit circular type definition in strict mode.
Type aliases support 'declaration merging' for recursive structures, whereas interfaces do not.
Interfaces cannot represent optional recursive properties, forcing the use of type aliases for linked-list data structures.
questions.correctAnswer: Interfaces can be directly referenced in their own declaration, while type aliases require an explicit wrapper or explicit circular type definition in strict mode.
questions.explanation: TypeScript interfaces are lazily evaluated and can refer to themselves directly. Type aliases often require explicit type annotation or handling to avoid 'circular reference' errors in specific configurations, although they are mostly interchangeable for simple recursive types.
questions.hint: Consider how the compiler validates circularity during interface vs. type resolution.
questions.relatedConcept: Recursive type definitions and compiler resolution
questions.codeSnippet:
type RecursiveType = { next: RecursiveType | null };
interface RecursiveInterface { next: RecursiveInterface | null };
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how the compiler resolves recursive types helps in building complex data models like trees or graphs in TS.

questions.question: When using TypeScript's 'satisfies' operator versus explicit type annotation, what is the primary advantage regarding object literal inference?
options: It forces the object to be read-only, preventing subsequent mutation of properties.
It removes the need for type narrowing when accessing properties, as the object is cast to the interface type.
It validates the object structure against a type while preserving the specific, narrow literal types of the object's properties.
It optimizes the bundle size by stripping the interface definition during the transpilation process.
questions.correctAnswer: It validates the object structure against a type while preserving the specific, narrow literal types of the object's properties.
questions.explanation: The 'satisfies' operator checks that an expression matches a type without coercing the expression to that type, keeping the specific literal values (e.g., 'red' vs 'string') intact for better type inference.
questions.hint: Think about whether 'satisfies' changes the inferred type to a wider supertype.
questions.relatedConcept: Type narrowing vs. type assertion
questions.codeSnippet: const palette = { primary: 'red', secondary: 'blue' } satisfies Record<string, string>;
questions.interviewTip: This is a key feature of modern TS (4.9+) used to improve type safety without losing metadata.

questions.question: What is the exact behavior of TypeScript's 'override' modifier when used in a derived class method?
options: It is emitted into the compiled JavaScript output as a runtime check to enforce method overriding semantics.
It is a compile-time check ensuring that a method with the same name exists in a superclass.
It makes the method automatically public and un-overridable by any further subclasses.
It is purely an IDE documentation hint and is completely ignored by the TypeScript compiler.
questions.correctAnswer: It is a compile-time check ensuring that a method with the same name exists in a superclass.
questions.explanation: The 'override' modifier (introduced in TypeScript 4.3 with the '--noImplicitOverride' flag) is purely a compile-time check. It ensures that if a method is marked with 'override', a corresponding method with the exact same name must exist on one of the base classes, preventing accidental overriding due to typos or base class refactoring. It is completely stripped out during JavaScript compilation.
questions.hint: Think about whether TypeScript modifiers always translate to runtime statements or if some are purely for static analysis.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript override modifier and static compilation guarantees
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of TypeScript's type-erasure model versus C# or Java-like languages that retain metadata or enforce overrides at runtime.

questions.question: In TypeScript, what is the behavior of the 'readonly' modifier when applied to an interface property that holds a reference to a mutable object, such as an array?
options: The code fails to compile because the array contents are implicitly readonly.
The code compiles successfully, and the array can be mutated.
The code compiles, but attempting to call .push() results in a runtime TypeError.
The code fails to compile because readonly interfaces cannot contain reference types.
questions.correctAnswer: The code compiles successfully, and the array can be mutated.
questions.explanation: The 'readonly' modifier in TypeScript prevents re-assignment of the property itself, but it does not perform a 'deep' freeze on the object it refers to. Therefore, the array instance can still be mutated via its methods like push().
questions.hint: Think about whether readonly creates a shallow or deep immutability.
questions.relatedConcept: Readonly modifier mechanics
questions.interviewTip: Understanding the difference between reference immutability and deep immutability is crucial for avoiding subtle state-mutation bugs in large TS applications.

questions.question: In TypeScript, what is the outcome of the following code snippet regarding the behavior of the 'in' operator on a partial object?
options: hasAge is true, because the key 'age' exists in the object at runtime.
hasAge is false, because the property 'age' is not initialized.
hasAge is false, because 'Partial' removes the property from the runtime object.
A runtime error occurs because 'in' operator cannot be used with partial types.
questions.correctAnswer: hasAge is false, because the property 'age' is not initialized.
questions.explanation: The 'Partial<T>' utility type only modifies the type signature to make properties optional for compile-time checking. It does not alter the runtime representation of the object. Since the object 'partialUser' was initialized without the 'age' key, the property does not exist in the object, so 'age' in partialUser evaluates to false.
questions.hint: Utility types like Partial affect compile-time types, not runtime object structure.
questions.relatedConcept: Runtime vs Compile-time semantics of TypeScript Utility Types
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands that TypeScript's type system is erased during compilation and utility types do not modify the actual JavaScript object literal structure.

questions.question: What is the final evaluated type of the variable 'result' in the following TypeScript snippet?
options: string
string | number
Container<string> | number
any
questions.correctAnswer: string | number
questions.explanation: When a conditional type with an 'infer' clause is applied to a union type, TypeScript distributes the conditional type over the union members. For 'Container<string>', it extracts 'string'. For 'number', the conditional condition fails, returning 'number'. Thus, the result is 'string | number'.
questions.hint: Conditional types distribute over union types automatically.
questions.relatedConcept: Distributive Conditional Types
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how conditional types interact with unions is crucial for writing sophisticated utility types in advanced TypeScript development.

questions.question: What is the primary compilation and type-checking behavior of TypeScript's `as const` assertion when applied to an object literal?
options: It compiles the object into a frozen JavaScript object using Object.freeze() at runtime, preventing mutations.
It makes all properties readonly and infers narrow literal types for the values rather than widening them to primitive types.
It transforms the object into a TypeScript interface type definition rather than a concrete value.
It suppresses all strict type-checking errors for properties nested within the object literal.
questions.correctAnswer: It makes all properties readonly and infers narrow literal types for the values rather than widening them to primitive types.
questions.explanation: The `as const` assertion is a type-system construct that signals to TypeScript to infer the most specific (narrow) literal type for an expression, and recursively marks properties as `readonly`. It does not emit runtime calls like `Object.freeze()` unless explicitly combined with runtime code, nor does it convert objects into interfaces.
questions.hint: Consider how literal types are widened (e.g., string to 'string') during standard inference versus when using a const assertion.
questions.relatedConcept: Const assertions and literal type narrowing
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers often ask this to verify whether a candidate understands the boundary between TypeScript's compile-time type system and runtime JavaScript behavior.

questions.question: What are the resolved types of Result1 and Result2 in the following TypeScript code?
options: Result1 is (string | number)[], and Result2 is string[] | number[]
Result1 is string[] | number[], and Result2 is (string | number)[]
Both Result1 and Result2 are resolved to (string | number)[]
Both Result1 and Result2 are resolved to string[] | number[]
questions.correctAnswer: Result1 is string[] | number[], and Result2 is (string | number)[]
questions.explanation: In TypeScript, conditional types distribute over union types if the checked type parameter is 'naked' (i.e., not wrapped in another generic or a tuple). Thus, Box<string | number> distributes into Box<string> | Box<number>, resulting in string[] | number[]. By wrapping T inside a tuple [T], the type parameter is no longer naked, which disables distribution. Consequently, NonDistBox evaluates the union as a single consolidated type, yielding (string | number)[].
questions.hint: Think about how TypeScript conditional types behave when acting on naked type parameters vs wrapped tuple types.
questions.relatedConcept: Distributive Conditional Types
questions.interviewTip: Understanding distributive conditional types is crucial when writing advanced utility types or design system components in TypeScript, especially when you need to conditionally format or match unions without splitting them.

questions.question: What is the behavior of the following TypeScript snippet concerning type narrowing within a conditional block involving a user-defined type guard?
options: The type of 'input' is inferred as 'string'.
The type of 'input' is inferred as 'string | number'.
The type of 'input' is inferred as 'never'.
The type of 'input' is inferred as 'unknown'.
questions.correctAnswer: The type of 'input' is inferred as 'string | number'.
questions.explanation: In TypeScript, when multiple type guards are joined by a logical OR (||) operator, the compiler only narrows the type if the resulting narrowing is sound for all branches of the expression. Because 'input' can be either a string or a number in the condition, TypeScript cannot guarantee a specific singular type within the block, reverting the union type to its original state.
questions.hint: Consider if the union type is fully exhausted by the combined conditions.
questions.relatedConcept: Type Guard union narrowing limitations
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how the TypeScript compiler handles complex control flow analysis helps candidates write more predictable code and avoid unnecessary type assertions.

questions.question: In TypeScript, what is the outcome of the following interaction between type narrowing and array methods?
options: The code fails to compile because 'arr' is inferred as string[] and cannot accept a number
The function returns an array of type (string | number)[]
The code compiles, but 'arr' is inferred as type 'any[]'
The function returns a tuple type [string, number]
questions.correctAnswer: The function returns an array of type (string | number)[]
questions.explanation: TypeScript uses control flow analysis to narrow the type of 'input' to 'string'. When 'const arr = [input]' is executed, TypeScript infers the array type based on the initial element as 'string[]'. However, subsequent mutations like 'arr.push(123)' trigger a widening of the inferred type to '(string | number)[]' to maintain type safety, allowing the push to succeed without compilation errors.
questions.hint: Consider how TypeScript's type inference handles array mutation after initial declaration.
questions.relatedConcept: Type inference and array mutation widening
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how TypeScript balances strictness with developer ergonomics in array literals is key to debugging unexpected 'Type is not assignable to' errors.

questions.question: What is the final evaluated type of the variable 'result' in the following TypeScript snippet, given strict null checks are enabled?
options: any
string | number
number
string
questions.correctAnswer: string | number
questions.explanation: TypeScript uses union types to track the potential values of a variable. Since 'arg' can be either type A or type B, and both have a property 'val', TypeScript infers the type of 'result' as the union of the types of those properties, which is 'number | string'.
questions.hint: Consider the intersection of properties available across all members of the union type.
questions.relatedConcept: Union Type Property Access
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how TypeScript performs narrowing versus union inference is key to writing safe generic code.

questions.question: Consider the following TypeScript code. What is the compile-time type of the variable 'result'? type StrictParam = { id: number; name: string }; type LooseParam = { id: number }; function process(config: StrictParam | LooseParam): void { // ... } const myConfig: StrictParam = { id: 1, name: 'Test' }; const result = process(myConfig);
options: StrictParam
void
LooseParam
Unknown because the parameter type is a union
questions.correctAnswer: void
questions.explanation: In TypeScript, when a parameter is typed as a union (A | B) and you pass a value that matches one of the specific constituent types (StrictParam is assignable to StrictParam | LooseParam), the compiler does not infer a specific return type based on the input's runtime shape. It simply uses the declared return type of the function, which is explicit as 'void'. The union in the parameter position accepts the input, but the return value is determined solely by the function signature, not by the specific input assigned. Therefore, 'result' has the type 'void'. A common trap is thinking TypeScript will narrow the return type to match the input, or that the union in the parameter 'contaminates' the return type.
questions.hint: Look at the function declaration's return type annotation, not the parameter type.
questions.relatedConcept: Function Return Type Inference and Union Parameter Acceptance
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands that parameter types dictate what you can *pass in*, while return types dictate what you get *out*. It checks for confidence in typing function signatures and avoids overthinking type narrowing on void functions.

title: UI/UX (Design) - Test 1: Core Fundamentals & Patterns
description: Comprehensive technical evaluation for UI/UX (Design) covering runtime mechanics, design principles, and problem solving.

questions.question: [UI/UX (Design) • Test 1 • Q1] In digital product design, what is the primary benefit of established typographic scales (Type Scale)?
options: Minimizes the download size of TTF font files.
Prevents CSS layout reflows on mobile devices.
Creates distinct visual hierarchy that guides scanning eyes from primary titles to metadata efficiently.
Enforces monochromatic color palettes across all screens.
questions.correctAnswer: Creates distinct visual hierarchy that guides scanning eyes from primary titles to metadata efficiently.
questions.explanation: A harmonic type scale (e.g., Major Third 1.25 or Golden Ratio 1.618) establishes intuitive relationships between headers, subheads, and body copy.
questions.hint: Harmonic font scale guides scannability and visual flow.
questions.relatedConcept: UI/UX (Design) - Typographic Hierarchy & Visual Scanning
questions.interviewTip: Maintain high line-height (1.5 - 1.6) on body text to maximize reading comfort.

questions.question: [UI/UX (Design) • Test 1 • Q2] What does Fitts's Law predict about user interaction with on-screen target elements?
options: The time required to rapidly move to a target is a function of the ratio between distance to the target and width of the target.
Users can hold at most 7 items in short-term memory (Miller's Law).
Decision time increases logarithmically with number of choices (Hick's Law).
Users perceive objects close together as belonging to the same group.
questions.correctAnswer: The time required to rapidly move to a target is a function of the ratio between distance to the target and width of the target.
questions.explanation: Fitts's law dictates that primary call-to-action buttons should be larger and closer to the user's cursor/thumb reach zone.
questions.hint: Target size and distance dictate acquisition time.
questions.relatedConcept: UI/UX (Design) - Fitts's Law in Interface Usability
questions.interviewTip: Screen corners and edges have infinite theoretical width because cursor cannot overshoot them.

questions.question: [UI/UX (Design) • Test 1 • Q3] According to Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.1 AA), what is the minimum contrast ratio required for standard body text?
options: 2.0:1 for all text elements.
7:1 for all text (this is AAA level).
4.5:1 against its background (3:1 for large text >= 18pt or bold >= 14pt).
10:1 strictly across dark mode interfaces.
questions.correctAnswer: 4.5:1 against its background (3:1 for large text >= 18pt or bold >= 14pt).
questions.explanation: WCAG AA compliance mandates at least 4.5:1 contrast for normal text to ensure readability for users with moderate visual impairments.
questions.hint: 4.5:1 for standard text; 3:1 for large text.
questions.relatedConcept: UI/UX (Design) - WCAG Accessibility Color Contrast
questions.interviewTip: Never rely on color alone to convey error states or interactive affordances.

questions.question: [UI/UX (Design) • Test 1 • Q4] In digital product design, what is the primary benefit of established typographic scales (Type Scale)? (Variant 1.4)
options: Creates distinct visual hierarchy that guides scanning eyes from primary titles to metadata efficiently.
Minimizes the download size of TTF font files.
Prevents CSS layout reflows on mobile devices.
Enforces monochromatic color palettes across all screens.
questions.correctAnswer: Creates distinct visual hierarchy that guides scanning eyes from primary titles to metadata efficiently.
questions.explanation: A harmonic type scale (e.g., Major Third 1.25 or Golden Ratio 1.618) establishes intuitive relationships between headers, subheads, and body copy.
questions.hint: Harmonic font scale guides scannability and visual flow.
questions.relatedConcept: UI/UX (Design) - Typographic Hierarchy & Visual Scanning
questions.interviewTip: Maintain high line-height (1.5 - 1.6) on body text to maximize reading comfort.

questions.question: [UI/UX (Design) • Test 1 • Q5] What does Fitts's Law predict about user interaction with on-screen target elements? (Variant 1.5)
options: Users can hold at most 7 items in short-term memory (Miller's Law).
Decision time increases logarithmically with number of choices (Hick's Law).
The time required to rapidly move to a target is a function of the ratio between distance to the target and width of the target.
Users perceive objects close together as belonging to the same group.
questions.correctAnswer: The time required to rapidly move to a target is a function of the ratio between distance to the target and width of the target.
questions.explanation: Fitts's law dictates that primary call-to-action buttons should be larger and closer to the user's cursor/thumb reach zone.
questions.hint: Target size and distance dictate acquisition time.
questions.relatedConcept: UI/UX (Design) - Fitts's Law in Interface Usability
questions.interviewTip: Screen corners and edges have infinite theoretical width because cursor cannot overshoot them.

questions.question: [UI/UX (Design) • Test 1 • Q6] According to Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.1 AA), what is the minimum contrast ratio required for standard body text? (Variant 1.6)
options: 4.5:1 against its background (3:1 for large text >= 18pt or bold >= 14pt).
2.0:1 for all text elements.
7:1 for all text (this is AAA level).
10:1 strictly across dark mode interfaces.
questions.correctAnswer: 4.5:1 against its background (3:1 for large text >= 18pt or bold >= 14pt).
questions.explanation: WCAG AA compliance mandates at least 4.5:1 contrast for normal text to ensure readability for users with moderate visual impairments.
questions.hint: 4.5:1 for standard text; 3:1 for large text.
questions.relatedConcept: UI/UX (Design) - WCAG Accessibility Color Contrast
questions.interviewTip: Never rely on color alone to convey error states or interactive affordances.

questions.question: [UI/UX (Design) • Test 1 • Q7] According to Hick's Law, how does the average decision time change when a menu expands from 4 equally likely options to 8 equally likely options?
options: It doubles
It increases by 50%
It stays the same
It halves
questions.correctAnswer: It increases by 50%
questions.explanation: Hick's Law states RT = a + b·log₂(N). Log₂(4)=2 and Log₂(8)=3, so decision time grows by a factor of 3/2 = 1.5, i.e., a 50 % increase. The other options misinterpret the logarithmic relationship.
questions.hint: Compare log₂(4) and log₂(8).
questions.relatedConcept: Hick's Law – decision time vs. number of choices
questions.interviewTip: Shows whether the candidate knows fundamental quantitative UX principles that affect menu design.

questions.question: [UI/UX (Design) • Test 1 • Q8] Which design adjustment best applies the Gestalt principle of proximity to make related form fields appear grouped together?
options: Use the same background color for all fields
Add decorative icons next to each field
