questions.relatedConcept: Component lifecycle cleanup and memory leaks
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to evaluate practical production awareness regarding memory management and cleanup habits in single-page applications.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q11] In Vue 3 Composition API, when should side effects that mutate DOM elements or perform asynchronous data fetching be executed relative to the component lifecycle?
options: Directly inside the setup() function body during synchronous execution to ensure immediate setup
Inside computed properties to leverage memoization for performance optimization
Inside template expressions to keep data binding declarative and side-effect free
Inside onMounted or watcher callbacks to guarantee the reactive scope and DOM nodes are fully initialized
questions.correctAnswer: Inside onMounted or watcher callbacks to guarantee the reactive scope and DOM nodes are fully initialized
questions.explanation: In Vue 3, setup() executes before the component is mounted to the DOM. Executing DOM mutations or async fetching directly in setup() lacks access to rendered DOM elements and can cause SSR hydration mismatches. Using lifecycle hooks like onMounted ensures proper DOM availability.
questions.hint: Think about when the actual DOM nodes are created and attached in a component's lifecycle.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 setup lifecycle and side effect management
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers check this to see if candidates understand Vue's reactivity initialization vs. DOM-dependent side effects.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q12] How does Vue 3 handle state updates when multiple reactive properties are mutated synchronously within a custom asynchronous event handler or macro task?
options: All mutations are batched into a single microtask queue and flushed asynchronously before the next browser paint
Each individual property mutation triggers an immediate, synchronous DOM re-render
Vue blocks the JavaScript main thread until all component sub-trees are fully synchronized
Mutations inside async tasks are ignored unless wrapped explicitly in $forceUpdate()
questions.correctAnswer: All mutations are batched into a single microtask queue and flushed asynchronously before the next browser paint
questions.explanation: Vue queues state mutations and buffers them in a queue to avoid redundant DOM re-renders when multiple state variables change within the same tick. The batching is flushed asynchronously via microtasks (like Promise.resolve() or MutationObserver).
questions.hint: Consider how Vue optimizes multiple synchronous state changes before updating the DOM.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue asynchronous rendering queue and DOM batching
questions.interviewTip: This tests deep knowledge of Vue's internal scheduler and asynchronous update cycle performance optimizations.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q13] When developing a Vue 3 application using the Composition API, you notice that mutating a property of a reactive object inside a nested child component does not trigger the expected UI update in a parent component computed property. Which of the following root causes best explains this symptom?
options: Provide/inject injections are read-only by default and silently block mutation attempts across component boundaries.
Destructuring reactive objects strips away their proxy reactivity wrappers, decoupling the local variable from the reactive source.
Nested objects inside reactive() calls automatically convert to shallowReactive, requiring manual deep tracking.
Computed properties cannot depend on values injected from a parent component unless explicitly wrapped in a watchEffect.
questions.correctAnswer: Destructuring reactive objects strips away their proxy reactivity wrappers, decoupling the local variable from the reactive source.
questions.explanation: Destructuring a reactive object created via reactive() breaks the reactivity connection because primitive values obtained via destructuring are plain values, not getter/setter proxies. The mutation or usage of the destructured variable will not track dependencies.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to JavaScript references when you destructure properties from a reactive proxy.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 reactive destructuring caveat and proxy loss
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates understand the limitations of JavaScript proxies when dealing with destructuring in Vue 3.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q14] In a Vue 3 application, a component's lifecycle hook `onMounted` fires, but attempts to query or manipulate a DOM element via a template ref yield `null`. Which of the following code patterns typically causes this specific symptom?
options: Template refs in Vue 3 cannot be accessed inside `onMounted` and must be delayed using `nextTick` unconditionally.
The `ref` variable name does not match the string attribute name provided in the template.
The element is conditionally rendered via `v-if`, and its initial evaluation evaluates to false during the mount phase.
Script setup syntax scopes template refs locally, preventing them from being exposed to lifecycle hooks.
questions.correctAnswer: The element is conditionally rendered via `v-if`, and its initial evaluation evaluates to false during the mount phase.
questions.explanation: If an element has a `v-if` directive that evaluates to false when the component mounts, it does not exist in the DOM, resulting in the template ref remaining `null` even inside `onMounted`.
questions.hint: Check conditional rendering directives attached to the element carrying the template ref.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue template refs with conditional rendering (v-if)
questions.interviewTip: This tests practical debugging skills regarding conditional rendering interactions with template refs in Vue.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q15] What happens when you pass a reactive object returned by `reactive()` directly into a Vue 3 `provide` call and consume it using `inject()` in a deeply nested descendant component?
options: The injected object loses reactivity because provide/inject strips Proxies during the context transfer.
Vue throws a runtime warning because reactive objects cannot be passed down via provide/inject without being wrapped in a computed property.
Mutations throw a readonly error unless the injected object is explicitly declared inside a readonly wrapper.
The injected object remains fully reactive, and mutations to its properties trigger updates across all consuming components.
questions.correctAnswer: The injected object remains fully reactive, and mutations to its properties trigger updates across all consuming components.
questions.explanation: In Vue 3, objects wrapped in `reactive()` maintain their Proxy-based reactivity when passed via `provide` and consumed via `inject`. Mutations made on the injected reference in descendant components will properly trigger reactivity updates.
questions.hint: Consider whether Vue's Proxy wrappers are preserved across the dependency injection context boundary.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Composition API Provide/Inject Reactivity Preservation
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to test your understanding of how Vue 3 maintains state synchronization and reactivity across component tree boundaries via provide and inject.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q16] In Vue 3, what is the precise behavior of the `v-memo` directive when its dependency array is passed as an empty array `v-memo="[]"`?
options: The template block is cached permanently after the initial render and will never update, even if component-level reactive dependencies change.
The template block re-evaluates and updates on every single component re-render cycle, effectively disabling optimization.
Vue throws a compilation error because `v-memo` requires at least one dependency expression inside its array.
The block behaves identically to `v-once`, but only caches internal child components rather than DOM nodes.
questions.correctAnswer: The template block is cached permanently after the initial render and will never update, even if component-level reactive dependencies change.
questions.explanation: When an empty array `[]` is passed to `v-memo`, the memoized template block will never re-evaluate or update after its initial render, since none of its dependencies ever change. This is functionally similar to `v-once` but scoped to a specific DOM subtree.
questions.hint: Think about what an empty dependency array means for conditional re-evaluation triggers in memoization algorithms.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 v-memo Directive Optimization Behavior
questions.codeSnippet: {{ expensiveComputation }}
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to verify whether candidates know advanced performance optimization techniques beyond standard computed properties and lazy loading.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q17] In Vue 3, how does the behavior of `v-model` change when applied to a custom component compared to Vue 2?
options: Vue 3 automatically infers the prop name from the component's internal name attribute rather than requiring explicit prop definitions.
Vue 3 replaces the default 'value' prop and 'input' event with 'modelValue' prop and 'update:modelValue' event, while supporting named model arguments.
Vue 3 removes custom component v-model support entirely, forcing developers to use explicit property bindings and custom event emitters.
Vue 3 retains the exact same 'value' prop and 'input' event contract from Vue 2, but wraps them in a Proxy for reactivity.
questions.correctAnswer: Vue 3 replaces the default 'value' prop and 'input' event with 'modelValue' prop and 'update:modelValue' event, while supporting named model arguments.
questions.explanation: Vue 3 standardizes `v-model` on custom components to use `modelValue` as the prop and `update:modelValue` as the emitted event by default, and introduces argument syntax like `v-model:title` to support multiple bindings on a single component.
questions.hint: Think about what props and events are automatically generated by the compiler for v-model in Vue 3.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Custom Component v-model API Changes
questions.codeSnippet: <MyComponent v-model:title="pageTitle" />
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers often ask this to verify migration knowledge from Vue 2 to Vue 3 and understanding of template compilation semantics.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q18] What is the primary architectural difference in how Vue 3 handles multiple root nodes in a Single File Component (SFC) template compared to Vue 2?
options: Vue 3 automatically injects a hidden <div> wrapper around multiple roots during compilation to satisfy DOM tree requirements.
Vue 3 throws a compilation error unless a single functional wrapper or <template v-slot> is provided.
Vue 3 supports Fragments out of the box, allowing components to have multiple root nodes without a wrapper element by explicitly patching the VNode children array.
Vue 3 delegates multiple root management entirely to the browser's native Shadow DOM implementation.
questions.correctAnswer: Vue 3 supports Fragments out of the box, allowing components to have multiple root nodes without a wrapper element by explicitly patching the VNode children array.
questions.explanation: Unlike Vue 2 which strictly enforced a single root element per SFC template, Vue 3 introduces Fragment support natively, allowing a component to render multiple root nodes and intelligently managing them via a flat VNode children array structure.
questions.hint: Consider the concept of 'Fragments' introduced in modern frontend frameworks to avoid unnecessary wrapper DOM nodes.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Template Fragments and Multi-Root Architecture
questions.codeSnippet:
<template>
  <header>Header</header>
  <main>Content</main>
</template>
questions.interviewTip: This question tests understanding of virtual DOM improvements and DOM structure optimization in Vue 3.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q19] When testing a Vue 3 component that uses Pinia stores via Vitest, what is the primary consequence of failing to call `setActivePinia()` before mounting the component with `mount()`?
options: The component will mount successfully, but all reactive store properties will remain permanently undefined.
Vue Test Utils will automatically create a fallback global Pinia store with default initial state values.
Vitest will intercept the missing store call and return mocked data using automatic file-system mocks.
Pinia will throw an active pinia was not found error because no store instance can be located or initialized.
questions.correctAnswer: Pinia will throw an active pinia was not found error because no store instance can be located or initialized.
questions.explanation: Pinia relies on an active instance of the pinia plugin to bind stores to the current Vue application context. Without `setActivePinia()` or passing a pinia instance directly to the test mount options (`global: { plugins: [pinia] }`), any attempt to use a store inside the component throws a runtime error stating that an active Pinia was not found.
questions.hint: Think about how Pinia tracks the current application context during unit testing outside of `app.use(pinia)`.
questions.relatedConcept: Pinia testing context and setActivePinia in Vue 3
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to verify practical experience with Vue 3 state management unit testing pitfalls and error diagnostics.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q20] How does Vue's Reactivity Transform (deprecated/experimental macro approach) or compiler-hinted error tracking behave when unref() is omitted in a custom Vue composition function diagnostic logger?
options: watchEffect tracks the ref object container itself rather than its .value property, causing the effect not to trigger on value mutations unless .value is accessed.
Vue's compiler automatically unwraps all arguments passed to custom functions inside watchEffect blocks.
Passing a ref directly to console.log throws a TypeError because refs cannot be read inside synchronous effects.
The effect executes once on mount and permanently unregisters itself due to type mismatch.
questions.correctAnswer: watchEffect tracks the ref object container itself rather than its .value property, causing the effect not to trigger on value mutations unless .value is accessed.
questions.explanation: Reactivity in Vue is tracked when `.value` is read, which triggers dependency collection (track). If you pass a `Ref` object directly into a logging function or watch effect without reading its `.value` property, the tracking mechanism binds to the `.value` property slot only if accessed, or fails to track property mutations accurately if the ref wrapper itself is monitored rather than its inner primitive value.
questions.hint: Consider how Vue's dependency tracking hooks into property and value accessors.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue reactivity dependency tracking and ref unwrapping pitfalls
questions.interviewTip: Used to test deep comprehension of Vue's Proxy-based reactivity tracking internals and debugging side effects.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q21] When utilizing the `v-html` directive in Vue to render untrusted user-supplied content, what is the primary security vulnerability introduced, and how does Vue's architecture handle it?
options: It triggers a hydration mismatch error during Server-Side Rendering (SSR) but is automatically sanitized by the Vue template compiler against XSS.
It introduces a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability because Vue does not sanitize HTML strings bound via v-html before inserting them into the DOM.
It automatically escapes script tags and malicious event handlers, protecting against XSS while allowing basic formatting.
It violates Content Security Policy (CSP) headers exclusively in production builds, disabling template compilation entirely.
questions.correctAnswer: It introduces a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability because Vue does not sanitize HTML strings bound via v-html before inserting them into the DOM.
questions.explanation: Dynamically rendering arbitrary HTML on your website can easily lead to XSS vulnerabilities because it's very easy for malicious third parties to inject arbitrary JavaScript execution vectors. Vue's `v-html` explicitly bypasses Vue's standard text interpolation (which automatically escapes content) and inserts raw HTML directly into the DOM.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to raw HTML strings when passed to innerHTML in a browser environment.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue v-html directive and Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) risks
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers ask this to test whether developers understand the security implications of bypassing Vue's template sanitization safeguards.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q22] What is the primary security risk of passing raw, untrusted user input directly into Vue's dynamic component or asynchronous component definitions (e.g., `:is='userInput'`), and how can it be mitigated?
options: It causes a memory leak because dynamic components are never garbage collected by Vue's reactivity system.
It leads to a prototype pollution vulnerability inside the Vue virtual DOM diffing algorithm.
It allows an attacker to instantiate arbitrary registered components, potentially exposing internal admin modules or triggering unwanted lifecycle side-effects if unvalidated.
It throws a compilation syntax error because dynamic component bindings only accept string literal identifiers, not variables.
questions.correctAnswer: It allows an attacker to instantiate arbitrary registered components, potentially exposing internal admin modules or triggering unwanted lifecycle side-effects if unvalidated.
questions.explanation: If a dynamic component's identifier (`:is`) is driven by unsanitized user input or unvalidated route parameters, an attacker might supply names of internal, sensitive, or unintended components registered globally or locally, leading to unauthorized UI exposure or logic execution.
questions.hint: Consider what `:is` resolves against in the component registry.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue dynamic components and security boundary enforcement
questions.codeSnippet: <component :is="userInputControl"></component>
questions.interviewTip: This tests advanced awareness of component registry hijacking and input validation boundaries in Vue applications.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q23] In Vue 3, what is the primary architectural advantage of using script setup (`<script setup>`) alongside Composition API compared to traditional Options API mixins for shared logic?
options: It automatically memoizes all reactive properties to prevent unnecessary DOM mutations.
It converts synchronous computation blocks into asynchronous Web Workers implicitly.
It allows direct manipulation of the Virtual DOM without passing through the Vue reactivity proxy system.
It eliminates namespace collision risks and maintains explicit variable provenance through direct lexical scoping.
questions.correctAnswer: It eliminates namespace collision risks and maintains explicit variable provenance through direct lexical scoping.
questions.explanation: Script setup uses true lexical scoping. When multiple mixins in the Options API contributed properties to the same component, property name collisions and unclear origin (provenance) of data were major maintenance issues. Composition API functions (composables) explicitly return values that are destructured or bound locally.
questions.hint: Think about how properties and methods merge or conflict when multiple logic chunks are brought into a single component.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 script setup lexical scoping vs mixin collision
questions.interviewTip: Senior interviewers look for migration experience and understanding why mixins were deprecated in favor of composables.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q24] When developing a high-performance Vue 3 application, why might an engineer choose `shallowRef()` over standard `ref()` for a large immutable dataset or external class instance?
options: To bypass deep recursive reactive proxy conversion, significantly reducing initialization CPU overhead and memory consumption.
To prevent the data from being garbage collected when the component unmounts.
To force Vue to perform synchronous DOM updates instead of batched asynchronous ticks.
To ensure that mutations to nested object properties automatically trigger watcher callbacks without requiring deep: true.
questions.correctAnswer: To bypass deep recursive reactive proxy conversion, significantly reducing initialization CPU overhead and memory consumption.
questions.explanation: shallowRef() tracks reactivity only on the .value access itself, rather than recursively converting all nested properties into reactive proxies. For huge third-party data structures or read-heavy datasets, this avoids massive performance penalties.
questions.hint: Consider the cost of traversing and wrapping large object graphs into Proxies.
questions.relatedConcept: shallowRef performance optimization and proxy overhead
questions.interviewTip: Crucial question for frontend performance optimization at scale.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q25] In Vue 3 with Composition API, what is the core reactivity hazard when directly destructuring properties from the object returned by `reactive()`?
options: Destructuring a reactive object automatically wraps all extracted primitives into computed properties under the hood.
The destructured variable loses reactivity connection, remaining a static primitive copy of its initial value.
It triggers a runtime TypeError because reactive objects prohibit property extraction without `toRef`.
Reactivity is fully preserved, but mutations made to the destructured variable bypass Vue's virtual DOM diffing queue.
questions.correctAnswer: The destructured variable loses reactivity connection, remaining a static primitive copy of its initial value.
questions.explanation: When you destructure a reactive object created by `reactive()`, you extract ordinary JavaScript values (like numbers or strings) which do not retain the reactive getters/setters. To preserve reactivity during destructuring, `toRefs()` or `toRef()` must be used.
questions.hint: Think about what JavaScript destructuring actually does to primitive values versus object references.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Reactive Destructuring Pitfalls
questions.interviewTip: Intermediary to advanced interviewers use this to verify whether candidates truly understand JavaScript value passing versus Vue's proxy-based reactivity mechanics.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q26] What is the primary rendering and memory optimization behavior of Vue's `v-memo` directive when applied to a large list or template block?
options: It completely destroys and re-creates DOM nodes every time any dependency updates to prevent memory leaks in large arrays.
It converts the template block into a static string during compilation, entirely disabling runtime reactivity for that element.
It caches the template sub-tree and skips both virtual DOM diffing and re-rendering unless one of the dependencies in the memo array changes.
It defers the rendering of the sub-tree until the browser main thread is idle using requestIdleCallback.
questions.correctAnswer: It caches the template sub-tree and skips both virtual DOM diffing and re-rendering unless one of the dependencies in the memo array changes.
questions.explanation: `v-memo` instructs Vue to memoize a sub-tree of the template. If the values provided in the dependency array remain identical on re-render, the entire sub-tree update is skipped, significantly speeding up rendering for heavy lists.
questions.hint: Consider memoization patterns in UI frameworks and what part of the rendering pipeline is bypassed.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue Performance Optimization with v-memo
questions.interviewTip: Great for assessing advanced Vue performance tuning knowledge beyond standard computed properties and lazy loading.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q27] What happens when you mutate a Vue 3 reactive proxy object directly inside a computed property getter function?
options: It successfully updates the reactive state without any warning or side effects.
Vue automatically intercepts the write and caches the value without triggering reactivity.
It throws a static compilation error during build time.
It triggers an infinite update loop and side-effect warnings or runtime errors.
questions.correctAnswer: It triggers an infinite update loop and side-effect warnings or runtime errors.
questions.explanation: Computed properties should be pure side-effect-free functions. Mutating state inside a computed getter triggers reactive dependencies that cause re-evaluations, leading to an infinite trigger loop that Vue detects and warns against at runtime.
questions.hint: Think about whether side effects are permitted inside computed property getters.
questions.relatedConcept: computed property side effects and infinite loops
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of Vue's reactivity system rules and functional purity in computed properties.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q28] In Vue 3, what occurs when a custom directive's `mounted` hook modifies a reactive state property that is also bound via `v-model` on the host element?
options: The state updates, which then propagates down to update the input's value via the reactivity system during the subsequent tick.
The directive execution is ignored because directives cannot modify setup state variables.
It causes an immediate unhandled exception due to direct mutation inside a lifecycle hook.
The input element is destroyed and recreated to prevent synchronization mismatches.
questions.correctAnswer: The state updates, which then propagates down to update the input's value via the reactivity system during the subsequent tick.
questions.explanation: Custom directives have full access to scope and reactive properties via bindings or closure. Mutating a reactive ref inside `mounted` behaves normally, scheduling a DOM update to sync the bound input element via the standard reactivity pipeline.
questions.hint: Directives run during component lifecycle phases and can interact with local closure variables.
questions.relatedConcept: custom directive lifecycle hooks and state mutation
questions.codeSnippet:
<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue';
const val = ref('initial');
const vCustom = {
  mounted(el) {
    val.value = 'modified';
  }
};
</script>
<template>
  <input v-model="val" v-custom />
</template>
questions.interviewTip: This tests advanced comprehension of how custom directives integrate with Vue's composition API scope and reactivity updates.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q29] In Vue 3, when using `v-memo` on a large `v-for` list, what is the primary structural trade-off regarding memory and rendering complexity?
options: It entirely eliminates the component instance lifecycle hooks for hidden items to reduce memory footprints, increasing initialization latency on toggle.
It caches the VNode tree to bypass virtual DOM diffing for that item, trading additional memory for cache arrays and optimized rendering throughput.
It forces synchronous DOM reflows across the entire list whenever any single tracked property mutates, prioritizing visual consistency over frame rate.
It disables reactivity tracking globally for the specified template scope, removing the memory overhead of dependency maps at the cost of manual patch triggers.
questions.correctAnswer: It caches the VNode tree to bypass virtual DOM diffing for that item, trading additional memory for cache arrays and optimized rendering throughput.
questions.explanation: v-memo caches the sub-tree's VNode representation based on an array of dependencies. While it speeds up diffing by skipping unchanged nodes, it incurs a minor memory cost to store the cached dependency arrays and previous values.
questions.hint: Think about what Vue compares between renders to determine whether to skip a sub-tree's diffing pass.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 v-memo performance optimization and VNode caching trade-offs
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates understand the inner workings of Vue 3's compiler-informed optimizations rather than just applying directives blindly.

questions.question: [Vue • Test 1 • Q30] What is the primary architectural advantage of using Vue 3's shallowRef over a standard ref when managing large, deeply nested third-party data models?
options: It makes the object completely immutable and read-only, preventing any accidental mutations from propagating to dependent computed properties.
It moves the state object entirely out of the JavaScript heap into WebAssembly memory to bypass garbage collection pauses.
It tracks reactivity only at the root `.value` assignment level, preventing the recursive Proxy wrapping overhead on thousands of internal nested properties.
It automatically memoizes all downstream getter functions to prevent redundant calculations during heavy re-renders.
questions.correctAnswer: It tracks reactivity only at the root `.value` assignment level, preventing the recursive Proxy wrapping overhead on thousands of internal nested properties.
questions.explanation: shallowRef bypasses the deep recursive traversal that turns nested objects and arrays into reactive Proxies, significantly reducing initialization time and memory consumption for large datasets where deep reactivity is unnecessary.
questions.hint: Consider how deep reactivity is achieved using JavaScript Proxies and the performance cost on large object graphs.
questions.relatedConcept: shallowRef performance implications and memory trade-offs in Vue 3
questions.codeSnippet: const largeModel = shallowRef(heavyObjectGraph);
questions.interviewTip: Often asked when discussing performance bottlenecks in dashboards or complex data visualization apps dealing with huge state trees.

questions.question: In Vue 3 with Composition API, what is the precise reactivity impact of destructuring properties directly from a reactive object returned by 'reactive()'?
options: The destructured variable 'count' maintains full two-way reactivity, automatically tracking component dependencies via Proxy getters.
The destructured variable 'count' loses reactivity, acting as a normal primitive copy that will not update when 'state.count' changes.
Vue's compiler intercepts the assignment and automatically wraps the variable in a getter/setter pair behind the scenes.
Destructuring a reactive object throws a runtime TypeError immediately in strict mode.
questions.correctAnswer: The destructured variable 'count' loses reactivity, acting as a normal primitive copy that will not update when 'state.count' changes.
questions.explanation: When you destructure properties from a reactive() object, you are extracting primitive values (like numbers or strings) by value. Because JavaScript primitives are passed by value, the extracted variable loses all connection to the original Proxy object's property, completely breaking reactivity. To preserve reactivity during destructuring, 'toRefs()' or 'toRef()' must be used.
questions.hint: Think about how JavaScript primitives handle assignment versus object references.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 reactive destructuring and primitive loss of reactivity
questions.interviewTip: Intervers love this question because destructuring reactive objects is one of the most common beginner bugs when transitioning from Options API to Composition API.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using the 'script setup' syntax, which behavior is guaranteed regarding the reactivity of a property destructured directly from a 'props' object?
options: The 'count' variable remains reactive and updates automatically when the parent prop changes.
The 'count' variable will lose reactivity, remaining fixed at the initial value passed from the parent.
A runtime error occurs because 'props' is read-only and cannot be destructured.
The 'count' variable is converted into a Ref automatically by the compiler.
questions.correctAnswer: The 'count' variable will lose reactivity, remaining fixed at the initial value passed from the parent.
questions.explanation: In JavaScript, destructuring a property from an object creates a new variable containing the value at that moment. Since 'props' are regular objects, 'count' becomes a primitive (or a reference to the value) and loses its connection to the reactive proxy of the props object. To maintain reactivity, one must use 'toRefs(props)'.
questions.hint: Consider how JavaScript destructuring works with object property access versus proxy-based reactivity.
questions.relatedConcept: Reactivity caveats with destructuring in Vue 3
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands the difference between standard JavaScript behavior and Vue's reactivity system when dealing with props.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using a functional component (defined as a plain function), how is the non-prop attribute inheritance behavior handled by default compared to a standard stateful component?
options: Functional components do not automatically inherit attributes unless explicitly defined via 'inheritAttrs: false' is absent or set to true, whereas stateful components always inherit them.
Functional components automatically inherit all non-prop attributes to the root element, whereas stateful components require explicit 'inheritAttrs' configuration.
Functional components ignore all non-prop attributes by default, while stateful components merge them into the root element automatically.
Both component types share identical attribute inheritance rules; they both automatically merge non-prop attributes into the root node regardless of implementation type.
questions.correctAnswer: Functional components automatically inherit all non-prop attributes to the root element, whereas stateful components require explicit 'inheritAttrs' configuration.
questions.explanation: In Vue 3, functional components (defined as functions) automatically inherit non-prop attributes (like class, style, or id) onto their root element. Stateful components, however, follow the 'inheritAttrs' property which defaults to 'true', but their implementation allows for finer-grained control and template-based root node definition, whereas the function-based component lacks a component instance to contextually bind separate attribute logic, defaulting to automatic pass-through.
questions.hint: Consider how Vue maps attributes when no component instance is available to manage the 'inheritAttrs' option.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Component Attribute Fallthrough
questions.interviewTip: Understanding how Vue handles DOM attributes is critical for building flexible component libraries where users expect standard HTML attributes to pass through correctly.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using a reactive object created with 'reactive()', what is the result of replacing the entire object with a new one via an assignment statement?
options: The original reactive proxy is updated in-place with the new object's properties, maintaining the original reactivity connection.
The original reactive proxy is replaced, and the reference to 'state' now points to a new reactive object, but the original connection to the UI is severed.
The assignment throws a TypeError because reactive proxies are read-only when assigned to a variable.
The original object's count increments to 1, but the variable 'state' remains a proxy to the original memory address.
questions.correctAnswer: The original reactive proxy is replaced, and the reference to 'state' now points to a new reactive object, but the original connection to the UI is severed.
questions.explanation: Because 'reactive()' creates a Proxy that wraps the original object, replacing the variable 'state' simply points the variable to a different proxy. Vue's dependency tracking is tied to the specific proxy instance created initially. Any template or effect that was observing the first proxy will not be updated by changes to the new object.
questions.hint: Consider that 'reactive()' returns a Proxy object, and assignment to a variable is just a pointer reassignment.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Reactivity Proxy limitations
questions.codeSnippet:
let state = reactive({ count: 0 });
state = reactive({ count: 1 });
questions.interviewTip: Understanding this distinction helps developers avoid common bugs when trying to reset state using simple assignments instead of updating properties.

questions.question: In Vue 3, how does the behavior of the `v-model` directive differ when applied to a custom component compared to native HTML elements under the default configuration?
options: On custom components, it automatically creates a two-way reactive computed property, whereas on native elements it mutates the DOM directly.

On custom components, it expands to passing a `modelValue` prop and listening for an `update:modelValue` event, whereas on native elements it binds to the `value` property and listens to the `input` or `change` event.
On custom components, it requires explicit registration via the `model` option in the component definition, which is not required for native elements.
On custom components, it binds to a `value` prop and emits an `input` event by default, identical to native elements in Vue 3.
questions.correctAnswer: On custom components, it expands to passing a `modelValue` prop and listening for an `update:modelValue` event, whereas on native elements it binds to the `value` property and listens to the `input` or `change` event.
questions.explanation: In Vue 3, `v-model` on a custom component was standardized to use `modelValue` as the prop and `update:modelValue` as the emitted event to support multiple v-models and cleaner syntax. On native form elements, it still maps to the respective element value and native events.
questions.hint: Think about the prop name and event name contract established in Vue 3 for custom component v-models.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 v-model custom component contract
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers often ask this to verify if the candidate has transitioned their knowledge from Vue 2 (where `value` and `input` were default) to Vue 3.

questions.question: In a Vue 3 Composition API component, you have a reactive counter and a watcher set up to read the DOM element's text content. If the user clicks the 'Increment' button (changing count from 0 to 1), what will be the updated value of 'domText.value' immediately after the watcher executes for the first time?
options: null
questions.explanation: By default, Vue 3 watchers run with a pre-render flush timing (flush: 'pre'). This means when a dependency changes, the watcher callback is executed before Vue updates the DOM. Therefore, when the count changes from 0 to 1, the watcher runs while the DOM still contains the old value, '0'. To access the updated DOM state in a watcher, you must specify { flush: 'post' } or use watchPostEffect.
questions.hint: Consider the default flush timing of Vue's reactivity system and when DOM updates actually occur relative to watcher execution.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Watcher Flush Timing
questions.interviewTip: Understanding the tick-based scheduling system of Vue is vital for managing DOM side effects. Candidates should know how to coordinate DOM-dependent logic using flush options like 'post' or nextTick.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using a 'reactive' object that contains a nested 'ref', what happens to the 'ref' when accessing it directly as a property of the reactive object?
options: It remains a Ref object, requiring access via state.count.value.
It is automatically unwrapped, returning the primitive value 0.
It triggers a TypeError because refs cannot be placed inside reactive objects.
It returns undefined because the reactive proxy does not track the ref property.
questions.correctAnswer: It is automatically unwrapped, returning the primitive value 0.
questions.explanation: In Vue 3, when a Ref is assigned as a property to a reactive object, the reactive proxy automatically unwraps the ref, allowing you to access its underlying value directly without using '.value'. This behavior is consistent with how refs are handled in template interpolation.
questions.hint: Consider the behavior of Vue's reactivity system regarding automatic unwrapping when nesting refs inside reactive proxies.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Reactivity Unwrapping
questions.interviewTip: This tests depth of knowledge regarding the reactivity system's internals and how Vue manages 'ref' vs 'reactive' syntax sugar.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using a custom ref created via `customRef`, what is the specific role of the 'track' and 'trigger' functions provided as arguments to the factory function?
options: track() saves the value to local storage, and trigger() forces the component to re-mount completely.
track() registers the dependency for the effect system, and trigger() notifies watchers that the value has changed.
track() forces an immediate DOM update, and trigger() resets the ref to its initial state.
track() validates the new value type, and trigger() executes the associated watcher callback synchronously.
questions.correctAnswer: track() registers the dependency for the effect system, and trigger() notifies watchers that the value has changed.
questions.explanation: In the Vue 3 reactivity system, `customRef` allows manual control over dependency tracking and update triggering. The `track` function tells Vue that the property is being accessed (dependency collection), and `trigger` informs Vue that the property has changed, allowing the effect system to queue the necessary re-renders or watcher re-executions.
questions.hint: Consider the relationship between dependency collection and the reactivity effect queue.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Custom Ref Reactivity Mechanics
questions.interviewTip: Understanding custom refs demonstrates a deeper grasp of how Vue's proxy-based reactivity system can be extended for advanced performance patterns like debouncing.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using 'v-for' on a template element, where must the ':key' attribute be placed to ensure correct DOM patching during list updates?
options: On the first child element inside the <template> tag.
On the <template> tag itself.
On both the <template> tag and the child element.
It is not required for <template> tags, only for component-based lists.
questions.correctAnswer: On the <template> tag itself.
questions.explanation: In Vue 3, the ':key' attribute must be placed on the <template> tag when used with 'v-for'. Prior to Vue 3, keys could not be placed on <template> tags, but Vue 3 explicitly supports placing the key directly on the loop wrapper to provide a stable identity for the fragment.
questions.hint: Vue 3 allows fragment-based lists; where does the identifier belong for the block as a whole?
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Template Fragments and list rendering keys
questions.interviewTip: Understanding Vue 3's improved fragment support demonstrates an understanding of how the virtual DOM tracks dynamic list reconciliation.

options: Both the computed getter and the method log only when `count` changes.
The computed getter logs only when `count` changes, while the method logs on every render.
Both the computed getter and the method log on every render.
The computed getter logs on every render, while the method logs only when `count` changes.
questions.correctAnswer: The computed getter logs only when `count` changes, while the method logs on every render.
questions.explanation: A `computed` property is cached; its getter runs only when one of its reactive dependencies (`count`) changes. The method is called during every render, so its console.log runs each time the component re‑renders, even if `count` hasn't changed.
questions.hint: Think about caching vs. plain function calls in the rendering cycle.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 computed property caching vs. methods in templates
questions.interviewTip: Shows whether the candidate understands Vue's reactivity and performance implications of using computed properties versus methods in templates.

title: Vue - Test 2: Technical Assessment
description: Test 2 for Vue. Every question is unique against the whole question database — no repeats, no renumbered or reworded variants of an existing question.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using the `<script setup>` syntax, what is the behavior of calling a function that is exported from a component using `defineExpose` inside a parent component that accesses it via a template ref?
options: The function throws a TypeError because refs in Vue 3 are read-only and cannot invoke methods.
The function executes successfully because defineExpose explicitly makes it part of the component's public instance.
The function call fails because the component instance is private by default and defineExpose does not affect template refs.
The function executes, but only if the component is wrapped in a markRaw call to prevent reactive tracking.
questions.correctAnswer: The function executes successfully because defineExpose explicitly makes it part of the component's public instance.
questions.explanation: In <script setup>, the component is closed by default. defineExpose is specifically designed to explicitly expose properties or methods to the parent component, which are then accessible via the template ref.
questions.hint: Think about the visibility of component instances when using the Composition API's setup script.
questions.relatedConcept: Component API encapsulation and explicit exposure
questions.interviewTip: Understanding encapsulation is vital for clean API design in large Vue applications.

questions.question: In Vue 3, what is the effect of using `shallowRef` to store an object that is subsequently modified inside a `watch` effect?
options: The watch callback triggers because Vue automatically deep-tracks any object assigned to a ref, regardless of its type.
The watch callback triggers because modifying a property of an object inside a ref counts as a side effect.
The watch callback does not trigger because shallowRef only tracks changes to the .value reference itself.
The code throws a runtime error because shallowRef objects are frozen in strict mode.
questions.correctAnswer: The watch callback does not trigger because shallowRef only tracks changes to the .value reference itself.
questions.explanation: shallowRef does not perform deep reactivity. Modifying a property of the object contained in the ref does not change the ref's value, therefore the watcher (which tracks the ref reference) does not detect the change.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between deep reactivity and shallow reactivity in terms of tracking depth.
questions.relatedConcept: Shallow reactivity and performance optimization
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate how they would optimize a large data structure to avoid unnecessary deep reactivity overhead.

questions.question: In Vue 3, what is the behavior of using `v-model` on a component prop when that prop is passed directly from a parent's reactive object?
options: It works correctly, provided the parent object is wrapped in a ref.
It creates a two-way binding, updating the parent object directly without emitting events.
It silently fails, and the parent reactive object remains unchanged.
It triggers a Vue warning because props are read-only and cannot be mutated by the child.
questions.correctAnswer: It triggers a Vue warning because props are read-only and cannot be mutated by the child.
questions.explanation: Vue props follow one-way data flow. Even though v-model is syntactic sugar, trying to bind a prop directly to a v-model inside the child component attempts to mutate the prop, which violates the strict immutability of props passed from parent to child, triggering a warning in development.
questions.hint: Consider the unidirectional data flow principle enforced in Vue.
questions.relatedConcept: Prop mutation restrictions and v-model mechanics
questions.codeSnippet: <ChildComponent v-model:title="parentReactiveObj.title" />
questions.interviewTip: An interviewer asks this to see if the candidate understands the difference between local component state and incoming data flow.

questions.question: What happens to a 'teleported' component's state if the Teleport component is unmounted from the DOM?
options: The component instance and its reactive state are destroyed.
The component instance remains in memory, but its DOM elements are removed.
The component is moved back to its original location in the DOM tree.
The component stays in the DOM, but its event listeners are deactivated.
questions.correctAnswer: The component instance and its reactive state are destroyed.
questions.explanation: Teleport only controls the DOM location, not the lifecycle of the component. If the component inside the Teleport is unmounted (e.g., via v-if), its instance is destroyed regardless of where the DOM elements were rendered.
questions.hint: Think about whether Teleport acts as a state wrapper or just a DOM portal.
questions.relatedConcept: Teleport lifecycle management
questions.codeSnippet: <Teleport to="#target"> <MyComponent v-if="show" /> </Teleport>
questions.interviewTip: This tests depth of knowledge regarding how Vue manages virtual DOM lifecycles independently of physical DOM layout.

questions.question: When using the 'shallowRef' API in Vue 3, how does the reactivity system react if you replace the entire value versus mutating a nested property within that value?
options: Both mutations and replacements trigger an effect due to proxy-based tracking.
Mutating a nested property does not trigger an effect, but replacing the value triggers an effect.
Both operations require calling 'triggerRef' to update the UI.
Mutating a nested property triggers an effect, but replacing the value does not.
questions.correctAnswer: Mutating a nested property does not trigger an effect, but replacing the value triggers an effect.
questions.explanation: shallowRef only makes the root level reactive. It tracks the .value property itself. Modifying nested properties does not trigger reactivity, while assigning a new object to .value updates the ref and triggers the effect.
questions.hint: Think about the scope of reactivity in 'shallow' variants compared to standard 'ref'.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 shallow reactivity boundaries
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands performance optimization vs deep reactivity pitfalls.

questions.question: In Vue 3, what is the behavior of the 'v-once' directive when applied to a component that uses a 'slot' or 'scoped-slot' containing dynamic content?
options: Only the component's internal template is frozen, while slots continue to re-render.
The directive is ignored for components and throws a warning in development.
The component and its entire slot content are rendered once and never updated.
The slot content is rendered once, but the component wrapper remains reactive.
questions.correctAnswer: The component and its entire slot content are rendered once and never updated.
questions.explanation: When v-once is used on a component, it signals the renderer to skip updates for the entire component subtree, including any slot content, because the component is treated as a static static-node.
questions.hint: Consider the scope of 'v-once' when applied to component tags vs simple HTML elements.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 rendering optimization and static tree hoisting
questions.codeSnippet:
<MyComponent v-once>
  <template #default="{ item }">
    {{ item.name }}
  </template>
</MyComponent>
questions.interviewTip: Understanding v-once is critical for performance tuning; knowing its scope prevents common bugs where developers expect parts of a component to stay reactive.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using `<script setup>` with a `defineExpose` macro, what is the impact on the component's public instance?
options: The component instance automatically exposes all internal variables regardless of defineExpose.
defineExpose merges the exposed properties with the default instance, making all internal methods public.
The 'count' property is exposed, but it becomes a static value and loses its reactivity.
The component instance will only expose the 'count' property, and private state remains encapsulated.
questions.correctAnswer: The component instance will only expose the 'count' property, and private state remains encapsulated.
questions.explanation: By default, components using <script setup> are closed, meaning nothing is exposed to the parent. defineExpose is an opt-in mechanism to expose specific variables or methods, effectively shielding the rest of the internal state.
questions.hint: Think about the encapsulation philosophy of <script setup> compared to Options API.
questions.relatedConcept: Component Instance Encapsulation
questions.codeSnippet:
<script setup>
const count = ref(0);
defineExpose({ count });
</script>
questions.interviewTip: Understanding component API boundaries is crucial for maintaining clean public interfaces in large-scale applications.

questions.question: What is the expected behavior when a `provide` call is executed inside a `watch` effect in a Vue 3 component?
options: It triggers a runtime error because provide() must be called during the component's setup phase.
It successfully updates the provided value for all child components reactively.
It only updates the value if the component is an asynchronous component.
It creates a local injection that is only available to the current component instance.
questions.correctAnswer: It triggers a runtime error because provide() must be called during the component's setup phase.
questions.explanation: Provide and inject are designed to be used during the synchronous execution of the setup() function or <script setup>. Calling them inside effects, callbacks, or nested functions is unsupported because the dependency graph for injection is established during component instantiation.
questions.hint: Consider when the dependency injection tree is constructed in the Vue component lifecycle.
questions.relatedConcept: Dependency Injection Lifecycle
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands the difference between state reactivity and the static nature of the DI tree.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using `shallowRef` to store a large object, what is the primary memory-saving behavior compared to a standard `ref`?
options: It prevents the entire object from being garbage collected until the component is unmounted.
It avoids recursively converting nested object properties into reactive proxies, reducing initialization overhead and memory footprint.
It automatically memoizes the object reference to prevent re-renders when internal properties change.
It forces the object to be stored in a non-reactive WeakMap to optimize for cross-component data sharing.
questions.correctAnswer: It avoids recursively converting nested object properties into reactive proxies, reducing initialization overhead and memory footprint.
questions.explanation: A standard `ref` uses `reactive()` internally for objects, which traverses the entire object tree to convert properties into proxies. `shallowRef` tracks only the .value property itself, skipping deep reactivity for performance.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between deep and shallow reactivity triggers.
questions.relatedConcept: Shallow Reactivity vs Deep Reactivity
questions.codeSnippet: const data = shallowRef({ nested: { val: 1 } });
questions.interviewTip: Ask about when they would choose shallowRef over ref to judge their understanding of Vue's performance overhead.

questions.question: When utilizing `v-once` on a large component tree, what is the specific effect on the component's update lifecycle during state changes?
options: The component is rendered only during the initial hydration phase and then automatically destroyed to save memory.
The component remains reactive to prop changes but prevents the DOM from updating until the user triggers a re-render.
The component is rendered once at runtime and then skipped by the update reconciliation process, even if props change.
The component is only rendered if the browser's main thread is idle, effectively debouncing the initial load.
questions.correctAnswer: The component is rendered once at runtime and then skipped by the update reconciliation process, even if props change.
questions.explanation: v-once instructs Vue to render the element or component once and then treat it as static, effectively excluding it from the diffing/patching process in future re-renders.
questions.hint: Think about the virtual DOM diffing process.
questions.relatedConcept: Static Content Optimization
questions.codeSnippet: <large-component v-once :data="items" />
questions.interviewTip: Good for assessing if the candidate understands how to prune the Virtual DOM for performance optimization.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using `watchEffect` to track reactive dependencies, what happens if an asynchronous operation is triggered inside the effect function and the dependency changes before the promise resolves?
options: Vue automatically cancels the previous promise execution because `watchEffect` tracks the async state.
The `result.value` update will be blocked by the Vue runtime if the dependency has changed since the promise started.
The async function will be re-executed immediately and the previous execution scope will be garbage collected by the proxy.
The effect function execution completes regardless of dependency changes, leading to a race condition where an older stale request may overwrite a newer one.
questions.correctAnswer: The effect function execution completes regardless of dependency changes, leading to a race condition where an older stale request may overwrite a newer one.
questions.explanation: watchEffect does not know about the asynchronous nature of the internal logic. If the dependency changes, the effect runs again, but the previous 'await' continues to execute in its own microtask, creating a classic race condition where the resolution of the earlier, stale call updates the state after the newer call.
questions.hint: Consider how the event loop handles unresolved promises during re-execution.
questions.relatedConcept: Async race conditions in effect scopes
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate how they would implement cleanup logic using the onCleanup callback provided by watchEffect.

questions.question: When defining a custom directive in Vue 3 with the `mounted` hook, what is the impact of modifying a reactive property that the host component's template relies on?
options: It triggers a re-render of the component, provided the reactive variable is part of the component's render context.
It fails silently because custom directives are restricted from mutating component state during the mount phase.
It causes an infinite update loop because the DOM element is still in the process of being attached.
It causes an immediate 'Uncaught TypeError' because the component instance is not yet fully initialized.
questions.correctAnswer: It triggers a re-render of the component, provided the reactive variable is part of the component's render context.
questions.explanation: Custom directives have access to the component instance via `binding.instance`. Modifying a reactive variable on that instance is a standard state mutation, which correctly triggers Vue's reactivity system to update the component's Virtual DOM.
questions.hint: Think about whether a custom directive is technically part of the component instance's context.
questions.relatedConcept: Directive lifecycle and reactivity system integration
questions.interviewTip: Discuss when it is appropriate to use custom directives versus component-level logic.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using `<script setup>`, a developer observes that a variable defined via `ref()` is not updating in the template despite the variable being reassigned. Which scenario most likely explains this behavior?
options: The 'ref' is not being accessed via '.value' inside the template, preventing automatic dependency tracking.
The variable 'count' was reassigned to a new Ref instance, breaking the original proxy binding to the template.
The 'increment' function is not wrapped in 'defineExpose', making it inaccessible to the template.
Vue 3 requires variables to be declared with 'const' inside 'script setup' to maintain reactivity.
questions.correctAnswer: The variable 'count' was reassigned to a new Ref instance, breaking the original proxy binding to the template.
questions.explanation: In Vue 3, 'ref' creates a reactive object. Reassigning the variable name to a new 'ref()' call replaces the original reactive wrapper with a plain object or a new proxy that the template is not tracking. The template is bound to the original object reference.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between modifying a property of an existing object and replacing the object itself.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Reactivity Proxy breakage via reassignment
questions.codeSnippet:
let count = ref(0);
const increment = () => { count = ref(count.value + 1); };
questions.interviewTip: This tests the developer's understanding of how JavaScript object references interact with Vue's proxy-based reactivity system.

questions.question: A developer attempts to use `provide` and `inject` to share a reactive state between a root component and a deeply nested child. The child receives the initial value but does not react to subsequent updates from the parent. What is the most likely cause?
options: The child is attempting to modify the injected value directly instead of using a provided mutation method.
The 'provide' key is not a Symbol, causing a collision with other injected values in the component tree.
The parent provided the reactive object directly, but the child is destructuring the object upon injection.
Reactive objects cannot be passed through provide/inject and must be wrapped in a 'ref' to maintain reactivity.
questions.correctAnswer: The parent provided the reactive object directly, but the child is destructuring the object upon injection.
questions.explanation: If the child uses ES6 destructuring on the injected object (e.g., 'const { name } = inject("user")'), the reactivity is lost because the extracted property is no longer a reactive proxy. The parent providing the reactive object is valid, but the consumer's handling is the failure point.
questions.hint: Focus on the lifecycle of the reactive proxy when it is accessed in the child component.
questions.relatedConcept: Loss of reactivity due to destructuring injected reactive objects
questions.interviewTip: This is a common 'gotcha' that distinguishes senior developers who understand proxy behavior from those who treat reactive objects like standard plain objects.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using `provide` and `inject` to pass data across a component tree, what occurs if the provided value is a standard (non-reactive) object and the providing component's template updates?
options: The injected value automatically updates in child components because Vue performs a deep watch on all provided objects.
The injected value triggers a full re-render of the entire component tree regardless of whether the object properties changed.
The application throws a runtime error stating that non-reactive objects cannot be provided in the Composition API.
The injected value remains unchanged in the child components because it was passed by reference to a static object.
questions.correctAnswer: The injected value remains unchanged in the child components because it was passed by reference to a static object.
questions.explanation: Provide/Inject is not reactive by default for primitive values or non-reactive objects. If a non-reactive object is provided, changes to the parent's data state that do not replace the object itself will not trigger an update in the injected child, as the child holds a reference to the initial static value.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between reactive state and static data in the dependency injection system.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Dependency Injection reactivity limitations
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate how they would make the injected value reactive if it were a static object.

questions.question: What is the result of using `v-if` and `v-for` on the same element in Vue 3, and how does this differ from Vue 2 behavior?
options: In Vue 3, `v-if` has higher priority than `v-for`, resulting in the `v-if` condition being evaluated before the loop, which can cause 'undefined' variable access inside the loop.
Vue 3 throws a compiler error because using both on the same element is deprecated and strictly forbidden in the template parser.
In Vue 3, `v-for` is given higher priority, meaning the `v-if` will be evaluated for every single iteration of the loop.
Both versions treat them equally; the directives are merged into a single internal render function call to maximize performance.
questions.correctAnswer: In Vue 3, `v-if` has higher priority than `v-for`, resulting in the `v-if` condition being evaluated before the loop, which can cause 'undefined' variable access inside the loop.
questions.explanation: In Vue 3, the compiler gives `v-if` higher priority than `v-for`. If `v-if` is placed on the same element as `v-for`, the condition cannot access the loop variable (e.g., 'item') because the loop hasn't run yet. Vue 2 gave `v-for` higher priority.
questions.hint: Think about the scope of the iterator variable in the template hierarchy.
questions.relatedConcept: Directive priority changes in Vue 3
questions.interviewTip: This tests whether the developer has kept up with breaking changes between major versions.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using a custom ref created via `customRef`, what is the technical requirement for the `track` and `trigger` functions to maintain reactivity consistency during asynchronous operations?
options: Both track() and trigger() must be executed within the same synchronous execution block as the getter/setter.
track() must be called synchronously inside the getter, while trigger() can be called asynchronously inside the setter.
trigger() must be called before the internal value is updated to ensure Vue captures the state change.
The track() function must be invoked manually after the value update to notify the dependency collector.
questions.correctAnswer: track() must be called synchronously inside the getter, while trigger() can be called asynchronously inside the setter.
questions.explanation: The 'track()' function must be called during the synchronous 'get' call to register the component effect as a dependency. 'trigger()' can safely be called asynchronously because it simply loops through and executes the collected effects associated with that dependency.
questions.hint: Think about when the dependency tracker needs to know about the variable access versus the change event.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 customRef reactivity tracking
questions.interviewTip: Understanding customRef is crucial for advanced reactivity patterns and debouncing input handling.

questions.question: When utilizing the `v-once` directive on a component containing multiple child elements, what is the precise impact on the virtual DOM reconciliation process?
options: Only the root element of the component is cached; child elements remain reactive to parent props.
It forces the component to be re-rendered only if the parent component's key changes.
The entire component subtree is skipped during subsequent patch updates, including all child elements.
It disables all lifecycle hooks for the component, including onMounted and onUpdated.
questions.correctAnswer: The entire component subtree is skipped during subsequent patch updates, including all child elements.
questions.explanation: When `v-once` is applied to a component, the entire rendered result is cached during the first render and completely skipped during subsequent reconciliation passes, rendering the child content static.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between applying a directive to a native element vs. a component.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue reconciliation and performance directives
questions.interviewTip: Distinguishing between component-level and element-level optimizations helps in large-scale Vue performance tuning.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using `provide` and `inject` to pass a `ref` from a parent to a descendant, what occurs if the parent provides the ref, and the descendant performs an assignment to the injected value without using the `.value` property?
options: The assignment correctly triggers reactivity because the dependency tracking system unwraps injected refs automatically.
The assignment throws a TypeError because the injected object is marked as non-writable by the provide mechanism.
The assignment updates the original ref's value because Vue uses a Proxy to intercept deep assignments on injected objects.
The assignment fails to update the reactive state, and the property 'count' is overwritten with a static number.
questions.correctAnswer: The assignment fails to update the reactive state, and the property 'count' is overwritten with a static number.
questions.explanation: Injecting a ref provides the ref object itself. If a developer assigns a value directly to the variable (e.g., count = 10), they are overwriting the variable reference with a primitive, losing the connection to the reactive system. The original ref remains unchanged, and the 'count' variable no longer points to the original ref object.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between assigning a new value to a variable holding a ref object versus modifying the .value property.
questions.relatedConcept: Reactivity system, Provide/Inject mechanics
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands the difference between the ref object shell and the value contained within, which is a common source of 'reactivity broken' bugs.

questions.question: What is the primary effect of using the `shallowRef` API instead of `ref` when managing an array of thousands of large objects, specifically regarding the browser's memory and CPU usage during Vue's dependency tracking?
options: It prevents deep reactivity, meaning Vue will not recursively create Proxies for every property of every object in the array.
It offloads the array management to the browser's garbage collector, completely bypassing Vue's reactivity system for the array contents.
It forces the template compiler to use static vnodes instead of dynamic ones, significantly reducing initial render time.
It triggers an immediate update of the entire array upon any mutation, ensuring that UI synchronization is faster than standard refs.
questions.correctAnswer: It prevents deep reactivity, meaning Vue will not recursively create Proxies for every property of every object in the array.
questions.explanation: shallowRef only tracks changes to the .value property itself. Unlike standard ref, it does not make the internal nested properties reactive, which prevents the costly performance overhead of creating proxies for thousands of objects.
questions.hint: Focus on the performance difference between deep and shallow reactivity.
questions.relatedConcept: Performance optimization, shallow reactivity
questions.interviewTip: Understanding when to use shallowRef vs ref is a key skill for building scalable applications; it shows the candidate considers memory pressure in the DOM.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using `shallowRef` to manage an array, why can updating the array elements directly via index (e.g., `data.value[0] = 'new'`) fail to trigger a view update?
options: Array indices are non-reactive by default in Vue 3 due to performance constraints in Proxy implementation.
shallowRef only tracks mutations to the .value reference itself, not properties within the nested structure.
shallowRef requires a manual call to triggerRef() only when replacing the entire array, not for partial updates.
The reactivity system cannot detect changes to arrays unless they are wrapped in a reactive() call instead of ref().
questions.correctAnswer: shallowRef only tracks mutations to the .value reference itself, not properties within the nested structure.
questions.explanation: shallowRef does not perform deep reactivity. It only watches for changes to the .value property itself. Modifying the contents of an object or array held by a shallowRef does not trigger re-renders because the reference to the array remains the same.
questions.hint: Consider how shallow reactivity differs from standard reactivity regarding nested objects.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Shallow Reactivity
questions.interviewTip: Ask this to see if the candidate understands the performance trade-offs of deep versus shallow reactivity.

questions.question: When utilizing the 'provide/inject' pattern in Vue 3, what is the safest way to ensure reactive dependency injection remains functional if the provided value is a primitive?
options: Primitive values are inherently reactive in Vue 3 if they are injected into a setup() function.
You must define the provide key as a Symbol imported from vue to ensure the reactivity bridge is established.
You must provide a ref or reactive object instead of a raw primitive to maintain a reactive connection.
You must wrap the injected value in a computed property to allow the child to track changes.
questions.correctAnswer: You must provide a ref or reactive object instead of a raw primitive to maintain a reactive connection.
questions.explanation: Provide/inject loses reactivity with primitives because primitives are passed by value. To share state that updates in the child when changed in the parent, a ref or reactive object must be provided, which is passed by reference.
questions.hint: Reflect on the difference between passing by value versus passing by reference in JavaScript.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Provide/Inject Reactivity
questions.codeSnippet:
provide('theme', 'dark'); // parent
const theme = inject('theme'); // child
questions.interviewTip: This question highlights a common architectural bug when beginners try to share simple status flags via provide/inject.

questions.question: In a Vue 3 application, what is the primary difference in behavior between using `shallowRef` and `ref` when updating nested object properties?
options: The component will re-render for both updates as Vue recursively tracks properties regardless of the ref type.
The component will only re-render if the object is explicitly wrapped in `toRaw` before mutation.
The component will re-render automatically because `shallowRef` triggers a shallow ref update cycle for all child object properties.
The component will not re-render because `shallowRef` only tracks changes to the .value reference, not nested mutations.
questions.correctAnswer: The component will not re-render because `shallowRef` only tracks changes to the .value reference, not nested mutations.
questions.explanation: A shallowRef only tracks the .value property itself. Modifying properties deep inside the object does not trigger a dependency effect for the component's render function, unlike a standard ref which converts the object into a reactive proxy.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between deep reactivity and shallow reactivity.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Shallow Reactivity
questions.interviewTip: Understanding shallow reactivity is vital for performance optimization when dealing with large, immutable data structures.

questions.question: When utilizing `provide/inject` in Vue 3, what occurs if you inject a reactive object provided by a parent, and then attempt to modify that object directly within the child component?
options: The mutation will be reflected globally across all components injecting that object, as the object is passed by reference.
The mutation will be ignored because `inject` creates a read-only copy of the provided value.
The child component will throw a TypeError because injected properties are immutable by default.
The parent component will lose reactivity on the 'config' object and stop observing further changes.
questions.correctAnswer: The mutation will be reflected globally across all components injecting that object, as the object is passed by reference.
questions.explanation: Vue's reactivity system passes objects by reference. When you provide a reactive object, the injected reference points to the same underlying reactive proxy, allowing child components to trigger global updates.
questions.hint: Think about how JavaScript handles object references vs. how Vue proxies manage state.
questions.relatedConcept: Cross-Component State Communication
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate about the risks of this pattern for state management traceability.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using the `<script setup>` syntax, what is the effect of calling `defineProps` inside a standard JavaScript function defined within the same component?
options: It successfully defines the props object and returns it for local usage within that specific function scope.
It triggers a compile-time error because defineProps is a compiler macro that must be used at the top-level scope.
It works correctly but only if the function is called inside the onMounted lifecycle hook.
It creates a reactive binding that updates automatically whenever the parent passes new data.
questions.correctAnswer: It triggers a compile-time error because defineProps is a compiler macro that must be used at the top-level scope.
questions.explanation: defineProps is a compiler macro in Vue 3 that is replaced by the build tool; it cannot be called inside nested functions or conditional blocks because the compiler expects it at the top-level scope of <script setup>.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between a runtime function and a build-time compiler macro.
questions.relatedConcept: Compiler macro limitations in script setup
questions.codeSnippet: function updateConfig() { const props = defineProps(['config']); console.log(props); }
questions.interviewTip: This tests if the candidate understands the difference between standard JS execution and Vue's build-time transformations.

questions.question: When utilizing the `v-model` directive on a custom component, what is the default behavior regarding the prop name and event name if no argument is provided to v-model?
options: It defaults to passing a 'value' prop and listening for an 'input' event.
It defaults to passing a 'model' prop and listening for a 'change' event.
It defaults to passing a 'modelValue' prop and listening for an 'update:modelValue' event.
It defaults to passing a 'v-model' prop and listening for an 'update' event.
questions.correctAnswer: It defaults to passing a 'modelValue' prop and listening for an 'update:modelValue' event.
questions.explanation: In Vue 3, v-model (without arguments) defaults to using 'modelValue' as the prop and 'update:modelValue' as the event, which is a change from the Vue 2 'value/input' convention.
