questions.hint: Check how Vue 3 standardizes v-model for custom components.
questions.relatedConcept: v-model custom component default conventions
questions.codeSnippet: <MyComponent v-model="count" />
questions.interviewTip: This is a standard question to differentiate developers who transitioned from Vue 2 to Vue 3.

questions.question: When utilizing `v-model` on a custom component in Vue 3, what happens if the component fails to emit the default 'update:modelValue' event, but instead emits a custom event name while using the standard v-model directive on the parent?
options: Vue automatically maps the custom event to the bound variable if it is the only event emitted.
The component will throw a runtime warning, and the v-model binding will be silently disabled.
The component state becomes desynchronized, but the parent variable updates via deep reactivity tracking.
The parent's bound variable will not update because Vue expects the 'update:modelValue' event by default.
questions.correctAnswer: The parent's bound variable will not update because Vue expects the 'update:modelValue' event by default.
questions.explanation: Vue 3's v-model syntax compiles to a prop named 'modelValue' and an event listener for 'update:modelValue'. Unless specified (e.g., v-model:propName), the framework strictly looks for that specific event signature to update the parent state.
questions.hint: Recall the compiled contract between v-model and the underlying prop/event pair.
questions.relatedConcept: Custom component v-model contract
questions.interviewTip: Understanding the 'contract' behind syntactic sugar prevents bugs in component libraries.

questions.question: In Vue 3, consider a scenario where a reactive object is wrapped in a `shallowRef`. If you replace the entire object using `.value = newObject`, what is the consequence for the reactivity of the new object's properties?
options: The properties of the new object will not be reactive, as shallowRef only triggers updates when the value is replaced, not when nested properties change.
The properties become reactive because shallowRef performs a recursive conversion on the new value assigned to .value.
The entire state loses its connection to the DOM and will not trigger a re-render even if replaced.
The component will throw an error because shallowRef does not support object replacement.
questions.correctAnswer: The properties of the new object will not be reactive, as shallowRef only triggers updates when the value is replaced, not when nested properties change.
questions.explanation: A shallowRef only tracks the .value reference itself. Unlike ref, it explicitly skips deep reactivity. Replacing the object triggers the ref update, but the internals of the new object remain plain, non-reactive JavaScript objects.
questions.hint: Contrast the behavior of ref() versus shallowRef() regarding depth.
questions.relatedConcept: Shallow reactivity mechanics
questions.codeSnippet:
const state = shallowRef({ count: 0 });
state.value = { count: 1 };
questions.interviewTip: This distinguishes junior developers from those who understand performance optimization patterns like shallowRef.

questions.question: In Vue 3, what is the primary technical reason that 'shallowRef' is more performant than 'ref' when managing large arrays of complex data objects?
options: It prevents the array from being stored in the virtual DOM until the next tick.
It avoids the overhead of recursively converting every property of the objects in the array into reactive proxies.
It caches the array reference at the compiler level, skipping deep diffing during patch operations.
It disables the Vue reactivity system for the array entirely, treating it as a plain static constant.
questions.correctAnswer: It avoids the overhead of recursively converting every property of the objects in the array into reactive proxies.
questions.explanation: ref() creates a deep reactive object that traverses all nested properties, which can be computationally expensive for large datasets. shallowRef() only tracks the value property itself, avoiding the recursive proxy conversion of nested objects.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between deep reactivity and shallow reactivity in proxy overhead.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Reactivity Performance Optimization
questions.interviewTip: Ask the candidate when they would trade deep reactivity for performance, and how that affects child component updates.

questions.question: When using the 'keep-alive' component in a high-frequency route navigation scenario, what happens to the state of child components that are deactivated but not unmounted?
options: The component instance is destroyed to free memory, but its data is serialized to sessionStorage to allow recreation.
The component is forced into a 'paused' state where all reactivity is disabled until it is re-activated.
The component instance remains in memory, and its state is preserved without triggering its 'beforeUnmount' or 'unmounted' lifecycle hooks.
The component is kept in the DOM as a hidden element (display: none), continuing to execute internal 'setInterval' or 'setTimeout' logic.
questions.correctAnswer: The component instance remains in memory, and its state is preserved without triggering its 'beforeUnmount' or 'unmounted' lifecycle hooks.
questions.explanation: keep-alive preserves the component state by caching the instance in an internal cache object rather than destroying it. It uses 'activated' and 'deactivated' hooks instead of unmount/mount.
questions.hint: Think about whether the component lifecycle is interrupted or merely transitioned.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue Component Caching Lifecycle
questions.interviewTip: Discuss how memory usage scales when caching many complex components with keep-alive.

questions.question: In Vue 3, what is the primary architectural difference between defining props using `defineProps(['propName'])` versus using type-based declaration `defineProps<{ propName: string }>()`?
options: Runtime string-array declarations provide better runtime performance because they completely bypass the JavaScript virtual machine's type-checking phase during compilation.

Type-based declarations rely on TypeScript compiler macros (and build-time transform) to declare runtime props, whereas runtime string-array declarations cannot infer TypeScript types automatically without extra casting.
Type-based declarations allow declaring reactive default values using standard ES6 destructured assignments, whereas runtime string arrays do not.
Runtime string-array declarations support complex generic type constraints, whereas type-based declarations are restricted strictly to primitive types.
questions.correctAnswer: Type-based declarations rely on TypeScript compiler macros (and build-time transform) to declare runtime props, whereas runtime string-array declarations cannot infer TypeScript types automatically without extra casting.
questions.explanation: Type-based macro declarations in Vue 3 SFCs allow developers to leverage TypeScript types directly for props. During compilation, Vue's compiler transforms these type annotations into equivalent runtime runtime `prop` options. Runtime string arrays ('defineProps(['id'])') only provide runtime validation and require manual TypeScript interfaces if static type-checking is needed.
questions.hint: Consider how Vue's compiler handles build-time macros versus runtime arrays for prop definitions.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 script setup type-based vs runtime prop declarations
questions.interviewTip: Interweaves TypeScript integration with Vue 3's compiler macros, assessing deep knowledge of how `<script setup>` is processed.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using the Composition API, what is the precise reactivity behavior of an object property passed as a prop if you destructure it directly within the setup() function or script setup?
options: The property 'name' remains reactive because Vue 3 automatically proxies all destructured primitive values from props.
The property 'name' loses its reactivity and will not trigger component re-renders when the parent updates the object.
The component throws a runtime error because direct destructuring of prop objects is forbidden in Vue 3.
The property 'name' is automatically wrapped in a ref, maintaining its connection to the parent's source state.
questions.correctAnswer: The property 'name' loses its reactivity and will not trigger component re-renders when the parent updates the object.
questions.explanation: In Vue 3, props are reactive, but the reactivity is bound to the proxy object itself. Destructuring a property from a reactive object results in a local constant containing the value at that moment. Since JavaScript primitives (like strings) are passed by value, the binding is broken, and subsequent changes to the prop in the parent will not update the destructured local variable.
questions.hint: Consider how JavaScript handles primitive values during destructuring versus how Vue's proxy-based reactivity system works.
questions.relatedConcept: Reactivity loss via destructuring in Composition API
questions.interviewTip: An interviewer asks this to see if the candidate understands the difference between standard JavaScript destructuring and Vue's reactivity system, which requires `toRefs` to maintain links.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using 'v-for' on a component, what is the impact of not providing a unique 'key' attribute when the list items are dynamic?
options: The component will fail to render entirely, throwing a runtime error during the component initialization phase.
Vue will output a warning in the console and default to 'in-place patch' strategy, potentially causing UI state synchronization errors.
Vue automatically assigns a unique hash to each component instance based on the internal object reference, negating the need for a key.
The list will be rendered correctly, but performance will degrade significantly as Vue will force a full DOM node replacement for every update.
questions.correctAnswer: Vue will output a warning in the console and default to 'in-place patch' strategy, potentially causing UI state synchronization errors.
questions.explanation: Vue's virtual DOM diffing algorithm uses keys to track node identities. Without keys, Vue uses an 'in-place patch' strategy which is performant but dangerous for stateful components (like inputs or toggles) because it reuses existing DOM nodes instead of reordering them, leading to bugs where internal state doesn't match the new list item.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to the internal component state when items are reordered if there is no stable identifier.
questions.relatedConcept: Virtual DOM reconciliation and list rendering strategy.
questions.codeSnippet: <my-component v-for="item in items" :item="item" />
questions.interviewTip: Understanding the key attribute is essential for debugging rendering bugs in production applications.

questions.question: In Vue 3, when using 'shallowRef', which of the following scenarios triggers a DOM update?
options: Both mutating the count property and assigning a new object trigger updates.
Only assigning a new object to state.value triggers an update.
Only mutating state.value.count triggers an update.
Neither action triggers an update because shallowRef is immutable.
questions.correctAnswer: Only assigning a new object to state.value triggers an update.
questions.explanation: shallowRef only tracks changes to the .value property itself. Deep mutations of the inner object are not tracked by the reactivity system. Assigning a new object to .value updates the ref and triggers the update.
questions.hint: Think about the difference between deep reactivity and shallow tracking in the Composition API.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Reactivity System (shallowRef)
questions.interviewTip: Understanding when to use shallowRef is crucial for performance optimization in large-scale Vue applications involving complex data structures.

questions.question: In Vue 3 with the Composition API, what happens when you destructure a reactive object returned by 'reactive()' directly in the setup scope?
options: The template will automatically track count reactively due to automatic unwrapping.
The returned count property loses its reactivity because destructuring strips the proxy connection.
Vue throws a runtime TypeError because destructuring a reactive proxy is forbidden.
The count property remains fully reactive and updates when state.count changes.
questions.correctAnswer: The returned count property loses its reactivity because destructuring strips the proxy connection.
questions.explanation: When you destructure a reactive object created with reactive(), the extracted properties are disconnected from the original proxy. They become plain JavaScript primitives and lose their reactivity. To preserve reactivity during destructuring, you should use 'toRefs()'.
questions.hint: Think about how standard JavaScript destructuring works on object properties versus Vue's proxy tracking.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Composition API reactive destructuring and toRefs
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers often ask this to verify if the candidate understands the difference between 'reactive()' proxies and plain primitive values when passed to templates.

questions.question: In Vue 3 with the Composition API, what is the fundamental difference in reactivity tracking behavior between `reactive()` and `ref()` when dealing with primitive values versus objects?
options: reactive() can accept primitive values directly, whereas ref() throws a runtime TypeError if passed anything other than an object or array.

ref() uses getters and setters to intercept property access on a wrapper object containing the value, whereas reactive() uses ES6 Proxies to recursively intercept operations on the source object itself.
ref() tracks mutations using deep dependency injection, while reactive() is restricted to shallow-level root property tracking only.
reactive() creates an immutable read-only proxy layer over the underlying object, whereas ref() mutates the target reference in place without triggering side effects.
questions.correctAnswer: ref() uses getters and setters to intercept property access on a wrapper object containing the value, whereas reactive() uses ES6 Proxies to recursively intercept operations on the source object itself.
questions.explanation: ref() creates a RefImpl object that wraps any value (primitive or object) inside a `.value` property, utilizing getters/setters for tracking. reactive() wraps an object (or collection type) directly with an ES6 Proxy for deep reactivity without needing a `.value` wrapper, though it does not support primitive values directly.
questions.hint: Think about how primitives cannot be passed into standard ES6 Proxies directly, requiring a wrapper object.
questions.relatedConcept: Vue 3 Composition API Reactivity Fundamentals
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers frequently ask this to verify whether a candidate understands the internal mechanics of Vue 3's proxy-based reactivity system versus ref wrapping.

questions.question: In Vue 3's `<script setup>`, you destructure a prop directly from `defineProps` as shown in the snippet. Why does the `doubleCount` computed property fail to update when the parent component passes a new `count` value?
options: The defineProps macro returns an un-reactive plain object, and properties must be manually registered with reactive() to enable dependency tracking.
Destructuring the reactive props object breaks reactivity because it extracts the primitive value of the property at initialization, resulting in a static, non-reactive local variable.

questions.correctAnswer: The new object loses reactivity because the reference is replaced by a plain object, detaching it from the original Proxy handler.
